questions.original_query: How can I use an hybridization of ontology and machine learning for text summarization ?

query.text: How can I use an hybridization of ontology and machine learning for text summarization ?
query.answer: A practical way to hybridize ontology and machine learning for text summarization is to build a <cite id="285e1eb4-0">system that maps sentences to nodes of a hierarchical ontology</cite>, then use those ontology concepts as semantic features for an ML summarizer. In practice, use the ontology to detect domain entities, relations, and topic coverage; score sentences by concept importance/coverage for an extractive stage; and then feed the selected content plus ontology cues into an abstractive model, since <cite id="34548109-0">hybrid summarization combines extractive and abstractive methods</cite>. Recent work suggests two effective integration patterns: <cite id="63116e37-0">ontology-based prompt tuning with an abstractive summarizer</cite>, which was reported to make summaries <cite id="63116e37-0">more accurate and contextually relevant to the domain</cite>, and <cite id="7f1056fe-0">an ontology-aware knowledge-based document representation module</cite> inside a neural summarizer. So, a strong recipe is: <cite id="285e1eb4-0">map text to ontology concepts</cite> → rank sentences/concepts with ML → generate or rewrite the summary with an abstractive model guided by those concepts/prompts; this is aligned with evidence that ontology-guided extraction can <cite id="285e1eb4-0">outperform baseline sentence extraction</cite> and that ontology-aware neural architectures can improve ROUGE over strong baselines <cite id="63116e37-0">such as BART, BERT, and GPT-3.5</cite>.

questions.original_query: In robotics, what are the leading methods for learning terrain traversibility costs automatically from robot experience?

query.text: In robotics, what are the leading methods for learning terrain traversibility costs automatically from robot experience?
query.answer: In current robotics literature, the leading approaches for automatically learning terrain traversibility costs from robot experience are <cite id="94609037-0">self-supervised costmap learning that combines exteroceptive environmental information with proprioceptive terrain interaction feedback</cite>, because this directly uses the robot’s own interaction data instead of hand labels. A closely related direction is <cite id="2b62c6a1-0">self-supervised terrain representation learning</cite> from <cite id="2b62c6a1-0">easy-to-collect, unconstrained, and unlabeled robot experience</cite>, which learns terrain features useful for downstream navigation rather than predicting a fixed hand-engineered cost. Another important family is <cite id="40a35d3f-8">learning risk-aware costmaps</cite> that <cite id="40a35d3f-8">infer a CVaR costmap from the LiDAR pointcloud</cite> to explicitly model uncertainty in traversability. For generalizing across environments, researchers are also using <cite id="40a35d3f-0">a meta-learning framework for learning a global model that accurately and reliably predicts terrain</cite> traversability across domains. Finally, newer systems emphasize continual adaptation, with <cite id="d7fdfd4a-0">adaptive real-time traversability analysis</cite> that <cite id="d7fdfd4a-0">dynamically analyz[es] traversed areas during autonomous driving and updat[es]</cite> the traversability model online. Overall, the field is led by self-supervised multimodal cost learning, self-supervised representation learning, uncertainty/risk-aware mapping, meta-learning for transfer, and online adaptation.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the leading methods for learning costs automatically from experience?
fully_underspecified.answer: The main families are <cite id="e69c072a-8">inverse optimal control (IOC), which assumes demonstrations are solutions to an optimal control problem with unknown underlying costs and extracts those cost parameters</cite>, and <cite id="5426aee3-0">inverse reinforcement learning (IRL), which infers the reward function of an agent from its policy or observed behavior</cite>. A closely related line is <cite id="9a08a72c-4">apprenticeship learning, whose objective differs from IRL because it focuses on learning a policy rather than explicitly recovering the unknown reward</cite>. Among IRL methods, <cite id="9a08a72c-5">maximum-entropy IRL is a leading variant because it develops a probabilistic approach based on the principle of maximum entropy</cite>. Finally, modern human-in-the-loop methods often use <cite id="9a08a72c-8">preference-based reinforcement learning, which learns reward functions from human feedback</cite>, with broader RLHF-style systems likewise centered on <cite id="ee64361f-7">reward models where complex human preferences are learned</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the advantages and limitations of applying bias mitigation algorithms during pre-processing, training and inference stages of a model?

query.text: What are the advantages and limitations of applying bias mitigation algorithms during pre-processing, training and inference stages of a model?
query.answer:
<cite id="1561c89f-0,1d2f3b8b-7">Pre-processing methods change the training data—through re-weighting, resampling, or feature transformation—to remove discrimination before learning</cite>; <cite id="39a35b22-5">their main advantage is that they can create fairer training data that encourages downstream models to behave more fairly</cite>. <cite id="3e80bdb3-1,1561c89f-1">Their main limitation is that they usually require access to the training data and sensitive/demographic labels</cite>, and <cite id="1561c89f-2">in some applications those sensitive attributes are hard to use in practice because of legal constraints</cite>.  

<cite id="3e80bdb3-0,3e80bdb3-5">Training-stage (in-processing) methods add fairness constraints or regularization directly into the learning algorithm</cite>; <cite id="3e80bdb3-2">their key advantage is that they can optimize fairness during model training</cite> and <cite id="3e80bdb3-6,3e80bdb3-1">make the fairness–accuracy trade-off explicit, giving decision makers a range of candidate models</cite>. <cite id="3e80bdb3-2">Their limitation is that they require access to, and the ability to modify, the model’s optimization procedure</cite>, which generally means retraining rather than simply wrapping an existing model.  

<cite id="ca9cbf76-1,cbb6260e-6">Inference-stage (post-processing) methods modify predictions after training, so they do not require access to the training process</cite>; <cite id="3e80bdb3-3,cbb6260e-2,cbb6260e-3">this makes them especially useful for models already in production, black-box vendor models, or systems that cannot be retrained</cite>. <cite id="d0c3f1da-0,cbb6260e-0">Their limitation is that performance can depend strongly on having accurate sensitive-attribute information (or accurately inferred proxies)</cite>, and <cite id="d0c3f1da-1,d0c3f1da-3">many such methods work by calibration or group-specific thresholding</cite>, which can be operationally or legally contentious.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the advantages and limitations of applying bias mitigation algorithms during different stages of a model?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Bias mitigation is commonly applied at <cite id="af647d35-5,af647d35-2">three stages: pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing.</cite>

- <cite id="af647d35-1,159fc507-1">Pre-processing changes the training data before modeling</cite>. Its main advantages are that <cite id="af647d35-1">it aims to improve fairness metrics</cite> and <cite id="3ed6db1b-5">it is often viewed as a very flexible intervention point</cite>. Its main limitation is that <cite id="3ed6db1b-1">it can only be used when you are allowed to modify the training data before model building</cite>.

- <cite id="0ec94ce7-0">In-processing incorporates fairness directly into model optimization</cite>. The advantage is that <cite id="0ec94ce7-0">the trained model can achieve fairness even when the data are biased</cite>, and <cite id="0ec94ce7-1">it offers direct control over the fairness-versus-accuracy trade-off</cite>. The limitation is that <cite id="0ec94ce7-2">it often requires modifying the model architecture or learning objective by adding fairness constraints or objectives</cite>.

- <cite id="159fc507-0,af647d35-2">Post-processing changes a model’s predictions after training</cite>. Its main advantage is deployability: <cite id="159fc507-2,62c6cfe4-6">it offers an easier path for adding fairness to models that are already deployed or in production</cite>. Its limitations are that <cite id="af647d35-2">it acts on the predictions of an already biased model rather than fixing the underlying data or training process</cite> and <cite id="62c6cfe4-0,62c6cfe4-4">it can involve trade-offs between fairness and predictive performance</cite>.

In short, <cite id="3ed6db1b-5">pre-processing is flexible</cite>, <cite id="0ec94ce7-0,0ec94ce7-1">in-processing gives the most direct optimization control</cite>, and <cite id="159fc507-2,62c6cfe4-6">post-processing is easiest for existing systems</cite>; but their limitations differ in <cite id="3ed6db1b-1">data access</cite>, <cite id="0ec94ce7-2">training complexity</cite>, and <cite id="62c6cfe4-0,af647d35-2">output-only correction/performance trade-offs</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are the advantages and limitations of applying bias mitigation algorithms during pre-processing, training and inference stages of a model?
without_scope.answer: Bias mitigation has different trade-offs depending on when it is applied. <cite id="0e1774b0-0,25751149-0">Pre-processing changes the training data or its representation before learning, typically to reduce correlations with sensitive attributes.</cite> Its main advantage is that <cite id="0e1774b0-1,0e1774b0-5">pre-processing is classifier-agnostic and does not require modifying the ML method itself</cite>; its main limitation is operational, because <cite id="0e1774b0-2">if bias is discovered later, using pre-processing to recover fairness generally requires complete retraining of the model.</cite> <cite id="f6505697-1,f6505697-2">In-processing methods modify the training procedure itself by adding fairness constraints/objectives or even changing the model architecture during training.</cite> Their advantage is that <cite id="f6505697-1,f6505697-2">fairness is handled directly inside optimization</cite>, but the limitation is that <cite id="0e1774b0-1,f6505697-1">they are less plug-and-play than pre/post methods because they require access to and modification of the learner itself, rather than being classifier-agnostic.</cite> <cite id="25751149-1,8e888f18-4">Post-processing (inference-stage) methods adjust model outputs after training.</cite> Their main advantage is practicality: <cite id="bd84bab2-5,0dd922bc-0,8e888f18-0">they are well suited to already deployed systems and can improve fairness without changing the training data or retraining the model.</cite> Their main limitation is scope, because <cite id="25751149-1,8e888f18-4">they intervene only at the prediction stage rather than correcting the underlying data or learning process.</cite>

questions.original_query: What considerations are important for material selection in fabricating industrial robotic grippers?  What are the advantages and disadvantages of soft vs rigid gripper materials?

query.text: What considerations are important for material selection in fabricating industrial robotic grippers?  What are the advantages and disadvantages of soft vs rigid gripper materials?
query.answer:
For industrial robotic grippers, material selection should be driven first by the <cite id="1f727b21-0">workpiece and application requirements, considering factors such as payload capacity, cycle time, precision requirements, and environmental conditions</cite>. The material also has to strike the right <cite id="48031b28-0">balance between flexibility and strength</cite>, while surface-level properties matter because <cite id="54330dab-7">surface softness, elasticity, wear resistance, and chemical compatibility directly affect gripping stability and product protection</cite>. In food, pharma, or washdown settings, resistance to the process environment becomes especially important; for example, <cite id="54330dab-9">food-grade silicone is a popular material for soft gripper design due to its excellent resistance to heat and chemicals</cite>.

Soft materials are advantageous when you need <cite id="ad72830a-1">adaptability and safety</cite>: they can <cite id="ad72830a-2">accommodate a wide range of objects</cite> and <cite id="ad72830a-7">conform to the shape of the object... without damaging the item</cite>. Their main drawbacks are that purely soft designs can suffer from <cite id="45de45d0-0">lower payload capacity</cite> and <cite id="45de45d0-0">less stable grip</cite>. Rigid materials have the opposite profile: they generally offer <cite id="ad72830a-0">greater payload capacity in comparison to soft grippers</cite>, but <cite id="45de45d0-5">rigid grippers can struggle with dimensional variation, misalignment, or fragile surfaces</cite>. In practice, that means soft materials are better for variable or delicate parts, rigid materials are better for heavy, repeatable, high-precision handling, and hybrid soft-rigid designs are often attractive when both robustness and compliance are needed <cite id="45de45d0-0">to overcome the challenges faced by purely soft grippers</cite>.

questions.original_query: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period when designing a Kalman filter. query.text: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period when designing a Kalman filter. Leaving apart the computational cost, are there any other reasons, e.g., noise-related issues, to set a lower bound for the sampling period? And, if so, is there an optimal value between these bounds?
query.answer: Not in the same hard sense as Nyquist. For a discrete-time Kalman filter, the sampling period enters the model itself because the process-noise covariance is derived under a continuous-time white-noise assumption and depends on how you discretize over one sample interval. So if you make the period very small, you do not just get “the same filter more often”: the amount the state is expected to change over one sample time depends on the sample time \(T_s\). In an ideal linear-Gaussian world with correctly scaled \(Q(T_s)\) and \(R(T_s)\), the Kalman filter is recursively optimal given the model and incoming measurements, so there is no universal noise-based lower bound saying “sampling faster is bad.” In practice, however, there are good reasons not to make \(T_s\) arbitrarily small. First, standard Kalman filtering relies on white-noise assumptions, and colored/correlated noise violates those assumptions; real sensors often have finite bandwidth, so very fast sampling can give highly correlated successive measurements rather than much new information. Second, numerical stability can become an issue when the process-noise covariance \(Q_k\) is very small, which is exactly what happens as \(T_s\) shrinks for many continuous-time models. Third, tuning is time-scale dependent: Kalman filter tuning can be ambiguous, and one proposed remedy is to tune across multiple different prediction intervals, which is another way of saying there is no single universally “best” sample period independent of the model/noise structure. So the practical answer is: yes, there can be an effective lower bound set by sensor bandwidth/noise color, model validity, and numerical conditioning, but there is no universal optimal value between that and the Nyquist upper bound. The “best” \(T_s\) is application-specific and is usually chosen so that the dynamics are well resolved, the discretized \(Q(T_s)\) and \(R(T_s)\) remain physically meaningful, and successive measurements still provide substantial new information rather than mostly correlated noise.

fully_underspecified.text: Are there any reasons to set a lower bound for the sampling period, and if so, is there an optimal value between the bounds?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="780a4740-1,e1d12e95-2">Yes—there are practical reasons not to make the sampling period arbitrarily small: very small sampling times increase computing demand and can introduce numerical problems.</cite> <cite id="780a4740-1">At the other extreme, if the sampling period is too large, the discrete controller becomes a poor approximation of the continuous design.</cite> <cite id="e1d12e95-7">So the “best” value is usually not a universal optimum, but a tradeoff chosen according to the closed-loop dynamics of the system.</cite> <cite id="ed90a989-0,ed90a989-1">A common rule of thumb in digital control is to choose the sampling frequency at least about 30× the closed-loop bandwidth</cite> (equivalently, <cite id="ed90a989-0,ed90a989-1">the sampling period about 1/30 of the closed-loop bandwidth time scale</cite>), which gives a practical value between “too slow” and “needlessly fast.”

without_scope.text: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period when designing a Kalman filter. Are there any other reasons, such as noise-related issues, to set a lower bound for the sampling period? And, if so, is there an optimal value between these bounds?
without_scope.answer: Yes—but the classical Kalman/Bucy optimal filter is derived for systems whose measurements contain white noise, and there is separate literature on Kalman filtering for systems corrupted by finite-step autocorrelated measurement noise. So, if you sample so fast that your measurement errors are no longer well approximated as white/independent from sample to sample, a very small sampling period can violate the standard KF assumptions. Also, the discrete process-noise covariance is derived under a continuous-time white-noise assumption, so changing the sampling period changes the correct discrete-time noise model rather than just “giving you more data.” There is therefore not a universal lower bound analogous to Nyquist; instead, the best sampling period is application-specific. In practice, the choice is a tradeoff because steady-state performance depends on the chosen process- and measurement-noise covariances, and the ratio of process noise to measurement noise determines whether the filter trusts the motion model or the measurements more. Consequently, an “optimal” sampling period, when it exists, is the one that minimizes your chosen estimation error for your particular dynamics/sensor/noise model; indeed, some problem settings explicitly report an optimal sampling period, but it is not universal.

Leaving apart the computational cost, are there any other reasons, e.g., noise-related issues, to set a lower bound for the sampling period? And, if so, is there an optimal value between these bounds?
without_term.answer: <cite id="1c979cbe-0,1c979cbe-3">Yes—there can be practical lower-bound reasons not to make the sampling period arbitrarily small: fast sampling can make standard discrete-time formulations numerically ill-conditioned, which is precisely why delta-operator methods were introduced “to avoid the ill-conditioned problems under fast sampling,” and why common shift-operator solutions are reported to “become ill-conditioned for a sufficiently small sampling period.”</cite> <cite id="8ef0794b-1">More broadly, state estimation can become poorly conditioned when observability is weak, so taking samples “too close together” may add little new information while worsening conditioning.</cite> <cite id="b81870f2-0,70ea1d67-4">There is also a communication/quantization tradeoff: work on networked estimation explicitly optimizes sampling periods together with quantization bit lengths to obtain good estimation performance under bandwidth limits, which implies that the best sampling period is problem-dependent rather than universal.</cite> <cite id="b6fe0d3d-2,b6fe0d3d-5,b6fe0d3d-8">On the noise side, there is no general rule that “faster is noisier”; in fact, ADC oversampling and averaging can improve effective resolution and dynamic range.</cite> So the most defensible conclusion is: <cite id="1c979cbe-0,1c979cbe-3,b81870f2-0">the sampling theorem gives an upper bound on the period, while any lower bound is usually practical—numerical conditioning, observability, sensor/ADC characteristics, and bandwidth/quantization—not fundamental; and any “optimal” sampling period lies between those bounds only in a model- and hardware-specific sense.</cite>

without_preference.answer: The short answer is: <cite id="9fb03560-5">there is no universal, theory-imposed lower bound on the sampling period in Kalman filtering analogous to the Nyquist upper bound, because in the ideal limit one can move to a continuous-time Kalman filter when measurements are effectively continuous.</cite> <cite id="28caf093-4,9fb03560-0">Standard Kalman-filter formulations assume process and measurement noise are white, and the discrete process-noise covariance depends on how that continuous-time white noise is discretized.</cite> In practice, however, <cite id="75a06b14-0">the sampling rate is one of the timescales that strongly influences how well-conditioned the estimation task is and can affect convergence/performance,</cite> and <cite id="ed35b4b7-3">if the measurement noise is colored rather than white, a modified Kalman filter is needed.</cite> So any “lower bound” is usually <cite id="75a06b14-0,ed35b4b7-3">a practical bound coming from conditioning, model mismatch, non-white/correlated noise, sensor physics, or computation—not a universal noise law.</cite> Consequently, <cite id="9fb03560-5,75a06b14-0">there is no single universally optimal sampling period between the bounds; the best choice is application-dependent and is typically selected by trading estimation performance/conditioning against implementation constraints.</cite>

questions.original_query: What is the known evidence for pervasiveness of gaming of citation metrics like citation count and h-index?

query.text: What is the known evidence for pervasiveness of gaming of citation metrics like citation count and h-index?
query.answer: The evidence suggests that gaming of citation metrics is real and fairly widespread, though hard to measure precisely. At the author level, large survey work based on over 12,000 responses from more than 110,000 scholars across 18 disciplines found that misattribution practices are widespread, including cases where journal editors coerce authors to add citations that are not pertinent to their work and some authors pad their reference lists with superfluous citations. A widely cited Science study further reported that, from 6,672 survey responses, coercion is uncomfortably common and appears to be practiced opportunistically, identifying 175 journals as coercers. At the metric-design level, the h-index is demonstrably gameable: a simulation study concluded that authors can considerably inflate their h-index through self-citations. At the journal level, there is also direct evidence of systemic manipulation: several journals were banned from the Journal Citation Reports because of excessive self-citation by journals, which “inflates” the impact factor. And concern is not limited to isolated anecdotes: there are dedicated large-scale efforts to estimate reviewer-side manipulation using the citation patterns of 69,000 reviewers. Overall, the best-supported conclusion is that gaming of citation count, impact factor, and h-index is known to occur in multiple forms, including direct, co-author, collaborative, and coercive induced self-citation, with substantial evidence that it is not rare, even if its exact prevalence remains uncertain.

query.text: What are some practically-relevant properties of k-node subgraphs that can be counted in faster than cubic time in the size of the input graph?
query.answer: Some of the most practically relevant countable k-node subgraph properties are whether a vertex set forms a triangle, a 4-cycle, a clique, or more generally a specific small 3- or 4-node graphlet or 5-vertex pattern. For sparse real-world graphs, these can often be counted well below cubic time: all triangles can be enumerated in \(O(m\alpha)\) time, where \(\alpha\) is arboricity, and Chiba and Nishizeki gave linear-time algorithms for clique and 4-cycle counting for bounded-degeneracy graphs. In fact, for every fixed \(k<6\), counting all \(k\)-vertex subgraphs can be solved in linear time on bounded-degeneracy graphs. These properties matter in practice because small-subgraph frequencies are a fundamental technique in network analysis, most notably in bioinformatics and social networks, graphlets are widely used from social science to biology to characterize networks, and exact counts for all 5-vertex subgraphs have been computed on graphs with tens of millions of edges in minutes on a commodity machine.

questions.original_query: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering in scientific domains? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.

query.text: What are some of the challenges associated with creating a training dataset for question answering in scientific domains? Describe some recent methods that try to overcome these challenges.
query.answer:
Creating QA training data for scientific domains is hard because the source material is intrinsically difficult and the annotations are expensive. Scientific QA often requires <cite id="e39368f8-0">discourse-level understanding</cite> over <cite id="69d81ff7-0">document-level</cite> or even <cite id="2e6e266a-0">multiple documents</cite>, and papers can be very long—<cite id="69d81ff7-0">PeerQA serves as a challenging benchmark for long-context modeling, as the papers have an average size of 12k tokens</cite>. A second major problem is supervision cost: <cite id="e39368f8-0">the main bottleneck in building such models is the availability of human-annotated data</cite>. A third challenge is that many scientific questions are not answerable from a single passage or a single modality: some require <cite id="2e6e266a-0">synthesizing information across multiple documents</cite>, while others depend on <cite id="62f952ee-2">figures, tables, and full paper</cite> content rather than plain text alone. Finally, synthetic benchmarks can miss realistic user questions; PeerQA was motivated by this by using <cite id="69d81ff7-0">questions ... sourced from peer reviews</cite>, which reflect what expert readers actually ask.

Recent work tries to overcome these problems with more structured and scalable data-collection pipelines. ScienceQA addresses annotation scarcity by building the dataset <cite id="e39368f8-0">in a semi-automated fashion having more than 100k human-annotated context–question–answer triples</cite>, reducing the manual burden while still keeping human supervision. For harder reasoning data, MEQA introduces <cite id="6d3bb5bd-0">a novel semi-automatic question generation strategy by composing event structures from information extraction (IE) datasets</cite>, producing questions that require <cite id="6d3bb5bd-0">complex reasoning over entity-entity, entity-event, and event-event relations</cite> and even providing <cite id="6d3bb5bd-0">multi-step QA-format event reasoning chain (explanation)</cite> annotations. To handle cross-paper reasoning, MDA-QA uses <cite id="2e6e266a-0">a pipeline methodology</cite> that <cite id="2e6e266a-0">detect[s] communities based on citation networks</cite>, <cite id="2e6e266a-0">leverag[es] Large Language Models (LLMs)</cite> to generate QA pairs, and applies <cite id="2e6e266a-0">an automated filtering mechanism to ensure multi-document dependence</cite>. For multimodal scientific evidence, SPIQA builds <cite id="62f952ee-7">the first large-scale QA dataset specifically designed to interpret complex figures and tables</cite> and covers <cite id="62f952ee-6">270K questions</cite>, explicitly targeting the fact that scientific answers may require visual as well as textual evidence. And to improve realism, PeerQA sources <cite id="69d81ff7-0">questions ... from peer reviews</cite> and <cite id="69d81ff7-0">answers ... annotated by the original authors</cite>, while also highlighting that retrieval over scientific papers benefits from <cite id="69d81ff7-0">decontextualization in document-level retrieval</cite>.

Overall, the main dataset-creation challenges are scarcity of expert annotations, long and complex documents, multi-hop and multi-document reasoning, multimodal evidence, and the need for realistic expert-style questions. Recent methods respond with semi-automatic annotation, IE- and LLM-based generation pipelines, citation-network-guided document grouping, automated filtering for genuine cross-document dependence, multimodal benchmark construction, and real-world question sourcing from peer review.

fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="6d9b10b6-0,ffb33906-0">Models can be quite good at dataset-style tasks with in-context learning: GPT-3 was reported to achieve strong performance on many NLP datasets, including translation, question answering, and cloze tasks.</cite> <cite id="09c11cc6-1,09c11cc6-8">Performance generally improves a lot with scale, and large models can sometimes become competitive with fine-tuned systems in the few-shot setting.</cite> <cite id="6255b27e-1,6255b27e-4">But ICL is not uniformly reliable: even GPT-3 showed notable benchmark gaps and, on some tasks, remained well below human performance.</cite> <cite id="de72ffa4-8,5af50825-0">Results are also highly sensitive to prompt format, example choice, and example order,</cite> <cite id="de72ffa4-0,de72ffa4-1,de72ffa4-3">although calibration and better prompt-selection methods can improve few-shot accuracy substantially—reported gains range up to 30 percentage points on diverse tasks and about 13 points on nine text-classification datasets.</cite> <cite id="6255b27e-2,062c1586-6">So the short answer is: ICL works surprisingly well on many datasets, especially with large models and carefully chosen demonstrations, but it is still inconsistent enough that fine-tuning can outperform it on some benchmarks while ICL can win on others.</cite>

without_scope.text: How good are LLMs at solving tabular ML datasets using ICL?
without_scope.answer: Overall, LLM-style ICL for tabular prediction is promising but not uniformly strong: instructions can improve performance overall and yield quite strong results on some tasks, yet LLMs often ignore instructions and fail to predict specific instances correctly, even with examples. In the low-data regime, generic prompted LLM approaches can be surprisingly competitive: TabLLM applies LLMs to zero-shot and few-shot tabular classification and outperforms prior deep-learning-based tabular methods on several benchmark datasets, and it outperforms all baselines for zero and very few training examples. But the strongest results now come from specialized tabular ICL/foundation models, not general-purpose chat LLMs: TabPFN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on its benchmarks, including gradient-boosted decision trees, and TabICL is on par with TabPFNv2 across 200 TALENT classification datasets while being up to 10× faster. So the short answer is: ICL works well for tabular ML mainly in few-shot/small-data settings, but general-purpose LLMs are still less reliable than dedicated tabular ICL models, which are now near- or state-of-the-art on major benchmarks.

questions.original_query: Compare the various algorithms for compressing trees in terms of computation complexity.

query.text: Compare the various algorithms for compressing trees in terms of computation complexity.
query.answer: In terms of construction complexity, the cheapest well-established tree compressors are the DAG-based ones: the minimal DAG is unique and can be computed in linear time, and this is also stated for XML/tree DAG compression more generally, where the minimal dag of a tree is unique and can be constructed in linear time. The same source family also explains that a hybrid DAG is built by first constructing the minimal unranked DAG, then taking its first-child/next-sibling encoding, and then building the minimal DAG again, so hybrid/binary-DAG style methods remain structurally simple, though the snippets here do not give a tighter end-to-end bound than the linear-time DAG subroutines. For grammar-based compression, the picture is more complex. The hard optimization problem is exact smallest-grammar compression: finding a smallest SLT grammar for a given tree is NP-complete. In practice, however, common approximations are much cheaper: the same survey notes two linear-time approximation algorithms: BPLEX and TreeRePair, and TreeRePair is described in a primary source as a new linear time compression algorithm. So grammar-based methods offer stronger compression potential, but exact optimal compression is computationally intractable, while practical heuristics are linear-time approximations. For top-tree / top-DAG compression, the available results are also favorable computationally: the entire top DAG construction can thus be done in O(n_T) time, and the authors summarize it as linear time construction. Compared with plain DAGs, the benefit is not lower asymptotic running time but greater expressive power on repeated tree patterns rather than only repeated subtrees: top tree compression can compress exponentially better than DAG compression, while the minimal DAG only captures identical repeated subtrees. So the overall comparison is: DAG/minimal-DAG methods are the simplest and clearly linear-time; top-tree/top-DAG methods are also linear-time but usually target better compression on more general repeated patterns; and grammar-based methods are the most computationally nuanced, because optimal compression is NP-complete while practical algorithms such as TreeRePair and BPLEX are still linear-time approximations.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response directly answers the comparison without noting any ambiguity or asking for clarification; it simply states the complexity results for DAG, grammar-based, and top-tree compression methods.

fully_underspecified.text: Compare the various algorithms for compressing trees.
fully_underspecified.answer:
A useful way to compare tree-compression algorithms is to separate <cite id="92b93299-0,54e16041-2">dictionary-based methods—DAGs, hybrid DAGs, and straight-line context-free tree grammars—from succinct encodings</cite>. <cite id="011b29e9-6">The most widely studied methods are DAG compression, top-tree compression, and grammar-based compression</cite>, while succinct representations such as <cite id="7624838e-3">LOUDS, balanced parentheses, and DFUDS</cite> focus on near-information-theoretic space rather than aggressively exploiting repeated patterns.

**DAG compression** is the simplest repeat-based approach: <cite id="92b93299-1">a DAG lets a node have several incoming edges</cite>, and in practice it works by <cite id="54e16041-0">sharing repeated subtrees of a tree</cite>. This makes DAGs fast and conceptually simple, but their weakness is that they only capture exact subtree repetition. As a result, <cite id="54e16041-7">tree grammars can be exponentially smaller than the minimal DAG</cite> on some inputs.

**Hybrid DAGs** extend DAGs by exploiting a different redundancy pattern. In particular, <cite id="54e16041-0">while the dag shares repeated subtrees, the binary dag shares repeated sibling sequences</cite>. So hybrid/binary DAG-style methods are typically preferable when structure repeats horizontally among siblings rather than as whole identical subtrees.

**Grammar-based compression** is more powerful but algorithmically harder. The survey notes that <cite id="649d0eb9-1">finding a smallest SLT grammar for a given tree is NP-complete</cite>, so practical systems use heuristics/approximations such as <cite id="649d0eb9-1">BPLEX and TreeRePair</cite>. TreeRePair is attractive because <cite id="649d0eb9-0">it is a linear-time algorithm</cite> that <cite id="54e16041-3">generates straight-line linear context-free tree grammars</cite>, and empirically <cite id="54e16041-3">the produced grammars are smaller than those produced by previous compressors on the reported test corpus</cite>. In short, grammar methods usually compress more than DAG-like methods, but they are more complex and optimal compression is intractable.

**Top-tree compression** is designed to capture repeated tree *patterns*, not just repeated subtrees. Its key idea is that <cite id="011b29e9-1">it transforms the input tree into another tree in which tree-pattern repeats become subtree repeats</cite>. This gives it a strong theoretical advantage: <cite id="011b29e9-0">top-tree compression can compress exponentially better than DAG compression</cite> and is <cite id="011b29e9-0">never worse than DAG compression</cite>. Relative to grammar compressors, top trees occupy a middle ground: usually more structured and easier to reason about than unrestricted grammar compression, but more expressive than plain DAG sharing.

**Succinct tree representations** are different again: they are not mainly about finding repeated patterns, but about representing arbitrary trees in very small space while retaining navigational operations. Standard choices are <cite id="7624838e-3">LOUDS, balanced parentheses, and DFUDS</cite>, which <cite id="7624838e-6">use only about \(2n + O(n)\) bits</cite>. More recent <cite id="7624838e-1">hypersuccinct trees achieve asymptotically optimal compression for all tree distributions</cite> and <cite id="7624838e-2">combine that compression with the operation support of succinct tree data structures</cite>. These methods are best when the goal is guaranteed compact representation plus query support, not maximal exploitation of repetition.

So, in one sentence: <cite id="54e16041-0">DAGs are simplest and exploit repeated subtrees</cite>; <cite id="54e16041-0">hybrid DAGs also exploit repeated sibling sequences</cite>; <cite id="54e16041-7,649d0eb9-1">grammar-based methods are more powerful but harder to optimize</cite>; <cite id="011b29e9-0,011b29e9-1">top-tree compression captures repeated patterns and dominates DAGs theoretically</cite>; and <cite id="7624838e-1,7624838e-3,7624838e-6">succinct/hypersuccinct encodings aim for near-optimal space with navigation support rather than repetition-based compression</cite>.

without_preference.text: Compare the various algorithms for compressing trees in terms of computation complexity.
without_preference.answer: In terms of compression-time complexity, the main tree-compression families are surprisingly similar: the minimal DAG can be computed in linear time, BPLEX and TreeRePair are both linear-time approximation algorithms, and top-tree compression can also be iterated in linear time. The key difference is therefore less about asymptotic runtime and more about what kind of redundancy they exploit: minimal DAG compression is the simplest linear-time method but only merges repeated identical subtrees; TreeRePair computes small linear SLCF tree grammars in linear time, so it can capture more general repeated patterns; and top-tree compression can compress exponentially better than DAG compression while still keeping linear-time construction. For optimal grammar-based compression, the picture is worse computationally: finding a smallest SLT grammar for a given tree is NP-complete, so exact optimum methods are not practical at scale and the linear-time algorithms above are used as heuristics. As a separate category, succinct tree representations use 2n + o(n) bits and support many operations in O(1) time; they are more about near-information-theoretic storage than exploiting repeated subtrees, and one practical construction algorithm runs in O(n/p + lg p) time on p threads.

questions.original_query: How do different fairness metrics correlate with each other across various datasets and model architectures?

query.text: How do different fairness metrics correlate with each other across various datasets and model architectures?
query.answer: Across datasets and model architectures, fairness metrics <cite id="578d929a-1">do not exhibit one universal correlation structure; instead, researchers explicitly compute correlations between fairness metrics</cite> and <cite id="0787429d-0">seek “representative fairness metrics” because fairness has many definitions that depend on context</cite>. Empirically, one study <cite id="578d929a-8">used 8 datasets, 7 classification models, and 9 fairness metrics to discover empirical relationships</cite>, while another found that <cite id="2b369265-0">with 2 fairness metrics, 4 ML algorithms, 5 real-world datasets, and 1600 evaluation cycles, there was a linear relationship between data and model fairness metrics when training-data distribution and size changed</cite>, suggesting that observed metric relationships are shaped at least as much by dataset properties and data shifts as by architecture alone. At the same time, some metric pairs are theoretically incompatible rather than positively correlated: <cite id="b2d73fa4-0">Predictive Parity and Equality of Odds cannot both hold</cite>, and more generally <cite id="b2d73fa4-3">if \(A\) and \(Y\) are not independent, then Equalized Odds and Predictive Value Parity cannot simultaneously hold</cite>. So the short answer is: <cite id="578d929a-1,578d929a-8">fairness metrics often show structured, sometimes redundant empirical relationships</cite>, but <cite id="0787429d-0,2b369265-0">those relationships vary by dataset and modeling context</cite>, and <cite id="b2d73fa4-0,b2d73fa4-3">some important metrics are fundamentally in tension, not simply correlated</cite>.

fully_underspecified.answer: Different fairness metrics often <cite id="87a25e33-0">capture different notions of what is a “fair decision”</cite> and the literature emphasizes the <cite id="87a25e33-0">differences, implications and “orthogonality” between these notions</cite>. In practice, this means they are frequently weakly aligned or even in conflict rather than strongly positively correlated: for example, <cite id="ed8cab48-1">independence is strictly linked to what is known as Demographic Parity</cite>, while <cite id="ed8cab48-1">separation is related to Equality of Odds</cite>, so optimizing one family need not optimize the other. More strongly, when groups have different base rates, <cite id="bbfdf888-0">no single classifier can simultaneously satisfy demographic parity, equalized odds</cite> and <cite id="bbfdf888-1">predictive parity simultaneously</cite>, and <cite id="dcd7a770-6">Equalized Odds and Predictive Value Parity cannot simultaneously hold</cite>. So the best summary is: fairness metrics are usually not consistently correlated; they often trade off, and the “correlation” between them depends heavily on base rates, label distributions, and the classifier thresholding choices.

without_scope.text: How do different fairness metrics correlate with each other?
without_scope.answer: <cite id="520a6062-0">Fairness metrics are often grouped into three observational families—independence, separation, and sufficiency—and common metrics within a family are therefore more closely related; for example, demographic/statistical parity is linked to independence, while equality of odds and its relaxations are linked to separation.</cite> <cite id="14344d9f-1">Some relationships are structural: equalized odds is a combination of predictive equality and equal opportunity, so those metrics are nested rather than independent.</cite> <cite id="520a6062-1">Across different families, however, the metrics do not have a stable “one goes up, all go up” correlation; instead, impossibility results show that important measures such as independence, separation, and sufficiency cannot generally all be satisfied at once under reasonable conditions.</cite> <cite id="1816041c-4">For example, demographic parity and equalized odds cannot simultaneously hold when group membership and predictions are both related to the true outcome,</cite> and <cite id="07730d5c-1">predictive parity and classification parity cannot both be satisfied when base rates differ between groups.</cite> <cite id="73fa4829-1,73fa4829-0">Because these relationships depend on the data and model regime, recent work explicitly estimates correlations among fairness metrics and uses them to choose a small representative subset, rather than assuming any single metric stands in for all the others.</cite>

Best practices are to: 

1. <cite id="d05db5bc-0">Prefer well-vetted, reputable libraries</cite> and minimize what you include by <cite id="eb613bee-0">remov[ing] unused dependencies, unnecessary features, components, files, and documentation</cite>.  

2. 3. Automate vulnerability detection with SCA tooling: <cite id="eb613bee-5">Dependency-Check ... scan[s] applications (and their dependent libraries) and identify[ies] any known vulnerable components</cite>, and <cite id="57d7311a-1">all third-party modules should be tested for known vulnerabilities against the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) that are listed in the National Vulnerability Database</cite>.  

4. Continuously monitor and patch quickly by using tools that <cite id="eb613bee-3">periodically monitor SBOM</cite> and by <cite id="57d7311a-3">establishing an assessment, prioritization, and remediation approach that enables vulnerabilities to be remediated quickly</cite>.  

5. 6. questions.original_query: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?

query.text: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?
query.answer:
## Short answer

<cite id="S44,S45">For key exchange, Kyber is often in the same performance ballpark as X25519/ECDH on modern CPUs, and some optimized implementations even make key generation and decapsulation faster than X25519 while encapsulation is comparable.</cite> <cite id="S45">Cloudflare reports Kyber512 at 1.09 ms key generation, 0.34 ms encapsulation, and 0.29 ms decapsulation, versus 0.30 ms key generation and 0.09 ms ECDH for X25519</cite>; but <cite id="S53">on Cortex‑M4 microcontrollers, Kyber encapsulation/decapsulation were still 5× to 35× slower than ECDH, although key generation was 2× to 5× faster.</cite>

<cite id="S15,S41,S43">For signatures, Dilithium usually signs more slowly than Ed25519/ECDSA-class schemes but verifies competitively or faster.</cite> <cite id="S41">One Dilithium2 benchmark reports 529,106 cycles to sign and 179,424 to verify, compared with 48,188 to sign and 196,106 to verify for Ed25519</cite>; <cite id="S15">Cloudflare summarizes this as roughly 2–3× slower signing but up to 5× faster verification.</cite>

## Energy cost

<cite id="S23,S56">Energy broadly tracks runtime, so PQC often costs more energy than classical ECC on constrained devices, though the picture differs by algorithm.</cite> <cite id="S22,S53">Kyber is repeatedly reported as one of the best PQ KEMs on embedded platforms, offering a strong energy/communication tradeoff and being the most energy-efficient PQ KEM in one Cortex‑M4 study.</cite> <cite id="S56,S20">Dilithium had the lowest runtime among the tested PQ signature schemes on Cortex‑M4F, but it still consumed more energy than the ECC baseline because of heavier memory-access costs.</cite>

## Why the comparison is mixed

<cite id="S48,S49">Kyber512’s public key is about 800 bytes, versus 32 bytes for X25519</cite>, and <cite id="S50,S51">Dilithium2 uses a 1312-byte public key and a 2420-byte signature, versus 32-byte public keys and 64-byte signatures for Ed25519.</cite> That means <cite id="S22,S28">even when compute performance is competitive, PQC can impose materially higher communication, storage, and sometimes system-energy costs.</cite>

## How future hardware optimizations could change this

<cite id="S59,S60">Kyber and Dilithium are especially amenable to acceleration because their polynomial arithmetic and NTTs expose substantial data-level parallelism.</cite> <cite id="S34">Official Kyber benchmarks show AVX2 reducing Kyber512 from 126,878/161,348/177,296 cycles to 15,632/19,976/17,364 for keypair/encapsulation/decapsulation</cite>, and <cite id="S35">official Dilithium benchmarks show AVX2 reducing Dilithium2 from 478,032/532,653/136,128 cycles to 162,356/177,646/59,002 for keygen/sign/verify.</cite> Beyond SIMD, <cite id="S30,S31,S32">research on instruction-set extensions, FPGA designs, and hardware/software co-design reports speedups ranging from about 10× up to 246× in some PQC cases, including roughly 26–29× for Kyber FPGA operations and 62–71% cycle reductions for Dilithium co-designed implementations.</cite> <cite id="S63,S64">These optimizations can also improve performance-per-watt and reduce energy by cutting latency and exploiting parallel structure more efficiently.</cite>

## Bottom line

<cite id="S44,S45,S53">Today, Kyber is already close to classical ECDH on desktops/servers but can still be substantially slower and more energy-hungry on small embedded devices.</cite> <cite id="S15,S41,S56">Dilithium is generally a slower signer than Ed25519 but a strong verifier, with energy cost on small devices still worse than ECC despite being one of the better PQ signature options.</cite> <cite id="S34,S35,S59,S60,S30">Because lattice PQC maps well to SIMD/vector/NTT accelerators, future hardware is likely to improve Kyber and Dilithium disproportionately, potentially narrowing or even reversing some of today’s classical-vs-PQC performance and energy gaps in favorable deployment environments.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: how do cryptography methods compare to other methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?
fully_underspecified.answer:
In practice, the performance and energy cost of “cryptographic” privacy methods vary a lot by technique. Mature crypto like TLS adds relatively modest overhead, but heavier cryptographic PETs can be expensive: <cite id="7a99ee4d-0">measured energy increases ranged from 2× for TLS to 10× for searchable encryption and 100,000× for fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) versus non-private counterparts</cite>. Compared with non-cryptographic or hardware-assisted alternatives, <cite id="96edb817-0">hardware enclaves are described as far more efficient than cryptographic computation because the CPU ultimately computes on unencrypted data inside the processor</cite>, and <cite id="96edb817-1">TEEs are presented as a more pragmatic alternative for mitigating computational costs</cite>. For FHE specifically, <cite id="50ab3e39-2">even after 1,000× to 10,000× improvement over five years, it remains far slower than plaintext computation for heavy workloads</cite>. 

Future hardware could narrow—but probably not erase—this gap. Recent results show <cite id="50ab3e39-3">GPU optimization achieving up to 2.0× speedup over baseline and prior state of the art</cite>, <cite id="a95cd41c-7">an FPGA system delivering over 20× speedup for logistic-regression training compared with a state-of-the-art GPU solution</cite>, and <cite id="a95cd41c-4">reports of over 100× faster FHE bootstrapping through memory-centric GPU optimization</cite>. So the likely trajectory is that advanced cryptographic methods, especially FHE, become much more practical with specialized GPUs/FPGAs/ASICs, but <cite id="7a99ee4d-0">their current energy and runtime costs are still substantially above lighter cryptography and hardware-trust approaches</cite>.

without_scope.text: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?
without_scope.answer:
## Overall comparison

In current software benchmarks, <cite id="e72d481d-0">Kyber and Dilithium achieve efficient execution times, outperforming classical cryptographic schemes such as RSA and ECDSA at equivalent security levels.</cite> On modern server-class systems, the practical penalty can be small: <cite id="600e697c-0">contemporary server architectures can implement these algorithms with negligible performance impact (<5% additional latency)</cite>, and in one large AWS TLS experiment <cite id="04c8813d-4">the addition of Kyber adds approximately 0.3 milliseconds of overhead.</cite>

## Where the cost shifts

The main trade-off is not always raw CPU time. <cite id="07bef625-0">Post-quantum cryptographic primitives have a range of trade-offs compared to traditional public key algorithms, either having slower computation or larger public keys and ciphertexts/signatures, or both.</cite> That means Kyber/Dilithium can look very competitive in computation while still paying more in communication overhead; in networked protocols, <cite id="07bef625-0">packet loss rates above 3-5% start to have a significant impact</cite> on TLS connection establishment performance.

## Energy cost

The limited energy measurements available are surprisingly favorable to lattice PQC in some settings. One reported benchmark found that <cite id="ad28bbc8-0">Dilithium and Kyber provide improved energy consumption to ECDSA+ECDHE, but much better than RSA+ECDHE.</cite> A broader heterogeneous benchmark likewise reported that <cite id="e5ae0283-6">Kyber consistently demonstrates the lowest energy requirements for KEM operations</cite>, suggesting that for key exchange especially, PQC is not necessarily an energy loser.

## How future hardware optimizations could change the picture

The comparison is very implementation-sensitive because <cite id="4fc21144-3">the NTT computations are the main algorithmic efficiency bottleneck in Kyber and Dilithium.</cite> Recent work explicitly <cite id="e72d481d-0">evaluated the impact of AVX2 optimizations</cite>, and hardware-focused research is already targeting shared accelerators because <cite id="4fc21144-2">a unified and shared NTT architecture ... can support polynomial multiplication for both CRYSTALS-Kyber and Dilithium.</cite> The upside can be large: one optimized Kyber implementation reported that <cite id="4fc21144-7">Kyber-1024 can achieve a speedup of 26x, 36x, and 35x for each phase</cite> relative to the AVX2 implementation submitted to NIST.

So the short answer is: today, Kyber and Dilithium are often already competitive with—and sometimes faster or lower-energy than—RSA/ECDSA-class methods at matched security levels, especially on servers; their main remaining downside is usually larger messages rather than catastrophic compute cost. Because their hot paths are structurally amenable to vectorization and dedicated NTT hardware, future CPU, FPGA, ASIC, and library optimizations could improve their latency and energy profile even further, potentially making them look better relative to classical schemes than they do in today's baseline software measurements.

without_term.text: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as these compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?
without_term.answer:
## Short answer

For the main NIST-style post-quantum choices (especially lattice-based schemes like **ML-KEM/Kyber** and **ML-DSA/Dilithium**), the usual tradeoff versus classical public-key crypto is:

- **Computation:** they are often **competitive with or faster than RSA**, and sometimes **competitive with elliptic-curve methods** on modern CPUs.
- **Bandwidth / memory:** they usually have **much larger keys, ciphertexts, and signatures** than ECC, so communication and storage costs are higher.
- **Energy:** if you only look at local arithmetic, lattice-based PQC can be quite efficient; but **total energy can rise** when larger messages increase memory traffic, radio use, or network transfer.
- **Future hardware:** PQC performance could improve a lot with **SIMD/vector instructions, NTT accelerators, FPGA/ASIC support, and better memory layouts**, because many lattice operations are highly regular and parallelizable. That said, classical crypto also benefits from hardware acceleration, so the future comparison is likely to remain **workload-dependent**, not one-sided.

## What this means in practice

For **key establishment**, PQC KEMs often look better against **RSA key exchange** than against **X25519/P-256 ECDH**. For **signatures**, PQ signatures may be fast enough computationally, but they often pay a substantial cost in **signature size** and sometimes verification/signing overhead relative to compact ECC signatures.

For **servers and desktops**, the extra bytes may be acceptable, so PQC can look quite practical already. For **IoT, embedded, battery-powered, or low-bandwidth systems**, the communication and memory overhead can dominate the arithmetic cost, so the energy picture may be worse even when CPU cycles look reasonable.

## Likely effect of future hardware optimizations

Future hardware optimizations will probably help PQC **a lot**, especially lattice-based schemes, because they rely on structured polynomial arithmetic that maps well to:
- vectorized CPU instructions,
- dedicated modular-multiplication / NTT units,
- parallel hardware pipelines,
- memory-hierarchy-aware implementations.

So the most likely outcome is:
1. **latency and energy per operation drop significantly** for PQC,
2. the gap versus classical schemes narrows further for compute cost,
3. but **message-size overhead will still matter**, especially in constrained or wireless settings.

## Bottom line

If your baseline is **RSA**, modern lattice-based PQC is often surprisingly favorable in raw computation. If your baseline is **ECC/X25519**, PQC is usually less attractive on **size/bandwidth**, while compute can be anywhere from comparable to somewhat worse or better depending on platform and implementation. Over time, **hardware specialization is likely to improve PQC disproportionately on the compute side**, but it **cannot fully erase the larger key/signature/ciphertext sizes** that drive communication and energy costs in many real systems.

If you want, I can turn this into a **table comparing ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA vs RSA-3072, P-256, and X25519** in terms of latency, key sizes, signature sizes, and likely energy behavior.

query.answer: <cite id="18a32c0a-2">In demonstration-based automation systems, the tool typically has a record phase in which it records the user’s actions during a demonstration</cite>, and those demonstrations are <cite id="18a32c0a-0">represented as scripts using constructs such as actions, nodes, and trigger conditions</cite>. In programmatic learning-from-demonstration, <cite id="90afdd94-2">a set of user demonstrations is used to learn a policy in a programming language</cite>—that is, a DSL-style program that can later control the system’s behavior. For web automation specifically, <cite id="608b4225-0">users demonstrate the UI actions for task steps</cite>; then <cite id="42aa314a-0">the system learns mappings between steps and actions and automates the remaining steps</cite>, often <cite id="608b4225-0">generalizing GUI actions from the semantic meaning of the specification</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How are demonstrations represented in programs and used for tasks?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="c8d4e4a5-0">In programmatic learning from demonstration, demonstrations are represented by learning a policy in a programming language</cite>, and <cite id="11ab75a1-0">the resulting programs can include complex control-flow structures such as nested loops and multiple conditionals</cite>. <cite id="c8d4e4a5-0">These learned programs are then used to control a robot’s behavior</cite> for <cite id="11ab75a1-0">long-horizon tasks</cite>.

without_scope.text: How are user demonstrations represented in programs and used for automation tasks?
without_scope.answer: User demonstrations are typically captured as <cite id="ccb86bad-4">action traces</cite> or <cite id="ccb86bad-2">sequences of user actions</cite>, and Programming-by-Demonstration systems <cite id="c3796ce2-1">automatically generate programs from user demonstrations</cite>. In these synthesized programs, the raw traces are abstracted into higher-level structure such as <cite id="ccb86bad-0,ccb86bad-2">variables, loops, and even multiple nested loops</cite>, so the program can <cite id="ccb86bad-4">reproduce what the user did</cite> and also <cite id="ccb86bad-4">generalize</cite> beyond the exact example. For automation, the synthesized program is then executed to drive tasks—for example, <cite id="cf32f3c0-0">creating task automations by demonstrating using GUIs of existing mobile apps</cite> or <cite id="ccb86bad-5">constructing software bots for web RPA tasks</cite>—so users can automate work <cite id="4bdce277-8">without needing to write programs</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the leading techniques for person-following robot navigation (which must track the person and potentially re-identify if occluded)?

query.text: What are the leading techniques for person-following robot navigation (which must track the person and potentially re-identify if occluded)?
query.answer:
Leading person-following robot systems are usually built as a <cite id="5adc1620-0">two-stage “identify then follow” pipeline, where the system performs tracking and possibly ReID to locate the target person, then plans and executes the follow behavior</cite>. On the perception side, the main technique families are: <cite id="80ded6fc-1,b70de91b-9">range/depth sensing with LiDAR, laser, or RGB-D cameras</cite>, <cite id="b70de91b-0,b70de91b-2">monocular-camera tracking-and-identification frameworks</cite>, and <cite id="b70de91b-4">stereo-vision CNN trackers that are designed to cope with occlusions, appearance changes, pose changes, crouching, and illumination variation</cite>. In crowded scenes, a common pattern is <cite id="ced60150-0">multi-person tracking followed by target-person identification via the corresponding ID</cite>.

For maintaining identity under occlusion, the strongest current pattern is appearance-based person ReID: <cite id="cb9ff608-2">in practical robot person-following scenarios, people are often occluded, so re-identification is necessary</cite>; <cite id="07e41720-8">when the robot loses the person because they move out of view or are occluded, it can resume following by re-identifying them from a learned target-person model</cite>. Representative ReID modules use <cite id="7261b632-0">360-degree visual registration, neural re-identification from multiple body parts such as faces and torsos, and a motion model predicting the person’s future position</cite>. Simpler but still effective systems also use <cite id="dbe142f5-0">deep person detection plus color features such as HSV histograms for target identification</cite>.

For partial occlusion specifically, leading methods increasingly use structure beyond whole-body appearance. <cite id="cb9ff608-4">One approach estimates the target location from the visible body joints under partial occlusion</cite>, while <cite id="5adc1620-2">if the person is totally occluded, an appearance-based ReID module is used to recover the track when the person reappears</cite>. Another important enhancement is prediction-based tracking: <cite id="176911d7-0">real-time systems combine trajectory prediction with scene semantics and social influence from nearby people, and this improved MOTA by over 5% in the reported evaluation</cite>.

Finally, successful person-following is not just perception but navigation integration. Strong systems pair the tracking/ReID module with <cite id="dbe142f5-0">SLAM and LiDAR-based obstacle avoidance</cite>, and also support <cite id="7261b632-0">searching for the person when they move out of camera sight and collision avoidance while following</cite>. So, in practice, the leading recipe today is: <cite id="ced60150-0,7261b632-0,176911d7-0">detect/track multiple people, maintain target identity with appearance-based ReID, use pose or motion prediction to survive occlusion, and couple that perception stack to safe local navigation and obstacle avoidance</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the leading techniques for robot navigation?
fully_underspecified.answer: The main “leading” techniques in robot navigation are <cite id="e7631e65-1">localization and SLAM</cite>, <cite id="e7631e65-1,8696c99c-1">path planning</cite>, and <cite id="e7631e65-1,e7631e65-0">obstacle avoidance</cite>. For mapping and self-positioning, <cite id="7a5a52cd-4,7a5a52cd-5">SLAM is the standard approach, because it lets a robot build a map while localizing itself in an unknown environment</cite>. For global path planning, <cite id="02fd1aaf-3">A* and RRT are among the most used algorithms for mobile robots</cite>, and <cite id="02fd1aaf-2">path-planning algorithms are used to identify safe, efficient routes</cite>. For local motion control and collision avoidance, <cite id="7a5a52cd-9">prominent techniques include artificial potential fields (APF), the Dynamic Window Approach (DWA), and Model Predictive Control (MPC)</cite>. More recently, <cite id="8696c99c-0,7a5a52cd-1">deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has become a leading learning-based approach, especially for navigation in dynamic or crowded environments</cite>. In practice, the strongest systems usually <cite id="e7631e65-0,7a5a52cd-6">combine SLAM or localization with path planning and obstacle avoidance, sometimes adding learning-based components</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are the leading techniques for robot navigation that must track a person and potentially re-identify them if occluded?
without_scope.answer: The strongest current approach is a <cite id="6a55a890-0">two-stage stack in which the robot first identifies the target person using tracking and possibly re-identification (ReID), and then follows using planning and control</cite>. In practice, the perception side is usually <cite id="7af07534-0">tracking-by-detection, e.g., YOLOv3 for person detection, Deep SORT for track association, and OSNet for person ReID</cite>, often strengthened with <cite id="94d8c7b1-0">lightweight ReID plus gating to preserve the target identity through occlusions and appearance changes</cite>. For harder losses of visibility, leading systems add <cite id="a72f0ad7-0">appearance-memory methods such as 360-degree target registration, local+global feature descriptors, and candidate matching, which can recover a person after complete occlusions or when they leave and re-enter the field of view</cite>; some also use <cite id="6a55a890-0">online continual learning to make ReID features more discriminative for long-term following</cite>. Under partial occlusion, a strong technique is <cite id="4e22f660-1">pose/keypoint-based localization that estimates the person’s location as a weighted sum of visible human keypoints</cite>. Robust systems increasingly use <cite id="4fe86ba3-0">multimodal embeddings from color, depth, and thermal sensing to handle viewpoint changes, dynamic camera motion, and long-term occlusion</cite>. On the navigation side, the leading methods are <cite id="0144d3ea-0">human-aware planners that combine human motion prediction (e.g., Interacting Multiple Model), proxemics, dynamic occupancy maps, and Model Predictive Control for safe obstacle-avoiding following</cite>, sometimes wrapped in <cite id="6e9c0f6e-0">state-machine control to stay stable through occlusion and illumination changes</cite>.

In practice, the strongest systems are usually <cite id="0d09e5e1-0,b8ffca5b-7,592ce90c-1">hybrid stacks that fuse perception, tracking, localization, obstacle avoidance, and human-aware behavior control</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are leading methods for generating hard examples of the boolean satisfiability problem, and what are their strengths and weaknesses?

query.text: What are leading methods for generating hard examples of the boolean satisfiability problem, and what are their strengths and weaknesses?
query.answer:
The main families of hard SAT generators are:

1. **Uniform random \(k\)-SAT near the phase transition.**  
   This is the classical baseline because <cite id="ae1633ed-7">“The really hard instances tend to occur at the phase transition where the problems are finely balanced between being satisfiable and unsatisfiable.”</cite> For random 3-SAT, <cite id="ae1633ed-9">the phase transition occurs at roughly a clause/variable ratio of \(4.26\)</cite>.  
   **Strengths:** simple, tunable, and reliably hard on average near the threshold.  
   **Weaknesses:** they are often less representative of industrial SAT; in the community-structure work, <cite id="aa77b15d-0">high-modularity generators are used to model pseudo-industrial formulas, while low modularity gives formulas “very similar to classical random formulas”</cite>, implying plain random formulas miss important real-world structure.

2. **Planted / hidden-solution satisfiable generators.**  
   These are used when one wants guaranteed satisfiable hard instances: <cite id="decaba51-0">Achlioptas, Gomes, Kautz, and Selman propose a generator that “only outputs satisfiable problem instances” and show hardness can be finely controlled</cite>. Later hidden-solution methods explicitly try to make such formulas hard; for example, <cite id="e706a901-1">single-hidden-assignment generation is “highly biased towards formulas with many assignments clustered around \(A\)”</cite>, which is a weakness, and newer methods aim to fix this: <cite id="e39fd0de-0">KHidden-M is proposed as more effective than earlier M-hidden generators for producing random hard SAT instances</cite>.  
   **Strengths:** guaranteed satisfiable, hardness can be tuned, useful for testing incomplete/local-search solvers.  
   **Weaknesses:** naive planting introduces detectable bias or structure that solvers can exploit.

3. **Structured proof-complexity families, especially Tseitin and pigeonhole formulas.**  
   These are leading sources of *provably* hard UNSAT benchmarks. <cite id="7865da99-1">Tseitin formulas are parity constraints on a graph and “have been studied extensively in proof complexity”</cite>; <cite id="7865da99-4">they are “classical hard instances for proof systems”</cite>. Also, <cite id="7865da99-2">space lower bounds are known for both pigeonhole principle formulas and Tseitin formulas</cite>.  
   **Strengths:** strong theoretical hardness guarantees, excellent for studying proof systems and CDCL/resolution behavior.  
   **Weaknesses:** they are highly specialized and often less representative of application structure than industrial benchmarks.

4. **Pseudo-industrial / community-structured generators.**  
   A major modern direction is to generate formulas with graph/community structure similar to real-world SAT. <cite id="aa77b15d-0">The Community Attachment model is designed to capture modularity seen in industrial instances</cite>, and <cite id="aa77b15d-0">the authors show modern solvers “do actually exploit this community structure”</cite>.  
   **Strengths:** more realistic for benchmarking modern SAT solvers than plain random formulas.  
   **Weaknesses:** realism does not automatically imply hardness; in fact, <cite id="6dbcf637-2">modern solvers often solve many industrial instances efficiently</cite>, so these generators are better for realism than for guaranteed worst-case difficulty.

5. **Search-based and evolutionary hard-instance generation.**  
   Instead of sampling from a fixed distribution, these methods optimize formulas against a solver or hardness objective. <cite id="709f55f3-0">One line of work uses local search to produce SAT instances “harder to solve than randomly generated k-CNF formulae”</cite>.  
   **Strengths:** can generate very hard instances for specific solvers or solver classes.  
   **Weaknesses:** the hardness may overfit to the target solver and may not transfer broadly; these methods usually provide empirical hardness rather than proof-theoretic guarantees.

6. **Learned generators (emerging).**  
   More recent ML-based methods try to imitate real SAT distributions: <cite id="e706a901-6">G2SAT generates formulas that “closely resemble given real-world SAT instances, as measured by both graph metrics and SAT solver behavior”</cite>.  
   **Strengths:** potentially the best match to a target benchmark distribution.  
   **Weaknesses:** the focus is resemblance, not formal hardness guarantees, so they are promising for realism but less established as hard-instance generators in the proof-complexity sense.

**Bottom line:** if you want **simple average-case hardness**, use <cite id="ae1633ed-7">phase-transition random \(k\)-SAT</cite>; if you need **hard satisfiable instances**, use <cite id="decaba51-0">planted/hidden-solution generators</cite> but beware <cite id="e706a901-1">bias</cite>; if you want **provable hardness**, use <cite id="7865da99-4">Tseitin</cite> and related proof-complexity families; if you want **realistic modern benchmarks**, use <cite id="aa77b15d-0">community-structured</cite> or <cite id="e706a901-6">learned generators</cite>; and if you want **solver-targeted adversarial instances**, use <cite id="709f55f3-0">evolutionary/search-based generation</cite>.

ambiguity_judge.evidence: The response directly lists methods and their strengths/weaknesses without noting any ambiguity or asking for clarification.

fully_underspecified.text: What are methods for generating difficult examples of a problem, and what are their strengths and weaknesses?
fully_underspecified.answer:
A good way to think about this is that <cite id="ad8c4287-0">instance difficulty depends on the features of a problem instance that affect difficulty in terms of algorithmic performance</cite>, so “hard examples” are usually generated relative to a target solver or solver family.

**1. Random/statistical generation, often tuned to known hard regions.** <cite id="1c9ede23-6">Traditionally, researchers apply statistical or pseudo-random methods to create instances with which to validate their proposals.</cite> In SAT, <cite id="c363fd01-4">the really hard instances tend to occur at the phase transition where the problems are finely balanced between being satisfiable and unsatisfiable.</cite> A strength of this family is control: <cite id="ad8c4287-7">one can finely control the hardness of satisfiable instances</cite> and even <cite id="43d26c75-0">generate SAT instances with multiple predefined solutions that could be hard to solve</cite>. Its main weakness is realism: <cite id="43d26c75-3">defining a model that captures all the properties of real-world instances is not trivial</cite>, which is why <cite id="5d74f711-1">new models of random SAT instances generation that capture realistically the features of real-world problems can be beneficial</cite>.

**2. Feature-guided or instance-space generation.** A more targeted method is to generate cases with desired measurable properties; for example, <cite id="1c9ede23-0">a methodology for generating new test instances with controllable properties, by filling observed gaps in the instance space</cite>. The strength here is coverage and controllability, but the weakness is that it relies on good features and a good map of the space, since <cite id="ad8c4287-0">we need to adequately characterize the features of a problem instance that have impact on difficulty</cite>.

**3. Evolutionary or adversarial search over instances.** Here, the generator directly searches for cases that make a solver fail or slow down: <cite id="c363fd01-1">evolutionary computation can be used to acquire difficult to solve combinatorial problem instances</cite>, and in adversarial/co-evolutionary variants <cite id="0e9d87f9-1">the generator is optimized to produce increasingly difficult problem instances</cite>. The strength is that this can produce very challenging benchmarks—<cite id="0e9d87f9-0">experimental results demonstrate that EALG generates significantly harder instances than current benchmarks</cite>—and it is useful to <cite id="1c9ede23-1">gain insights into strengths/weaknesses of certain algorithms or to build a set of instances with strong performance differences</cite>. The main weakness is cost: <cite id="b472e10b-6">expensive optimization problems require expensive or even unaffordable costs for evaluating candidate solutions</cite>, and <cite id="b472e10b-2">traditional evolutionary algorithms tend to fail when they need many such expensive evaluations</cite>.

**4. Learning-based or generative models.** These methods learn a distribution of hard or realistic instances from data. Their big strength is realism: <cite id="5d74f711-0">G2SAT can generate SAT formulas that closely resemble given real-world SAT instances, as measured by both graph metrics and SAT solver behavior</cite>, and <cite id="43d26c75-8">SATGEN generates Boolean satisfiability formulas which resemble instances that arise in real-world settings</cite>. Some methods also improve generation efficiency, because <cite id="ad8c4287-3">the proposed method is able to use warm-starts to generate instances incrementally, resulting in enhanced efficiency</cite>. Their weakness is the data burden: <cite id="43d26c75-4">generating labeled data for hard problem instances is non-trivial</cite>, especially because <cite id="43d26c75-4">SAT is NP-complete</cite>.

In short, the main options are <cite id="1c9ede23-6,c363fd01-4">random/phase-transition methods</cite>, <cite id="1c9ede23-0">feature- or instance-space methods</cite>, <cite id="c363fd01-1,0e9d87f9-1">evolutionary/adversarial search</cite>, and <cite id="5d74f711-0,43d26c75-8">learning-based generation</cite>. The tradeoff is usually between <cite id="1c9ede23-0,ad8c4287-7">control</cite>, <cite id="5d74f711-0">realism</cite>, <cite id="0e9d87f9-0">difficulty achieved</cite>, and <cite id="b472e10b-6,43d26c75-4">the cost of evaluating or labeling candidate instances</cite>.
