questions.original_query: Many papers study optimal scaling laws for training compute. Has anyone analyzed optimality for inference-time compute? For instance, self-consistency samples many outputs to find the right answers. While this is effective, can't we just sample once if we have a stronger model?

query.text: Many papers study optimal scaling laws for training compute. Has anyone analyzed optimality for inference-time compute? For instance, self-consistency samples many outputs to find the right answers. While this is effective, can't we just sample once if we have a stronger model?

fully_underspecified.text: Has anyone analyzed optimality for compute? For instance, one method samples many outputs to find the right answers. While this is effective, can't we just sample once if we have a stronger model?
fully_underspecified.answer: Yes. Recent work explicitly studies “compute-optimal inference,” focusing on the trade-offs between model sizes and generating additional tokens, and even how to select an optimal size for the language model and an effective inference strategy such as greedy search, majority voting, or best-of-N. The main takeaway is that scaling inference compute with inference strategies can be more computationally efficient than scaling model parameters, so “just use a bigger model once” is not always the best use of compute. But naive repeated sampling is also not a free lunch: the effectiveness of repeated sampling quickly reaches diminishing and even negative returns. So the answer is: sometimes a stronger model with one sample is better, but there is no universal dominance; the optimal choice depends on the task, budget, and inference method, and compute-optimal strategies can be more than 4× more efficient than a best-of-N baseline on math reasoning.

fully_underspecified.text: do we know how true this is? Is it true for all areas or only for more visible aspects? Does supervised fine-tuning on a large instruction dataset teach models new knowledge?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Best current evidence says: <cite id="f34fad75-0">supervised fine-tuning on instruction data usually does not robustly teach LLMs much new factual knowledge; models “struggle to acquire new factual knowledge through fine-tuning,” and such examples are “learned significantly slower” than examples consistent with what the model already knows.</cite> The same study concludes that <cite id="f34fad75-0">LLMs “mostly acquire factual knowledge through pre-training, whereas fine-tuning teaches them to use it more efficiently.”</cite> So if by “teach” you mean deep, general, reliable world knowledge, the answer is mostly no; if you mean behavior that is more helpful, aligned, and better at expressing existing knowledge, then yes: <cite id="f10faf2d-0">instruction fine-tuning is critical for aligning LLMs with user intentions and helping them follow instructions</cite> and <cite id="f10faf2d-3">it improves controllable model behavior.</cite>

It is also <cite id="d33d1724-0">not equally true in all areas or formats: question-answer training data gives much stronger knowledge generalization than document/article-style training data.</cite> And there are signs the boundary is not absolute: <cite id="48c6cb24-0">pre-instruction-tuning before continued training on documents “significantly enhances the ability of LLMs to absorb knowledge from new documents,” outperforming standard instruction-tuning by 17.8%.</cite> But that result still points to <cite id="48c6cb24-0">instruction tuning helping knowledge absorption/extraction when paired with continued training on documents</cite>, not ordinary large-scale instruction SFT by itself being a strong mechanism for adding broad new knowledge. So the safest summary is: <cite id="f34fad75-0">instruction SFT mainly changes visible behavior and knowledge use; it can sometimes implant narrow facts, but this is weaker, slower, and less general than pretraining or continued pretraining.</cite>

A model’s knowledge and capabilities are learnt almost entirely during pretraining, while alignment teaches it which subdistribution of formats should be used when interacting with users

without_term.answer: The short version is: the “Superficial Alignment Hypothesis” says most knowledge and capabilities are learned in pretraining, and alignment/post-training mainly teaches the model how to respond. There is real evidence for this in some domains: LIMA found that simple fine-tuning on a very small, high-quality dataset was enough to learn specific response formats and compete strongly with much larger alignment pipelines, which supports the hypothesis. And more broadly, instruction tuning clearly improves zero-shot performance, which is consistent with the idea that post-training often elicits capabilities already present in the pretrained model rather than creating them from scratch. This is reinforced by a 2024 ACL paper arguing that instruction-tuned LMs are “better knowledge elicitors,” and that their focus is on eliciting factual knowledge with instruction tuning on QA data; similarly, a recent survey says instruction tuning can model a response style rather than impart new knowledge. But the stronger, universal version of the hypothesis does not seem to hold. “Revisiting the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis” reports that, with appropriate post-training, a model’s ability to integrate new knowledge greatly improves on downstream tasks like multihop question answering, which is direct evidence that post-training can change more than just surface style. Also, work on knowledge editing shows that traditional methods can refine LLMs via fine-tuning on texts containing specific knowledge, so parameter-updating stages after pretraining can indeed alter a model’s factual content at least in targeted settings. So my best synthesis is: the hypothesis is approximately true for many highly perceivable interaction-layer properties—things like response format, instruction following, and likely a chunk of “helpfulness” behavior—because small amounts of post-training can strongly reshape how the model presents what it already knows. But it is not true in full generality: post-training can improve knowledge integration and can even update facts, though standard supervised instruction tuning is often better viewed as elicitation than as major knowledge acquisition. Useful papers to read: 1. Zhou et al., “LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment” 2. Raghavendra et al., “Revisiting the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis” 3. Wei et al., “Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners” 4. Jiang et al., “Instruction-tuned Language Models are Better Knowledge Elicitors” 5. Zheng et al., work on knowledge editing / updating factual knowledge by fine-tuning

without_preference.text: do we know how true the “superficial alignment hypothesis” is? A model’s knowledge and capabilities are learnt almost entirely during pretraining, while alignment teaches it which subdistribution of formats should be used when interacting with users. Is it true for all domains/aspects or is it only true for more perceivable aspects like helpfulness? Does SFT on a huge instruction dataset teach models new knowledge?
without_preference.answer:
The “superficial alignment hypothesis” looks <cite id="99877b8a-0">roughly true as a first approximation</cite>, but <cite id="3e64bec0-0">too strong as a universal claim</cite>. On the “superficial” side, instruction tuning appears to mainly reshape how pretrained knowledge is accessed and expressed: <cite id="99877b8a-0">it helps models recognize the instruction parts of prompts</cite>, <cite id="99877b8a-0">makes attention heads capture more relationships around instruction verbs</cite>, and <cite id="99877b8a-0">rotates pre-trained knowledge toward user-oriented tasks</cite>. That supports the view that post-training often changes <cite id="99877b8a-0">instruction-following and response selection</cite> more than it creates capabilities from scratch. But it is not true in all domains or aspects, because <cite id="3e64bec0-0">supervised fine-tuning can significantly benefit the model</cite>, <cite id="3e64bec0-0">the model can already solve some tasks after pre-training, while fine-tuning most benefits datasets where the model does not show capability during pre-training</cite>, and <cite id="3e64bec0-0">continual pre-training improves the model in a latent way that manifests after fine-tuning</cite>. Also, post-training is not purely cosmetic: <cite id="3e64bec0-0">it may forget previously known domain knowledge and tasks that are not seen during fine-tuning</cite> and <cite id="3e64bec0-0">it increases sensitivity to evaluation prompts</cite>, which shows it can alter substantive behavior, not just surface politeness or helpfulness.  

On whether SFT on a huge instruction dataset can teach new knowledge: <cite id="a5e12710-0">yes, it can, but unevenly and often brittly</cite>. A large 2025 study reports that <cite id="a5e12710-0">the conventional wisdom is that injecting knowledge via finetuning results in brittle performance and poor generalization</cite>, yet also argues that <cite id="a5e12710-0">“task customization” and “knowledge injection” are not fundamentally different categories</cite>. Instead, success depends on the kind of knowledge and data format: <cite id="a5e12710-0">question-answer training data generalizes much better than document/article-style finetuning data</cite>, <cite id="a5e12710-0">numerical information is harder to retain than categorical information</cite>, and <cite id="a5e12710-0">models struggle to use finetuned knowledge in multi-step reasoning even when trained on similar examples</cite>. Strikingly, that same study finds <cite id="a5e12710-0">it is not fundamentally more difficult to finetune information about a real-world event than information about a model’s writing style</cite>. So the best current answer is: the hypothesis is <cite id="99877b8a-0">more accurate for visible alignment properties like instruction following/helpfulness</cite> than as a blanket statement about all cognition; <cite id="a5e12710-0">SFT can teach some new knowledge</cite>, but <cite id="a5e12710-0">the learned knowledge is much more format-, domain-, and reasoning-dependent than knowledge acquired during pretraining</cite>.

questions.original_query: Have anyone tried training with 4-bit quantization? Did you observe some performance difference with higher precision?

query.text: Have anyone tried training with 4-bit quantization? Did you observe some performance difference with higher precision?
query.answer: Yes—<cite id="0c925059-0">QLoRA showed that you can fine-tune a model with a 4-bit base model</cite>, and <cite id="8b3c6a18-0">the common supported setup for 4-bit in bitsandbytes is training only extra parameters</cite> rather than updating all quantized weights directly. In practice, <cite id="8b3c6a18-1">“pure 4bit training” is not possible in that stack</cite>; instead, <cite id="0c925059-6,8b3c6a18-2">the frozen base model is stored in 4-bit precision while LoRA/adapters are trained in higher precision such as BF16/FP16</cite>. On quality, the main reported result is that <cite id="0c925059-0">QLoRA can replicate 16-bit full fine-tuning performance with a 4-bit base model and LoRA adapters</cite>, and Hugging Face’s summary likewise says <cite id="de950a2c-4">it reduces memory usage “without performance tradeoffs compared to standard 16-bit model finetuning”</cite>. So the short answer is: <cite id="0c925059-0,8b3c6a18-1">yes, 4-bit training/fine-tuning has been tried extensively, but usually as 4-bit-backed adapter fine-tuning rather than full end-to-end 4-bit weight training; reported performance is often very close to 16-bit, with the main benefit being much lower memory use</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Have anyone tried training with quantization? Did you observe some performance difference with higher precision?
fully_underspecified.answer: Yes—<cite id="e009e537-0">training with quantized / low-precision weights and activations has been studied extensively</cite>, and one classic result reports that <cite id="e009e537-0">QNNs achieve prediction accuracy comparable to their 32-bit counterparts</cite>. In practice, <cite id="a94306c9-2">mixed-precision training is widely used because it can preserve accuracy compared to full precision training</cite> while improving efficiency. But if you push precision too low, <cite id="24b30be6-1">quantization can cause lost accuracy, particularly at low-bit precision</cite>, so methods like QAT are used because <cite id="24b30be6-0">they provide a smoother transition from higher to lower precisions, often yielding greater accuracy recovery</cite>. So the short answer is: yes, people absolutely train with quantization; <cite id="a94306c9-2">16/32-bit mixed precision often shows little or no accuracy drop versus higher precision</cite>, but <cite id="24b30be6-1">more aggressive low-bit quantization can hurt performance unless carefully trained</cite>.

without_preference.text: Have anyone tried training with 4-bit quantization? Did you observe some performance difference?
without_preference.answer: Yes — <cite id="65912409-1">QLoRA is a 4-bit quantization approach for LLM fine-tuning</cite>, and it specifically <cite id="65912409-0">backpropagates through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into LoRA adapters while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance</cite>. So for adapter-based fine-tuning, the reported performance difference was essentially negligible relative to full 16-bit fine-tuning <cite id="65912409-0,65912409-1">in the tasks they evaluated</cite>. More recently, 4-bit has also been pushed into pretraining: <cite id="0c5afe95-1">NVFP4 extends 4-bit precision from inference to pretraining</cite>, and the reported result is that it <cite id="0c5afe95-0">achieves training loss and downstream task accuracies comparable to an FP8 baseline</cite>. In short: <cite id="65912409-0">yes, people have trained with 4-bit</cite>, and <cite id="65912409-0,0c5afe95-0">with specialized methods, the observed quality drop can be very small or even comparable to higher-precision baselines</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are some of the key advantages and challenges of building multilingual evaluation datasets by translating existing English datasets into other target languages? Or more specifically, how do these translated datasets impact the quality and reliability of cross-lingual evaluations, and what potential pitfalls should be considered when using translations as a primary method for creating non-English benchmarks?

query.text: What are some of the key advantages and challenges of building multilingual evaluation datasets by translating existing English datasets into other target languages? Or more specifically, how do these translated datasets impact the quality and reliability of cross-lingual evaluations, and what potential pitfalls should be considered when using translations as a primary method for creating non-English benchmarks?
query.answer: Translation-based multilingual benchmarks are useful because they can <cite id="2f050742-1">extend an existing English benchmark to many languages, as XNLI does for 15 languages</cite> and create <cite id="2f050742-6">fully parallel benchmarks for measuring how well models transfer across languages</cite>, which makes cross-language comparisons much cleaner than using unrelated test sets. The main downside is that translations can reduce evaluation validity: <cite id="9f8f6682-3">translated datasets fail to reflect naturally occurring multilingual data due to translation artifacts that distort linguistic patterns</cite>, and <cite id="d11b38a5-4">machine translationese in evaluation datasets can inflate performance assessments</cite>. Score distortion can also go in the opposite direction, since <cite id="2f050742-0">for XQuAD, automatically translated test sets underestimated mBERT’s true performance by 3.0 F1 / 0.2 EM points</cite>. A further risk is cultural mismatch: <cite id="2a4a8a8f-1">multilingual benchmarks are commonly translations of English benchmarks, thereby lacking the cultural nuances found in other languages</cite>. So, translated datasets are valuable for fast and controlled cross-lingual evaluation, but if used as the primary way to build non-English benchmarks they can overstate or understate model quality, miss culture-specific phenomena, and should ideally be supplemented with native data and <cite id="2a4a8a8f-7">expert verification rather than relying on machine-translated benchmarks alone</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some of the key advantages and challenges of building evaluation datasets by translating existing datasets into other languages? How do these translated datasets impact the quality and reliability of evaluations, and what potential pitfalls should be considered when using translations as a primary method for creating benchmarks?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Translating an existing benchmark into other languages has two big practical advantages: <cite id="8ae6aa3f-2">it can rely on existing professional translation services rather than requiring expertise in multiple languages</cite>, and <cite id="8ae6aa3f-2">it can create parallel evaluation sets that offer a meaningful measure of the cross-lingual transfer gap of different models</cite>. That makes translation an attractive way to scale multilingual evaluation quickly, especially when native benchmark creation is expensive or slow <cite id="af7f7a61-0">recent research has adopted translating existing benchmarks as one of the main approaches to multilingual LLM evaluation</cite>.  

The main challenge is that translation can change the benchmark itself. Prior work finds that <cite id="8ae6aa3f-1">machine translation affects model behavior in cross-lingual evaluation</cite> and that many multilingual benchmarks built this way <cite id="079751ff-0">propagat[e] source-language biases</cite>. These issues can hurt evaluation quality and reliability because <cite id="f91843ba-0">translation errors in machine-translated benchmarks affect multilingual LLM evaluation</cite>, and researchers now explicitly test whether they alter <cite id="8ae6aa3f-0">not only absolute scores but also relative system ordering</cite>. The risk is not just random noise: <cite id="8ae6aa3f-5">MT-based evaluation is reliable in some cases and misleading in others</cite>, and <cite id="af7f7a61-1">current language selections in multilingual datasets tend to overestimate LLM performance on low-resource languages</cite>. So, translated datasets are useful as a fast, comparable proxy, but as a primary benchmarking method they can mismeasure true native-language ability, import source-language assumptions, and produce unstable or inflated conclusions unless they are carefully audited and preferably human-verified <cite id="a7345415-1">reliability of machine-translated benchmark evaluation benefits from corpus audit, targeted repairs, and sentence-level quality profiling</cite>.

How do these translated datasets impact the quality and reliability of cross-lingual evaluations, and what potential pitfalls should be considered when using translations as a primary method for creating non-English benchmarks?

<cite id="f129ba9e-0">The main challenge is that translation quality significantly influences benchmark results,</cite> so <cite id="fe419275-0">better translation methods can produce more reliable evaluations.</cite> <cite id="4759c5f8-1">Poorly translated datasets may suffer from semantic drift and context loss, which can lead to misleading performance metrics.</cite> <cite id="53f0abcc-4">Another major limitation is that translated benchmarks often lack the cultural nuances of non-English settings,</cite> and <cite id="f129ba9e-8">even expert human translations may not be sufficient to guarantee effective evaluation in a target language.</cite> In practice, that means translated benchmarks are useful for fast, controlled, apples-to-apples testing across languages, but they should not be treated as a complete substitute for natively created, culturally grounded non-English benchmarks, especially when tasks depend on local knowledge, pragmatics, or natural language use.

questions.original_query: What are the benefits of LNP-based drug delivery compared to other nanoparticle-based applications?

query.text: What are the benefits of LNP-based drug delivery compared to other nanoparticle-based applications?
query.answer: Compared with other nanoparticle drug-delivery platforms, LNPs are often favored because <cite id="49d2598d-0">they are a highly adaptable nanocarrier with structural flexibility, biocompatibility, and the ability to encapsulate diverse therapeutic agents ranging from chemotherapeutics to nucleic acids and imaging tracers</cite>. In practice, this means <cite id="49d2598d-0">they can support targeted treatment with improved efficacy and reduced systemic toxicity</cite>, and <cite id="49d2598d-0">they can be engineered for ligand-mediated targeting and pH- or temperature-responsive release</cite>. LNPs are especially strong for RNA medicines because <cite id="486a5866-0">ionizable lipid nanoparticles enable safe and efficient cytosolic delivery of therapeutic nucleic acids</cite>, while <cite id="486a5866-4">biodegradable lipids improve tolerability by allowing fast metabolism</cite>. Compared with polymeric nanoparticles, whose classic advantages are often <cite id="e6b79177-0">controllable size, shape, and surface charge</cite>, LNPs stand out more for <cite id="49d2598d-0">biological compatibility and broad cargo delivery</cite>. They also have stronger real-world translation than many inorganic nanoparticle systems: <cite id="d11cc78a-0">there are FDA-approved lipid-based nanoparticles</cite>, whereas <cite id="5c84c4b7-0">very few inorganic nanoparticle systems have entered the clinic</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the benefits of drug delivery compared to other applications?
fully_underspecified.answer: If by “drug delivery” you mean <cite id="c89cd1f5-0">modern/targeted drug delivery systems compared with conventional drug administration</cite>, the main benefits are that they offer <cite id="c89cd1f5-0">enhanced performance, automation, precision, and efficacy</cite>. They can <cite id="11244c0c-0">improve drug solubility, target site accumulation, patient acceptance, and compliance, and reduce drug toxicity</cite>. In targeted or nano-based forms, they also <cite id="c89cd1f5-2">outperform free drugs in treatment efficacy</cite> and <cite id="c89cd1f5-2">reduce systemic toxicity compared to conventional drug therapy</cite>. Another major advantage is <cite id="11244c0c-7">precise and sustained drug release</cite>, which can <cite id="11244c0c-4">reduce the need for multiple doses and greatly improve patient compliance</cite>. So, overall, drug delivery is valued because it <cite id="11244c0c-2">improves efficacy and reduces toxicity via targeted drug delivery and controlled drug release</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the biochemical analytical tools to assess the integrity and stability of LNPs?

query.text: What are the biochemical analytical tools to assess the integrity and stability of LNPs?
query.answer:
To assess LNP integrity and stability, researchers usually use an <cite id="c54e6ec3-5">orthogonal approach to lipid nanoparticle analysis</cite>. Core tools include <cite id="36b9993e-0">LNP size (Z-average) and polydispersity index (PDI)</cite>, typically measured by <cite id="c54e6ec3-0">DLS, a long-standing, fast and very widespread technique for sizing and quality control of nanoparticles</cite>; <cite id="ae927d10-0">zeta potential measurements of RNA-LNPs</cite> to monitor surface charge and colloidal stability; and imaging methods such as <cite id="e3a07ea9-0">Cryo-TEM ... to gain insight into lipid nanoparticle surface morphology and detailed inner structure</cite>. For payload retention, <cite id="36b9993e-0">encapsulation efficiency</cite> is a key integrity readout, commonly measured with the <cite id="ba4fe6e0-7">RiboGreen assay ... used routinely to determine the mRNA encapsulation efficiency and the concentration of encapsulated</cite> RNA, while <cite id="c54e6ec3-3">capillary gel electrophoresis with laser-induced fluorescence</cite> can also determine encapsulation efficiency and <cite id="ba4fe6e0-5">confirm mRNA degradation</cite>. For chemical stability of the lipid components, <cite id="ae927d10-1">LC-MS</cite> is used to analyze <cite id="c54e6ec3-2">LNPs ... [where] LC–MS</cite> supports compositional/impurity assessment, and <cite id="c54e6ec3-0">differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)</cite> can probe thermal/phase behavior linked to formulation stability. Additional complementary methods include <cite id="176815d2-3">TEM, SEM, and X-ray studies</cite> for morphology/structure and <cite id="176815d2-4">nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA)</cite> as a sizing complement to DLS.

In practice, the most useful biochemical/biophysical panel is: <cite id="36b9993e-0,c54e6ec3-0">DLS/PDI</cite>, <cite id="ae927d10-0">zeta potential</cite>, <cite id="e3a07ea9-0">cryo-TEM</cite>, <cite id="ba4fe6e0-7,c54e6ec3-3">RiboGreen or CGE for encapsulation/free RNA</cite>, <cite id="ba4fe6e0-5">gel/CGE for RNA integrity</cite>, <cite id="ae927d10-1,c54e6ec3-2">LC-MS for lipid identity/degradation and impurities</cite>, and <cite id="c54e6ec3-0">DSC</cite> for thermal stability.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the analytical tools to assess the integrity and stability of these particles?

without_term.text: What are the biochemical analytical tools to assess the integrity and stability of lipid nanoparticles?
without_term.answer:
The most useful toolkit is an <cite id="f64d7f87-0,e5601d2b-1">orthogonal set of analytical methods that covers chemical composition, drug loading, particle size/concentration/stability, and structure/morphology</cite>. In practice, the core tools are:

- <cite id="29bfd16b-0,158167db-0">Dynamic light scattering (DLS), often alongside MALS, for particle size distribution, polydispersity, aggregation, and routine quality control</cite>.
- <cite id="29bfd16b-1,158167db-9">Zeta-potential measurements, typically by electrophoretic light scattering (ELS), because surface charge is a key critical quality attribute tied to colloidal stability</cite>.
- <cite id="f64d7f87-3,f64d7f87-1">Cryo-EM/cryo-TEM for direct assessment of LNP morphology, particle shape, lamellarity, and structural heterogeneity</cite>.
- <cite id="e5601d2b-0">RiboGreen fluorescence assays for encapsulation efficiency, by distinguishing free (unencapsulated) RNA from total RNA after LNP disruption</cite>.
- <cite id="f64d7f87-0,4f460404-5,4f460404-1">Chromatographic and mass-spectrometric methods—especially LC/HPLC and LC-MS/MS—for chemical composition, lipid quantification, impurity/degradation profiling, and molecular-mass confirmation of lipid components</cite>.
- <cite id="4f460404-3,4f460404-0">Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and often X-ray methods, for higher-level fingerprints of LNP structure/composition and for detecting structural or compositional changes during storage</cite>.

So, the key analytical tools to assess LNP integrity and stability are <cite id="29bfd16b-0,29bfd16b-1,f64d7f87-3,e5601d2b-0,4f460404-5,4f460404-3">DLS/MALS, zeta-potential (ELS), cryo-EM/cryo-TEM, encapsulation assays such as RiboGreen, LC/HPLC/LC-MS, and DSC/X-ray techniques</cite>.
