query.text: How can user modeling techniques be improved to capture and leverage individual preferences more effectively in personalized recommendation systems?
query.answer: To improve user modeling, personalized recommenders should move beyond a single static user embedding and instead: (1) <cite id="2b4a11a6-0">capture and extract the user's multiple and diverse interests</cite>, because <cite id="2b4a11a6-1">existing recommendation methods struggle to model users' multifaceted preferences due to the diversity and volatility of user behavior</cite>; (2) make profiles <cite id="d18185df-4">consider the change in users' preferences over time</cite> and use <cite id="d18185df-1">runtime identification of contextual information</cite> to <cite id="d18185df-1">boost recommendation performance</cite>; (3) enrich user representations with features that <cite id="43a50692-0">exploit the rich side information associated with users or items (e.g., user reviews and item images)</cite> and <cite id="43a50692-1">integrate diverse data types including images, text, audio, and video</cite>; (4) apply causal debiasing, since <cite id="38b81606-6">various confounding factors are present and lead to data biases</cite> and <cite id="38b81606-6">make it difficult to accurately determine a user’s true preference</cite>, so methods that <cite id="38b81606-1">model item Exposure and user Satisfaction simultaneously with Causal Inference</cite> are useful; and (5) support privacy-preserving personalization through federated settings that <cite id="38b81606-3">mitigate the risk of user privacy leakage with local data</cite> while <cite id="38b81606-4">balancing growing demands for data security and personalized experiences</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How can techniques be improved to capture and use preferences more effectively in recommendation systems?
fully_underspecified.answer: Preference capture in recommender systems can be improved by <cite id="169fadd5-5,2aca1e5a-1">combining explicit feedback with implicit behavioral signals, since recommender systems learn from both, and implicit feedback only indirectly reflects user preference</cite>. Systems should also <cite id="24e9acd9-4,24e9acd9-1,24e9acd9-0">model preferences as dynamic rather than static: user behavior modeling is critical, sequential recommenders use interaction history to improve personalization, and modeling multiple heterogeneous behaviors is necessary</cite>. In addition, recommenders can better use preferences by <cite id="0f8d717c-1,0f8d717c-7">incorporating context—whether explicit or latent, static or dynamic—because users may have different preferences in different situations</cite>. For sparse or changing preferences, <cite id="2e309bc8-0,2e309bc8-1">conversational and interactive elicitation helps by repeatedly asking targeted questions and adapting to user responses over multiple turns to capture current needs</cite>. Finally, preference use becomes more faithful when models <cite id="22ef4661-5,22ef4661-0,22ef4661-2">correct for biases such as selection, position, exposure, and popularity bias, since these can enter at multiple stages and distort what the system learns and recommends</cite>.

without_preference.text: How can user modeling techniques be improved to capture and leverage individual preferences more effectively in recommendation systems?
without_preference.answer: User modeling in recommendation systems can be improved by replacing a single static user profile with a richer, adaptive representation. First, models should track preference drift, because <cite id="f26961d7-0">individual preferences change over time, requiring recommendation systems to adapt to dynamic user preference changes</cite>; one concrete direction is <cite id="f26961d7-2">attention-based dynamic user preference modeling</cite>. Second, they should represent users with multiple latent interests rather than one embedding, since <cite id="a8dd3fdc-0">multi-interest recommendation explicitly extracts multiple interest representations from users' historical interactions</cite>. Third, user models should include situational signals, as <cite id="c4f78dd5-0">context-aware recommender systems incorporate contextual information to achieve better recommendations</cite>. Fourth, they should fuse more evidence about taste, because <cite id="07ff0869-9">multimodal recommendation jointly exploits diverse item metadata (images, text, audio) and collaborative signals to model user preferences</cite>. Finally, stronger personalization and robustness are likely to come from newer representation-learning and correction methods—recent surveys highlight <cite id="bcc4b43e-0">graph-based, transformer-based, self-supervised, causality-aware, and LLM-enhanced</cite> paradigms, and debiasing can help by adding <cite id="bcc4b43e-6">penalty constraints for items based on their popularity</cite> so the learned user model reflects true preference rather than exposure bias.

questions.original_query: How can complex word identification (CWI) models be personalized to improve their performance for individual users with different language backgrounds and proficiency levels?

query.text: How can complex word identification (CWI) models be personalized to improve their performance for individual users with different language backgrounds and proficiency levels?
query.answer: Complex word identification can be personalized by <cite id="f5668281-0">predicting which words are likely to be considered complex by a given target population</cite> rather than assuming one universal notion of difficulty. This matters because <cite id="794232aa-0">there are sizable differences between the lexical complexity assignments of L1 and L2 English speakers</cite>, and for L2 users <cite id="794232aa-0">word frequency, length, syllable count, familiarity, prevalence, and number of derivations have a greater effect on perceived lexical complexity</cite>. In practice, a good approach is to build user-aware CWI models that condition on learner metadata such as <cite id="578a581d-6">L1</cite> and proficiency-related information, and to train on personalized learner corpora such as <cite id="578a581d-1">LexComSpaL2, a novel corpus which can be employed to train personalised word-level difficulty classifiers for learners of Spanish</cite>. Model adaptation can be further improved by adding learner-relevant linguistic features: for example, <cite id="c022c3a3-0">adding word family knowledge as an extra feature</cite> in a <cite id="c022c3a3-0">personalised word difficulty classifier for L2 Spanish</cite> improved performance from <cite id="c022c3a3-0">F1 = 0.53</cite> to <cite id="c022c3a3-0">F1 = 0.62</cite>. Finally, when enough per-user data can be collected, <cite id="32585a0f-6">personal models are best when predicting word complexity for individual readers</cite>, and <cite id="32585a0f-6">a novel active learning framework</cite> suggests that selectively requesting a small amount of user feedback is a practical way to personalize predictions.

fully_underspecified.text: How can models be personalized to improve their performance for individual users?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="44ad7d7d-1,44ad7d7d-8">A common way to personalize models is to use three levers: prompting with personalized context, adaptation of the model, and alignment to user preferences.</cite> <cite id="92b67138-0,44ad7d7d-2,1122bfc1-0">In practice, this often means building a structured user-profile memory that stores relevant facts, entities, concepts, and past preferences, then retrieving that information at inference time so responses are conditioned on the individual user.</cite> <cite id="92b67138-7,92b67138-1">Models can also be adapted with user-specific fine-tuning or lightweight user models trained from feedback; personalized RLHF-style methods have been reported to produce responses more closely aligned with individual users.</cite> <cite id="9d2b20c8-0,9d2b20c8-1">Finally, personalization can happen even without retraining by modifying decoding at inference time so the model’s outputs better match a particular user’s preferences.</cite> Overall, <cite id="92b67138-1,9d2b20c8-0">the goal is to inject user-specific information and feedback into prompting, memory, training, or decoding so the model performs better for that individual.</cite>

without_scope.text: How can complex word identification (CWI) models be personalized to improve their performance for individual users?
without_scope.answer: <cite id="00aa6fa4-0,00aa6fa4-2">CWI can be personalized by training per-user “bespoke” models rather than relying on a single model for everyone, because personal models work best for predicting complexity for individual readers and outperform baselines and prior state-of-the-art systems.</cite> <cite id="d2b35ed3-0,d2b35ed3-3,00aa6fa4-2">A practical way to do this is to collect a small amount of user-specific feedback and use active learning to choose the most informative words for that user to label, which allows per-individual models to be trained without extensive annotation.</cite> <cite id="bd4c32f5-0">Personalization should also account for reader characteristics that systematically affect perceived difficulty—for example, L1 and L2 English speakers assign lexical complexity differently.</cite> <cite id="7057c4c5-1,7057c4c5-6">More broadly, building learner-specific corpora and training personalised word-level difficulty classifiers for particular populations is another effective route to user-adaptive CWI.</cite>

without_term.text: How can word identification models be personalized to improve their performance for individual users with different language backgrounds and proficiency levels?
without_term.answer: <cite id="ac34cc73-0">Word-identification models should be personalized by conditioning predictions on reader profiles, because perceived difficulty is subjective and is influenced by factors such as prior knowledge, language proficiency, and the reader’s background.</cite> <cite id="ac34cc73-0">A practical approach is to train profile-based models on annotations from the target audience, so the system is specialized to behave like that audience rather than relying only on generic linguistic features.</cite> <cite id="ee0a5d76-0">For users with different native languages, models can explicitly use the user’s L1 to detect cognates and false friends, since an adaptive pipeline based on native language changes which words are identified as difficult compared with standard frequency-based methods.</cite> <cite id="44f13141-0">This is important because L1 and L2 speakers assign lexical complexity differently, and for L2 readers features such as word frequency, length, syllable count, familiarity, prevalence, and number of derivations have a stronger effect on perceived difficulty.</cite> <cite id="44f13141-0">So, the best personalization strategy is to combine user metadata such as mother tongue and proficiency with lexical features whose weights vary by user group, yielding personalized lexical complexity or complex-word identification models for different target populations.</cite>

questions.original_query: In the domain of HCI or social science, there are many cases that researchers need to conduct studies with surveys and participants. How can large language models (LLMs) be used to simulate or represent diverse human populations in such social science applications?

query.text: In the domain of HCI or social science, there are many cases that researchers need to conduct studies with surveys and participants. How can large language models (LLMs) be used to simulate or represent diverse human populations in such social science applications?
query.answer:
## What LLMs can do in HCI/social-science studies

LLMs can be used as <cite id="S13">“silicon samples” or synthetic respondents</cite> to <cite id="S37">detect ambiguous wording, generate likely free-text themes, and screen manipulations for obvious failures</cite>. In HCI, they can also support <cite id="S41">“populated prototypes” of social computing systems</cite> that let teams <cite id="S41">preview discussion dynamics, moderation challenges, and onboarding frictions before costly field deployments</cite>.

A practical way to represent diversity is to prompt the model with <cite id="S11">demographic prompting</cite> or <cite id="S11">richer personas</cite>. But the evidence suggests that <cite id="S11">demographic prompting alone improves mean-level fit but collapses variance</cite>, and that <cite id="S27">models frequently break character, default to generic assistant norms, and produce stereotyped depictions for marginalized identities</cite>. This means simple “pretend you are a 22-year-old woman from X” prompting is usually not enough for realistic subgroup representation.

## Better ways to simulate diverse populations

A stronger approach is to build <cite id="S14">retrieval-augmented personas based on census microdata</cite> or other empirical records. These methods work better because <cite id="S14">retrieval-based personas better preserve joint distributions of attributes and produce more realistic open-ended responses</cite>, and <cite id="S35">retrieved neighborhood statistics, occupation information, and exemplar quotes from matched human respondents</cite> can improve realism over <cite id="S35">free-form role prompts</cite>.

Another promising strategy is to create participant-specific or subgroup-specific agents from real human data. For example, researchers have built <cite id="S22">generative agents using two-hour interviews and survey responses from 1,052 participants</cite>, and found that these agents <cite id="S22">predict individual responses to the General Social Survey, Big Five inventory, and behavioral economic games with significantly higher accuracy than demographic baselines or zero-shot LLM personas</cite>. More generally, <cite id="S23">“digital twins” of survey participants using interview transcripts and self-reports</cite> can capture <cite id="S23">stable preferences better than generic prompts</cite>.

A third useful layer is calibration. Studies propose <cite id="S5">post-stratification and group-aware prompting</cite> to align synthetic responses with empirical demographic distributions, and show that <cite id="S5">calibration substantially improves subgroup-level accuracy</cite>. Still, calibration has limits: <cite id="S34">post-stratification weighting reduces some compositional bias</cite> but <cite id="S34">cannot recover attitudes or behaviors absent from the model’s latent knowledge</cite>.

## Where current LLM population simulation fails

Across multiple evaluations, LLMs usually do better on averages than on diversity. They can <cite id="S2">match average human response distributions and basic correlations</cite> and <cite id="S3">approximate aggregate response distributions</cite>, but they also <cite id="S1">fail to accurately capture the heterogeneity of underrepresented and politically distinct subpopulations</cite>. Repeatedly, researchers find that models <cite id="S1">flatten differences across groups</cite>, <cite id="S3">systematically underestimate demographic heterogeneity</cite>, and <cite id="S3">fail to reproduce multivariate response structures</cite>.

These failures are especially important for marginalized or intersectional groups. Evidence shows that <cite id="S15">errors are substantially larger for groups with lower prevalence in the training data</cite>, with pronounced declines for <cite id="S15">racial minorities, politically extreme respondents, and respondents with intersecting marginalized identities</cite>. Similarly, in HCI contexts, LLMs may <cite id="S7">underrepresent accessibility-related concerns and the experiences of minority users unless those perspectives are explicitly modeled</cite>, and synthetic personas can miss <cite id="S25">caregiving burdens, safety concerns, and constraints tied to class and local infrastructure</cite>.

## Best-practice workflow for researchers

A good workflow is to treat LLMs as a **hybrid research tool**, not a replacement for participants. One recommended design is to use <cite id="S39">a small, diverse human sample to seed personas, calibrate the synthetic population, and identify failure modes</cite>, and then use the expanded simulation <cite id="S39">for scenario analysis rather than final inference</cite>. This fits the broader recommendation that useful simulations need <cite id="S32">realistic population construction, behavior models validated against human data, and evaluation of emergent macro-level patterns</cite>.

Validation should be stricter than just checking overall averages. Reviews recommend <cite id="S33">testing not only average response distributions but also subgroup calibration, temporal stability, network interactions, and sensitivity to prompt choices and model versions</cite>. That matters because <cite id="S29">responses are sensitive to prompt wording, sampling temperature, and safety tuning</cite>, so <cite id="S29">it is risky to interpret a single prompted persona as a faithful stand-in for a human subgroup</cite>.

## Bottom line

The most defensible use of LLMs in HCI and social science is to <cite id="S13">pilot survey instruments, stress-test experimental manipulations, and explore hypothesis space before costly studies</cite>, or to run <cite id="S41">early-stage design simulations</cite>. They are much less suitable when the goal is <cite id="S37">estimating treatment effects or heterogeneous responses</cite>, and they <cite id="S13">should not be treated as replacements for representative human samples when subgroup estimates or policy-sensitive conclusions are required</cite>. In short: use LLMs to **augment** human-subject research, especially through empirically grounded personas, calibration, and multilevel validation—not to bypass the need for real diverse participants.

fully_underspecified.text: How can models be used to simulate or represent human populations in studies?
fully_underspecified.answer: In studies, models can represent human populations at several levels. <cite id="8f0186de-2">Synthetic populations are built to create realistic populations for simulation</cite>, and <cite id="50f64559-5">spatial microsimulation generates individual-level data allocated to geographical areas</cite>, allowing <cite id="50f64559-0">high spatial, temporal, and demographic resolution</cite>. Researchers then use these synthetic people in <cite id="abc7ab69-3">agent-based models, which simulate interactions between people, places, things, and time</cite>; for example, <cite id="8f0186de-5">survey- and census-based synthetic agent populations have been used to reflect real-world populations in disease spread simulations</cite>. At a more aggregated level, <cite id="abc7ab69-6">compartmental models split a population into groups or compartments and model movement between them</cite>, and <cite id="abc7ab69-8">these are useful for quickly evaluating disease dynamics, while agent-based models offer more flexibility</cite>. Overall, models are used either to represent populations as <cite id="50f64559-3">synthetic populations for each target area</cite> or as interacting agents and groups, depending on whether the study needs detailed individual behavior or broader population trends.

without_scope.text: How can large language models (LLMs) be used to simulate or represent diverse human populations in social science applications?
without_scope.answer: LLMs can be used in social science as <cite id="0ac7488f-0">tools to synthesize public opinion data</cite> and <cite id="0ac7488f-1">to simulate consumer survey responses</cite> by treating the model as a set of synthetic respondents. A common method is <cite id="a899e5ec-1">persona prompting</cite>, where researchers ask the model to <cite id="a899e5ec-1">simulate views of various sociodemographic groups</cite>; related work also proposes <cite id="a9289839-8">synthesizing high-quality, population-aligned persona sets for LLM-driven social simulation</cite>. At the population level, researchers can use <cite id="8db47459-1">“random silicon sampling”</cite> to <cite id="8db47459-1">simulate human sub-population opinions using only group-level demographic information</cite>, or <cite id="a9289839-9">randomly choose personas and exemplars according to learned mixing weights to elicit diverse LLM responses during simulation</cite>. These approaches are being applied to <cite id="0ac7488f-9">simulate decision-making scenarios and even pilot social-science experiments</cite>, but they should be validated carefully because studies highlight <cite id="0ac7488f-2">challenges in using LLMs to simulate diverse human survey responses</cite>, including <cite id="a899e5ec-6">gender, racial, age, educational, and income biases</cite> and the difficulty of <cite id="a9289839-1">the scalable generation of representative</cite> personas.

without_term.text: In the domain of human-computer interaction or social science, there are many cases that researchers need to conduct studies with surveys and participants. How can large language models be used to simulate or represent diverse human populations in such social science applications?
without_term.answer:
<cite id="5ae438dd-0,595f84ce-0,6556670f-0">A common approach is to build “synthetic respondents” or “silicon samples” by prompting an LLM with demographic and attitudinal descriptors, biographies, or personas so the model answers as if it were a member of a target subgroup.</cite> <cite id="df55be50-0,df55be50-1">In HCI, the same idea is used to instantiate “synthetic users” with different goals, expertise levels, and backgrounds to stress-test interfaces, dialogue systems, or study protocols across more diverse usage scenarios.</cite>

<cite id="5ae438dd-1,6556670f-1,595f84ce-4">This works best as a population-level tool: studies report that persona-conditioned LLMs can sometimes reproduce subgroup-level survey distributions, align better with observed human opinion patterns than generic prompting, and even recover some experimental treatment effects, but this is much more reliable for aggregate patterns than for realistic individual persons.</cite> <cite id="5ae438dd-2,6556670f-3,df55be50-3,595f84ce-3">Because of that, the most defensible uses are low-cost pilot testing, hypothesis generation, scenario exploration, survey or instrument refinement, robustness checks, and formative design before running expensive studies with real people.</cite>

<cite id="595f84ce-0,595f84ce-1,595f84ce-2,df55be50-2">Researchers should be cautious, however, because synthetic populations are sensitive to prompt design and model choice, can fail on out-of-sample tasks or minority groups, may reproduce stereotypes from training data instead of genuine preferences, and often make users seem more coherent, compliant, and articulate than real participants.</cite> <cite id="5ae438dd-3,595f84ce-3,df55be50-3,595f84ce-5">So the best practice is to treat LLMs as complements—not replacements—for human participants: benchmark them against real survey data, report prompts and sampling settings transparently, and validate any consequential findings with actual people.</cite>

questions.original_query: In survey-based research, generating questions with different granularity is usually a heavy work. Are there any question-generation models that are controllable over the specificity of the questions?

query.text: In survey-based research, generating questions with different granularity is usually a heavy work. Are there any question-generation models that are controllable over the specificity of the questions?
query.answer: Yes. <cite id="c9eb10d7-2">The recent NQG survey explicitly identifies “controllable” question generation as a real subarea, where specific aspects of questions can be controlled.</cite> The <cite id="a206b6ea-0,a206b6ea-2">closest direct match to your need for specificity/granularity control is SQUASH (Specificity-controlled Question-Answer Hierarchies)</cite>, which <cite id="a206b6ea-0,a206b6ea-1">converts an input document into a hierarchy of question-answer pairs</cite> and <cite id="a206b6ea-8">determines that hierarchy by the specificity of the question.</cite> More broadly, recent reviews say controllable QG systems can be customized along dimensions such as <cite id="c9eb10d7-0">difficulty level and desired answer type</cite>, so the field is moving toward user-steerable generation even beyond specificity alone. A fair caveat is that <cite id="a206b6ea-0,a206b6ea-2">SQUASH is framed as a general text-generation/QG task</cite>, so if your application is survey research specifically, you may need adaptation rather than an off-the-shelf survey-focused model.

without_scope.text: Are there any question-generation models that are controllable over the specificity of the questions?
without_scope.answer: Yes. <cite id="d7542e23-1">SQUASH (“Specificity-controlled Question-Answer Hierarchies”)</cite> is a question-generation setup that <cite id="d7542e23-0">aims to convert a document into a hierarchy of question-answer pairs with controlled specificity</cite>; the project description also notes that <cite id="d7542e23-6">the hierarchy is determined by the specificity of the question</cite>. That said, <cite id="689fa2c5-3">most controllable question-generation work is described as focusing mainly on cognitive level and difficulty level</cite>, and there are also models that control <cite id="689fa2c5-2">question type</cite> or <cite id="689fa2c5-6">difficulty labels</cite>. So the short answer is: <cite id="d7542e23-1">yes, specificity control does exist</cite>, but <cite id="689fa2c5-3">it appears to be less common than other control dimensions like type or difficulty</cite>.

questions.original_query: In real research reading, scholar will search for relavent work or follow-up papers in order to get a more comprehensive understanding. Is there any work done to automate or assist in this process?

query.text: In real research reading, scholar will search for relavent work or follow-up papers in order to get a more comprehensive understanding. Is there any work done to automate or assist in this process?
query.answer:
Yes—<cite id="7c536f41-9">there is a substantial research area on scientific paper recommendation systems</cite>, including methods based on <cite id="7c536f41-9">paper citation graph</cite> and broader <cite id="7c536f41-9">citation recommendation tasks and methods</cite>. Beyond recommending individual papers, there is also work on <cite id="8886de73-3,7c536f41-5">automatic related work generation (RWG)</cite>, and a 2024 survey explicitly treats it as an academically and computationally important problem <cite id="8886de73-3">because literature review writing is challenging</cite>. 

There are also concrete systems aimed at helping scholars discover follow-up or adjacent work. For example, <cite id="8886de73-5,63053cdf-0">Relatedly proposes a novel approach to discovering and systematically reviewing literature by reading and exploring relevant related work sections</cite>. On the interactive-tool side, <cite id="b87916d2-0,b87916d2-2">Connected Papers is a visual tool to help researchers find and explore papers relevant to their field</cite>, and it can build <cite id="b87916d2-7">a graph of related papers based on co-citation and bibliographic coupling similarities</cite>. More recently, LLM-based approaches have gone further toward automation: <cite id="35ceae4b-4">an automated literature research and review-generation method based on large language models was proposed to overcome efficiency bottlenecks and reduce cognitive load</cite>. 

So the short answer is: <cite id="7c536f41-9,8886de73-3,63053cdf-0">yes—there is already significant work on automating or assisting the search for relevant and follow-up papers, ranging from citation/paper recommendation to related-work generation and literature-review support systems.</cite>

questions.original_query: Interdisciplinary research usually takes extra efforts to conduct. Are there any systems or approaches to facilitate interdisciplinary research and cross-domain discovery in scientific fields?

query.text: Interdisciplinary research usually takes extra efforts to conduct. Are there any systems or approaches to facilitate interdisciplinary research and cross-domain discovery in scientific fields?
query.answer: Yes. <cite id="b97913ad-2,b97913ad-0,658c424d-2">Literature-based discovery (LBD) is specifically designed for cross-disciplinary knowledge discovery: it uncovers hidden or previously unknown associations between disparate literatures and can generate novel hypotheses from large bodies of papers.</cite> <cite id="b97913ad-5,69553c1b-5">Scientific knowledge graphs are another important system; they organize data cohesively for centralized exploration, and cross-literature knowledge flow in such graphs can help scientists discover new research directions.</cite> <cite id="f04b19e4-1,f04b19e4-7">Bibliometric and network-mapping approaches can identify convergence patterns and emerging interdisciplinary areas by combining science mapping with network analysis.</cite> <cite id="f04b19e4-5,f04b19e4-6">At the organizational level, convergence and team-science approaches bring together knowledge and tools from multiple disciplines to co-create solutions across disciplinary boundaries.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: Are there any systems or approaches to facilitate research and discovery in scientific fields?
fully_underspecified.answer: Yes. <cite id="8b7f65be-1">Literature-Based Discovery (LBD) is a text mining technique used to generate novel hypotheses from vast amounts of literature sources</cite>, and <cite id="8b7f65be-2">literature-based discovery systems aim at discovering valuable latent connections between previously disparate research areas.</cite> Beyond LBD, <cite id="1b37d629-0">knowledge graphs are becoming core infrastructures for AI-driven scientific discovery</cite>. In domain-specific science, <cite id="1b37d629-1">artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming materials science by accelerating the design, synthesis, and characterization of novel materials.</cite> There are also experimental platforms: <cite id="8abc3038-4">self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate automation, robotics, and artificial intelligence to accelerate discovery through closed-loop experimentation</cite>, and <cite id="8abc3038-5">self-driving laboratories combine artificial intelligence with automated robotic platforms for the autonomous discovery of new materials.</cite> More broadly, <cite id="8b7f65be-7">new approaches to scientific process that use open systems to enable community-based research regarding complex</cite> problems are also being used to accelerate research.

without_scope.text: Are there any systems or approaches to facilitate interdisciplinary research and cross-domain discovery in scientific fields?
without_scope.answer: Yes. <cite id="251a3864-0">Literature-based discovery (LBD) addresses this challenge by uncovering previously unknown associations between disparate domains</cite>, and <cite id="251a3864-1">is a text mining technique used to generate novel hypotheses from vast amounts of literature sources</cite>. Another active approach is to build <cite id="251a3864-6">knowledge graphs</cite>, which <cite id="f8fbe64e-2">provide metadata and described data within a graph structure</cite> and can support <cite id="f8fbe64e-2">link prediction or node classification as means of knowledge discovery</cite>. Newer retrieval systems are also being designed specifically for cross-domain science: <cite id="73e0b39e-0">the Mechanism-Centric Cross-Domain Retrieval Framework (MCDF)</cite> is <cite id="73e0b39e-0">explicitly designed to operationalize cross-domain</cite> connections, motivated by the idea that <cite id="73e0b39e-1">cross-domain isomorphisms, hidden shared structural patterns across disparate fields, are critical for driving interdisciplinary innovation</cite>. There are also systems for finding interdisciplinary papers directly; for example, one recent method aims to <cite id="f8fbe64e-4">accurately identify potential cross-disciplinary literature and locate specific interdisciplinary pairs</cite>, providing <cite id="f8fbe64e-4">high-resolution intelligence for scientific research management and frontier exploration</cite>. So the answer is yes: current approaches include LBD, scientific knowledge graphs, mechanism-centric cross-domain retrieval, and fine-grained interdisciplinary literature identification.

questions.original_query: Citation graph is a good tool to find relevant work and to help understand the evolution of the domain. What recent research has been done to analyze scientific discourse and generate citation content using citation networks and related textual information?

query.text: Citation graph is a good tool to find relevant work and to help understand the evolution of the domain. What recent research has been done to analyze scientific discourse and generate citation content using citation networks and related textual information?
query.answer:
Recent work is converging on a <cite id="42a5f3b7-2,8b84b1cd-3,8b84b1cd-6,8e8e9ed2-6">graph-plus-text view of scientific discourse and citation writing</cite>: instead of modeling a citation from only its local sentence, researchers are increasingly combining <cite id="42a5f3b7-2">citation-phrase text with graph embeddings</cite>, <cite id="42a5f3b7-9">knowledge graphs built on citation datasets</cite>, <cite id="8b84b1cd-3">cited text spans that capture inter-document relationships</cite>, and <cite id="8b84b1cd-6">multiple sources of information for more accurate citation text generation</cite>.

On the analysis side, a strong recent theme is <cite id="42a5f3b7-2">citation intent prediction via graph embeddings</cite>. <cite id="42a5f3b7-2">GraphCite (2022) addresses citation intent prediction by going beyond textual clues in the citation phrase and using graph embeddings</cite>, while <cite id="42a5f3b7-9">a 2023 graph-based structure-aware method proposes text-free citation intent classification using a knowledge graph built on top of the SciCite dataset</cite>. Recent work has also moved toward richer supervision: <cite id="07eadeef-3">one line constructs a fine-grained citation graph in which citation intents and their supporting evidence are labeled between citing and cited papers</cite>.

On the generation side, the field has expanded from full related-work generation to finer-grained citation writing. <cite id="8e8e9ed2-1">A 2024 survey notes that, because scientific papers are very long documents, a newer version of related-work generation focuses on generating individual citation texts</cite>. Within that space, <cite id="42a5f3b7-3">Intent-Controllable Citation Text Generation (2022) introduces intent-controllable generation so that different citation texts can be produced according to the author’s citation intent</cite>. <cite id="8b84b1cd-5">Recent citation generation work explicitly frames the task as concisely and accurately describing the relationship between two scientific articles</cite>, and <cite id="8b84b1cd-3">2024 work on cited text spans treats span recognition as crucial for understanding inter-document relationships in scientific literature</cite>. Another recent method <cite id="8b84b1cd-6">improves contextual relevance and accuracy by integrating multiple sources of information</cite>.

There has also been important infrastructure work. <cite id="8b84b1cd-0">CiteBench (2023) unifies multiple diverse datasets and enables standardized evaluation of citation text generation</cite>, which helps compare models across task variants. And for longer-form literature review writing, <cite id="669a3d05-0">the 2024 survey emphasizes that good related-work writing is not a concatenation of generic summaries but a coherent story connecting prior work to the current paper</cite>; correspondingly, <cite id="8e8e9ed2-6">GRASP uses graph-aided reasoning for related-work generation and reports related-work sections that closely match human-written targets</cite>.

So, the recent picture is: <cite id="42a5f3b7-2,42a5f3b7-9,07eadeef-3">citation networks are being used not just for retrieval but for discourse analysis through intent, evidence, and graph structure</cite>, while <cite id="42a5f3b7-3,8b84b1cd-3,8b84b1cd-6,8e8e9ed2-6">citation content generation is becoming more controllable, evidence-grounded, multi-source, and graph-aware</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What recent research has been done to analyze scientific discourse and generate citation content?
fully_underspecified.answer: Recent research has split into two closely related lines. On the analysis side, <cite id="80546d5c-0,80546d5c-1">2025 work on paragraph-level functional structure recognition treats scientific papers as having automatically recognizable functional structures, with the goal of improving fine-grained information retrieval and reducing problems in full-text scholarly search</cite>, and <cite id="80546d5c-2">a 2024 study on PLOS articles reported that deep learning models show promise for paragraph-level structure-function recognition in scientific texts</cite>. On the generation side, <cite id="3b7a4343-0">recent NLP work has formalized citation text generation as the task of producing accurate textual summaries from the citing-paper context plus the papers to be cited</cite>; this now includes <cite id="3b7a4343-2">intent-controllable citation text generation</cite>, <cite id="3b7a4343-3">methods that use cited text spans to concisely and accurately describe relationships between scientific articles</cite>, and <cite id="9b613915-9">frameworks that explicitly model citation intent and retrieve appropriate references for academic citation generation</cite>. The field has become established enough that <cite id="96b08bbc-5">a 2024 survey summarizes the main approaches, task definitions, and open challenges in related-work and citation text generation</cite>.

On the <cite id="56a17d24-0">analysis of scientific discourse</cite> side, <cite id="56a17d24-0">FINECITE (ACL Findings 2025) argues that limiting citation context to the citing sentence “fails to cover the rich information of scientific discourse,” introduces a corpus of “1,056 manually annotated citation contexts,” and reports improvements of “up to 25%” over prior state of the art</cite>; more broadly, <cite id="1b370cc3-7">citation context analysis is used for the syntactic and semantic analysis of citation contexts to understand “how and why” citations are made</cite>. Overall, the trend is toward <cite id="56a17d24-0">richer discourse-aware citation contexts</cite> plus <cite id="16cfbfd8-0">better grounding in cited full text</cite> and <cite id="0eca3260-2">graph/network structure</cite> to produce more accurate analysis and citation content.

questions.original_query: For research paper reading, how can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections for scientific papers with the help of language models?

query.text: For research paper reading, how can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections for scientific papers with the help of language models?
query.answer:
## Short answer

To improve automatic related work generation for scientific papers, the most promising direction is to <cite id="87493039-0">treat it as a multi-stage problem involving retrieval-augmented generation, long-document understanding, and analysis of the relation between the target paper and prior work</cite>, rather than asking a language model to write the whole section in one shot. In practice, that means building systems that first retrieve and rank relevant papers/passages, then generate citation-grounded notes or citation texts, then organize them into a planned outline, and only then draft a coherent section with explicit evidence links and post-generation verification. This design directly addresses the fact that <cite id="cd013ba9-0">a good related work section is not a concatenation of generic summaries, but a coherent story connecting prior work and the current paper</cite>.

## Why one-shot generation is weak

The core difficulty is that related-work writing is a hard synthesis task, not just summarization. The survey on RWG emphasizes that <cite id="cd013ba9-0">writing an RWS is non-trivial</cite> because <cite id="cd013ba9-0">it is insufficient to simply concatenate generic summaries of prior works</cite>; instead, <cite id="cd013ba9-0">composing a coherent story that connects each related work and the current (citing) work</cite> is what authors actually need. That same survey also characterizes RWG as <cite id="87493039-0">a complex task</cite> involving <cite id="87493039-0">retrieval-augmented generation, long document understanding</cite> and relationship analysis.

A second problem is context length. Because <cite id="87493039-2">scientific research papers are very long documents</cite>, the field has increasingly shifted toward <cite id="87493039-2">generating individual citation texts</cite> as a more tractable subproblem. This suggests that better related-work systems should decompose the task into citation- or passage-level units before attempting full-section generation.

## What to change in the system design

### 1) Make retrieval the backbone, not an optional add-on

A related-work generator should begin with strong retrieval over candidate papers, relevant sections, and citation contexts. This follows naturally from the survey’s framing of RWG as a task that includes <cite id="87493039-0">retrieval-augmented generation</cite>, and from broader grounding work showing that <cite id="048fd7df-0">technical solution approaches such as retrieval augmented</cite> methods are central for grounding LLM outputs. The practical implication is to retrieve at multiple granularities: whole papers for coverage, abstracts/intros for positioning, and fine-grained passages for evidence-backed sentence generation.

A retrieval-first design is also supported by recent scientific-synthesis systems. For example, OpenScholar is described as <cite id="048fd7df-1">a specialized retrieval-augmented language model</cite> that works by <cite id="048fd7df-1">identifying relevant passages</cite>. For related-work writing, the analogue is clear: passage retrieval should feed the generator with directly citable evidence rather than expecting the model to rely on parametric memory.

### 2) Decompose generation into citation texts before section drafting

Because full related-work generation is long-context and discourse-heavy, a better approach is to first generate structured citation notes: what the cited paper did, how it differs from the target paper, and which theme it belongs to. This is consistent with the survey observation that <cite id="87493039-2">a new version of the RWG task arose: generating individual citation texts</cite> due to the length of scientific inputs. In other words, section generation should be treated as a composition step over verified citation-level units.

This decomposition helps in at least three ways. First, it reduces hallucination by forcing local grounding. Second, it makes discourse planning easier because the model organizes prepared building blocks rather than inventing everything jointly. Third, it enables targeted human correction at the citation level, which is much more practical for research workflows.

### 3) Add an explicit outline or discourse plan before writing prose

A major weakness of direct LLM generation is poor organization. Recent work outside RWG shows that planning helps long-form generation: <cite id="57aab20e-1">explicit outlines</cite> can guide LLMs toward <cite id="57aab20e-1">goal-oriented, high-quality text</cite>, and other work explicitly <cite id="57aab20e-3">integrate[s] planning into single-turn long-form text generation</cite>. For related work, this means the model should first decide the structure—such as themes, methods, datasets, or limitations—before writing paragraphs.

This is especially important because related-work sections are rhetorical objects, not just information dumps. Since a good RWS should present <cite id="cd013ba9-0">a coherent story that connects each related work and the current (citing) work</cite>, planning should include not only topical grouping but also comparative intent: which prior lines are similar, what gap remains, and how the current paper differs.

### 4) Train or adapt models specifically for grounding and citation generation

A strong system should not merely sound scholarly; it should produce verifiable claims tied to evidence. Grounding research notes that <cite id="048fd7df-0">grounding differs from factuality</cite>, and proposes <cite id="048fd7df-0">technical solution approaches such as retrieval augmented</cite> methods. More directly, AGREE shows that a specialized adaptation framework yields <cite id="dc42930c-2">improved grounding and citation generation</cite>, with <cite id="dc42930c-2">extensive experiments on two LLMs over five datasets demonstrating the effectiveness</cite> of the approach.

For related-work generation, this argues for fine-tuning or preference-optimizing models on tasks where every sentence is backed by retrieved snippets or citation spans. Concretely, the generator should output sentence-level evidence links during drafting, then a checker should verify that each comparative statement is actually supported by the cited passage. This is much safer than letting the model invent comparisons from latent memory.

### 5) Engineer the long-context format, not just the window size

Longer context windows alone are not enough. Recent work on long-context grounding argues for <cite id="048fd7df-2">the overlooked yet critical role of context format</cite> in long-context retrieval-augmented generation. For related-work systems, this means that how retrieved papers are arranged—e.g., grouped by theme, sorted by relevance, accompanied by extracted claims, or aligned against target-paper contributions—can materially affect output quality.

So instead of pasting ten PDFs into a prompt, systems should provide structured context packs. A useful format is: target-paper contribution summary, retrieved paper metadata, extracted contribution sentences, methods, datasets, limitations, and one-line “relation-to-target” notes. That structure better supports synthesis and comparison.

## A practical architecture for better related-work generation

A strong end-to-end pipeline could look like this:

1. **Target-paper analysis:** extract the target paper’s problem, method, data, and claimed contributions.  
2. **Hierarchical retrieval:** retrieve candidate papers, then relevant passages within them.  
3. **Citation-unit generation:** produce grounded citation texts for each selected paper.  
4. **Outline planning:** organize citation units into themes and paragraph order.  
5. **Section drafting:** write prose from the outline while preserving evidence links.  
6. **Grounding verification:** check every claim against retrieved passages and fix unsupported ones.  
7. **Human-in-the-loop revision:** let the researcher edit themes, emphasis, and novelty framing.

This architecture follows directly from the evidence that RWG is <cite id="87493039-0">a complex task</cite>, that long scientific inputs motivate <cite id="87493039-2">generating individual citation texts</cite>, that scientific synthesis benefits from <cite id="048fd7df-1">identifying relevant passages</cite>, and that better grounding and citation generation can be learned via adaptation frameworks such as AGREE <cite id="dc42930c-2">demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed AGREE framework</cite>.

## How to evaluate progress

Improvement should not be measured only by fluency. Because the task is long-form and scientific, evaluation should explicitly test grounding, structure, and usefulness. Recent benchmarking work points to the need for dedicated evaluation frameworks for <cite id="048fd7df-4">long-to-long scientific text generation</cite>, and controllability studies show the value of systematically evaluating <cite id="57aab20e-6">the controllability of large language models</cite>.

For related-work generation, the most important metrics are likely: retrieval recall of truly relevant papers, citation accuracy, sentence-level grounding, thematic organization quality, comparative faithfulness to the source papers, and human judgment of usefulness for researchers. Human evaluation is especially important because a section can be fluent yet still omit the key competing baselines or misstate the novelty gap.

## Bottom line

The best way to improve automatic related-work generation is to stop treating it as a single prompting problem and instead build a grounded scientific-writing pipeline. The evidence suggests combining <cite id="87493039-0">retrieval-augmented generation</cite>, <cite id="87493039-2">citation text</cite> decomposition, <cite id="57aab20e-1">explicit outlines</cite>, and model adaptation for <cite id="dc42930c-2">grounding and citation generation</cite>. In short: retrieve better, plan explicitly, generate at citation level first, ground every claim, and evaluate with scientific-writing-specific criteria.

fully_underspecified.text: How can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections?
fully_underspecified.answer: We can improve automatic related work generation by treating it as more than generic summarization. First, systems should <cite id="9a9ac943-0">combine reference retrieval and related work generation</cite>, because selecting the right papers is a core part of the task. Second, models should be <cite id="6c55314e-4">target-aware</cite>, since a related work section must <cite id="636d0adf-0">connect each related work and the current (citing) work</cite> rather than just list summaries. Third, generators should explicitly plan <cite id="628ceeb6-0">structure</cite> and <cite id="628ceeb6-0">novelty statements</cite>, because good related work sections are <cite id="628ceeb6-0">properly structured</cite> and <cite id="628ceeb6-0">clearly described novelty</cite>. Fourth, retrieval-augmented, citation-grounded generation should be used to improve faithfulness, since specialized RAG systems for scientific synthesis <cite id="9cb5c8dd-0">identify relevant passages</cite> and can achieve <cite id="9cb5c8dd-4">citation accuracy on par with human experts</cite>. Finally, progress depends on better benchmarks and metrics: recent work argues for <cite id="628ceeb6-0">automatic evaluation metrics for structure and novelty</cite> and validates them with <cite id="628ceeb6-0">human evaluation</cite>.

without_preference.text: How can we improve the automatic generation of related work sections for scientific papers with the help of language models?
without_preference.answer: We can improve LM-based related-work generation by designing systems that <cite id="c3ac2f88-1">treat RWG as a complex task involving retrieval-augmented generation, long document understanding, and query-focused multi-document summarization</cite>, instead of plain summarization. A stronger pipeline should <cite id="86d28e93-1,c3ac2f88-2">combine reference retrieval and related work generation in a unified framework based on the large language model</cite>, then <cite id="8976014f-1">generate structured related work with novelty statements</cite> rather than a flat text block. It should also use <cite id="90ee142c-5">retrieval-augmented, structure-aware models with a focus on citation information</cite> so that claims are better grounded in the literature. questions.original_query: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue due to residual optical absorption in the integrated optomechanical devices?

query.text: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue due to residual optical absorption in the integrated optomechanical devices?
query.answer: Some practical ways to address this are to <cite id="c7a3de95-1">redesign the device to reduce optical absorption and improve thermal anchoring</cite>, since <cite id="74c145ca-1">residual optical absorption can set the ultimate performance limit in integrated optomechanical systems</cite>. In particular, <cite id="504161a4-0,25aed24c-2">typical suspended optomechanical structures suffer from poor thermal anchoring</cite>, so using <cite id="c7a3de95-2">two-dimensional optomechanical-crystal geometries with increased thermal anchoring</cite> or <cite id="c7a3de95-0">release-free geometries developed to further improve thermal anchoring</cite> can help carry heat away. Another route is <cite id="28959017-4">choosing materials with low absorption and very high thermal conductivity, such as diamond</cite>, because <cite id="28959017-3">diamond’s low nonlinear optical absorption increases the allowed optical intensity</cite>. So, in short: improve heat sinking/thermal anchoring, reduce absorption through device design and fabrication, and use low-loss, high-thermal-conductivity materials like diamond.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue?

without_scope.text: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue due to residual optical absorption in integrated optomechanical devices?
without_scope.answer: Some of the main ways to overcome residual-absorption heating in integrated optomechanical devices are to <cite id="f5ba22c0-1,4472007b-7">use pulsed optical excitation/readout instead of continuous-wave drive, since pulsed operation is specifically used to study and limit transient heating</cite>; to <cite id="4bc40b1c-0,4bc40b1c-2,4472007b-2,4bc40b1c-9">improve thermal anchoring by moving away from poorly anchored suspended structures toward two-dimensional or release-free optomechanical crystals, whose better anchoring helps dissipate thermal phonons generated by optical absorption heating</cite>; and to <cite id="3dddbb30-5,4bc40b1c-5">reduce parasitic optical absorption itself, including absorption in coupling waveguides, by using lower-absorption platforms/fabrication approaches</cite>. In cryogenic systems, <cite id="e3eb62d7-0">good packaging and thermalization are also important because reduced thermal anchoring can otherwise cause prohibitive optical-absorption heating</cite>. A key caveat is that <cite id="e3eb62d7-1,e3eb62d7-7">optical absorption heating can increase faster as temperature is lowered</cite>, so <cite id="e3eb62d7-0,4bc40b1c-9">cryogenic operation works best when combined with strong thermal anchoring and low optical absorption</cite>.

query.answer: <cite id="75dfb965-0">One demonstrated cryogenic method is vertical coupling using grating couplers together with angle-polished fibers</cite>, since one study <cite id="75dfb965-0">demonstrate[d] a fiber-chip coupling technique, based on grating couplers and angle-polished fibers, and use[d] it for cryogenic measurements</cite>. query.text: What are ways to modulate the gigahertz surface acoustic waves?
query.answer: Ways to modulate gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs) include <cite id="9ab27f2f-0">electrical control on lithium niobate, which can modulate the phase and amplitude of traveling acoustic waves and even realize frequency shifting by serrodyne phase modulation</cite>; <cite id="fed89123-0">thermal control using on-chip microheaters, which locally change temperature to control SAW phase and can also produce amplitude modulation with acoustic Mach–Zehnder interferometers</cite>; and <cite id="c6344793-0">structural/phononic-crystal engineering, where local modulation of SAW phononic crystals creates band-gap-supported cavities or waveguides that capture and guide SAWs</cite>. There is also evidence for <cite id="c6344793-3">coherent control of gigahertz surface acoustic phonon modes</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are ways to modulate surface acoustic waves?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="da459146-0,da459146-2">SAWs can be modulated electrically by using the electro-acoustic effect to control the phase velocity of travelling acoustic waves on piezoelectric platforms such as lithium niobate.</cite> <cite id="340a98c7-3">They can also be modulated structurally with phononic crystals, which tailor the dispersion relation and transmission of acoustic waves.</cite> <cite id="340a98c7-0">Optical methods are another route: ultrafast laser excitation can generate high-frequency SAWs on nanoscale patterned surfaces.</cite> <cite id="4b11ff40-0,4b11ff40-3">Surface loading is a major modulation mechanism as well—added mass, viscosity changes, elastic-modulus variations, and other boundary-condition changes shift SAW frequency, phase, or velocity.</cite> <cite id="4b11ff40-2">Finally, temperature changes and electrical loading can also shift SAW resonance and therefore modulate the wave response.</cite>
