questions.original_query: What discoveries have been made regarding the topological charge corresponding to bound states in the continuum?

query.text: What discoveries have been made regarding the topological charge corresponding to bound states in the continuum?
query.answer: Research on optical bound states in the continuum (BICs) has shown that <cite id="9aabb778-4,83948dba-5">BICs are vortex centers in the polarization directions of far-field radiation and carry conserved, quantized topological charges.</cite> In symmetry-preserved photonic crystal slabs, <cite id="989f11e4-1,9aabb778-7">these BICs were further identified as topological defects of polarization vortices with integer topological charges,</cite> and later work found that <cite id="83948dba-3">topological-charge conservation makes fundamental BICs tunable as structural parameters vary, enabling controlled merging of multiple BICs.</cite> This picture was also <cite id="9aabb778-3">experimentally confirmed through the observation of a polarization vortex at an optical BIC.</cite> More recently, the concept has been extended beyond simple integer charges: <cite id="83948dba-0">vectorial topological charge was introduced to capture the full set of BIC polarization properties,</cite> and <cite id="9aabb778-0">its multicomponent nature was shown to let a BIC split into multiple pairs of half-integer pseudopolarization singularities under perturbation.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What discoveries have been made regarding the charge corresponding to bound states?
fully_underspecified.answer: If you mean the well-known physics literature on topological or solitonic bound states, the main discovery is that <cite id="de031a10-0,de031a10-2">certain zero-energy bound states can exhibit charge fractionalization</cite>. In particular, <cite id="de031a10-5">the occurrence of a fractional fermion number was first pointed out by Jackiw and Rebbi in 1976</cite>, and the Jackiw–Rebbi model is <cite id="de031a10-2">credited with predicting zero-energy bound states and charge fractionalization</cite>. In later realizations, this bound-state charge is often identified as <cite id="de031a10-1">a topological fractional charge of \(e/2\)</cite>.

questions.original_query: What physical platforms can be used to study the quantum properties of phonons?

query.text: What physical platforms can be used to study the quantum properties of phonons?
query.answer: Researchers study quantum phonons on several major hardware platforms. <cite id="5dce6d44-2">Trapped-ion crystals have collective modes of vibration, whose excitations are considered phonons</cite>, so trapped ions are one established platform for phonon-based quantum experiments. <cite id="542de8c0-5">Opto- and electromechanical platforms are also used for quantum state preparation and entanglement of mechanical systems</cite>, making nanomechanical and cavity-optomechanical resonators another key class. In hybrid solid-state devices, <cite id="8ddf91d1-5">coupling a superconducting qubit to a bath of piezoelectric surface-acoustic-wave phonons enables a platform for investigating open quantum systems</cite>. More broadly, <cite id="3c148a0e-0">surface acoustic waves coupled to quantum dots, trapped atoms and ions, and point defects have been proposed as quantum transduction platforms</cite>, so <cite id="8ddf91d1-0">quantum dots, trapped ions/atoms, nitrogen-vacancy centers, and superconducting qubits</cite> can all serve as physical platforms for studying the quantum properties of phonons.

fully_underspecified.text: What platforms can be used to study properties?
fully_underspecified.answer: If you mean real estate property research, common platforms include Zillow, Redfin, Realtor.com, and Trulia for residential properties, plus LoopNet for commercial properties. You can also use county assessor / property appraiser websites, GIS parcel maps, and local MLS-based brokerage sites to study ownership, tax history, parcel details, and recent sales. If you want, I can also break this down by purpose—finding comps, ownership records, rents, tax data, or commercial analysis.

questions.original_query: Which quantum states of phonons have been successfully prepared?

query.text: Which quantum states of phonons have been successfully prepared?
query.answer: Experiments have successfully prepared several kinds of phonon quantum states. In trapped-ion motional modes, researchers <cite id="d30e8c44-4">have created and analysed thermal, Fock, squeezed, coherent, Schrödinger-cat states, and other superpositions of Fock states</cite>. In mechanical resonators, <cite id="d09ef401-0">a mechanical resonator has been prepared in its quantum ground state and controlled at the single-phonon level</cite>, and <cite id="d09ef401-1">single quantum excitations (phonons) in the resonator</cite> have been created. More recently, trapped-ion experiments have also <cite id="24bab6b3-3">experimentally demonstrate[d] the generation of entangled coherent states with the two-dimensional motion of a trapped ion system</cite>. So the prepared phonon-state families include <cite id="d30e8c44-4">thermal, Fock/number, coherent, squeezed, Schrödinger-cat, and other Fock-state superpositions</cite>, plus <cite id="d09ef401-0,d09ef401-1">ground and single-phonon states</cite> and <cite id="24bab6b3-3">entangled coherent phonon states</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Which states have been successfully prepared?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="ceabf428-1">Schrödinger's cat states have been successfully prepared</cite> <cite id="2e802a6b-0">in various physical systems</cite>. \boxed{\text{Schrödinger's cat states}}

questions.original_query: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher network to a student network?

query.text: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher network to a student network?
query.answer: <cite id="S11,P2">In standard knowledge distillation, “dark knowledge” is the information in the teacher’s soft output distribution beyond the one-hot correct label—especially the relative probabilities assigned to incorrect classes.</cite> <cite id="P1,P3,P8">Those non-target probabilities encode how similar or plausible different classes are for a given input, so the student learns the teacher’s class relationships and uncertainty structure, not just the final answer.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What is the knowledge that gets distilled in knowledge distillation, where information is transferred from one network to another?
fully_underspecified.answer: In classic knowledge distillation, the “knowledge” is mainly the teacher model’s <cite id="9537ecb2-9">soft target</cite> output distribution rather than just hard labels: <cite id="dd2e0a44-3">the most popular response-based knowledge for image classification is known as soft targets … soft targets are the probabilities that the input belongs to</cite> each class. These softened probabilities encode <cite id="dd2e0a44-2">“almost all the knowledge”</cite> because they reveal inter-class similarities and uncertainty—often called <cite id="9537ecb2-4">“dark knowledge” of the soft target</cite>. More broadly, later KD methods also transfer other signals such as <cite id="288cd70f-1">the neural response</cite> and, in some variants, <cite id="288cd70f-5">feature based</cite> or <cite id="288cd70f-5">logic based</cite> information.

without_scope.text: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher network to a student network?
without_scope.answer: <cite id="9196a65e-2">In the standard Hinton-style formulation of knowledge distillation, the distilled “dark knowledge” is contained in the teacher’s soft targets</cite>—that is, <cite id="609188fb-3">the relative probabilities of incorrect answers</cite>, which <cite id="609188fb-3">tell us a lot about how the cumbersome model tends to generalize</cite>. Put differently, the student is trained to match not just the hard correct label, but <cite id="9196a65e-3">the teacher's relative confidence in those answers and its mistakes</cite>; this hidden information in the non-argmax class probabilities is what is meant by <cite id="9196a65e-1">dark knowledge</cite>.

without_term.text: What exactly is the "dark knowledge" that gets distilled in the standard formulation of knowledge distillation, wherein information is transferred from a teacher model to a student model?
without_term.answer: <cite id="d3d2127a-2">This "dark knowledge", which is practically invisible in the class probabilities, defines a similarity metric over the classes</cite>. In the standard knowledge-distillation setup, what gets distilled is therefore <cite id="d3d2127a-9">the teacher's relative confidence across classes</cite>—especially the information carried by the non-argmax / wrong-class probabilities, i.e. the softened output distribution rather than just the hard label. <cite id="d02aeeca-5">The popular name for the signal carried in those wrong-class probabilities is "dark knowledge"</cite>.

questions.original_query: Can classifier-free guidance be extended beyond conditional diffusion models in image generation to NLP tasks?

query.text: Can classifier-free guidance be extended beyond conditional diffusion models in image generation to NLP tasks?
query.answer: Yes. <cite id="76a374eb-0">Classifier-free guidance was originally proposed as a post-training way to trade off mode coverage and sample fidelity in conditional diffusion models.</cite> But it has also been extended to NLP settings: <cite id="f702fc5a-6">the IJCAI 2023 paper “Diffusion Models for Non-autoregressive Text Generation” explicitly discusses training with classifier-free guidance</cite>, and <cite id="76a374eb-5">a separate work on “Classifier-free Diffusion Models for Machine Translation” explores diffusion models with classifier-free guidance for neural machine translation.</cite> So the answer is yes—<cite id="f702fc5a-6,76a374eb-5">CFG has moved beyond image generation into diffusion-based NLP tasks such as text generation and machine translation</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Can guidance be extended beyond models in generation to tasks?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="S6">Yes—recent generative-model work argues that guidance can move beyond model-internal or classifier-based signals to task objectives.</cite> <cite id="S6">A unified training-free framework says guidance can use “arbitrary differentiable objective functions,” enabling “task-specific control without retraining.”</cite> <cite id="S8">Another summary of the same line of work says it “generalizes guidance beyond classifier and model-based methods by allowing arbitrary differentiable task objectives at inference time.”</cite> <cite id="S9">Related work on Universal Guidance likewise states that gradients from external losses can steer sampling, enabling “flexible conditioning and inverse-problem solving.”</cite>

without_scope.text: Can classifier-free guidance be extended beyond conditional diffusion models to NLP tasks?
without_scope.answer: <cite id="2c3e6bb4-2">Yes—classifier-free guidance has been extended beyond conditional diffusion models to NLP.</cite> <cite id="2c3e6bb4-2">EleutherAI’s “Stay on topic with Classifier-Free Guidance” reports that CFG “can be used broadly as an inference-time technique in pure language modeling,”</cite> and <cite id="6e81eb26-2">the paper states that it applies CFG “to the decoding” process of language models.</cite> It has also appeared in other NLP generative settings: <cite id="6e81eb26-0">“Classifier-free Diffusion Models for Machine Translation” describes CFG as an approach where the model learns conditional data distributions itself,</cite> and <cite id="6e81eb26-3">a machine-translation benchmarking paper notes that DiffuSeq uses CFG “to model a conditional diffusion process.”</cite> So the answer is that <cite id="2c3e6bb4-2,6e81eb26-0">CFG is not limited to its original conditional image-diffusion use; it has been adapted to language modeling and MT-style NLP tasks as well.</cite>

without_term.text: Can guidance without a classifier be extended beyond conditional diffusion models in image generation to natural language processing tasks?
without_term.answer: Yes. <cite id="20131cf5-1">The authors demonstrate that CFG, which has primarily been used in text-to-image generation, can bring improvements in pure language modeling.</cite> More specifically, <cite id="cefb81fd-2">this paper adapts the classifier-free guidance from text-to-image diffusion model into text generation to have better control on the generation</cite>, and related work also applies it to NLP tasks such as <cite id="20131cf5-0">machine translation</cite> with diffusion language models. Therefore, guidance without a classifier has indeed been extended beyond image generation into NLP.

questions.original_query: In knowledge distillation, the teacher model is typically a larger (more powerful) network than the student model. Has there been work showing that the teacher model is size-matched or smaller (but perhaps more targeted in knowledge) than the student model, and for knowledge transfer to still be effective?

query.text: In knowledge distillation, the teacher model is typically a larger (more powerful) network than the student model. Has there been work showing that the teacher model is size-matched or smaller (but perhaps more targeted in knowledge) than the student model, and for knowledge transfer to still be effective?
query.answer: Yes. <cite id="74f78e39-0">Born-Again Neural Networks demonstrates that knowledge distillation between networks of identical architecture and capacity consistently enhances performance</cite>, and related self-distillation work likewise states that <cite id="0f144cc3-0">in self-distillation, both teacher and student models have the same network architecture</cite>. There is also evidence for the teacher being smaller than the student: <cite id="b23c5cf2-0">Noisy Student Training extends distillation using equal-or-larger student models</cite>, and the CVPR version emphasizes <cite id="b23c5cf2-6">using student models that are as large as (if not larger than) the teacher</cite>, while still <cite id="b23c5cf2-6">improv[ing] ImageNet classification</cite>. Finally, for “more targeted knowledge” rather than raw size, <cite id="856782b4-3">single-task models effectively teach a multi-task model</cite>, and that approach <cite id="2366ddc6-0">consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training</cite>. So the answer is clearly yes: effective transfer has been shown with size-matched teachers, with smaller teachers, and with specialist teachers whose advantage is task focus rather than scale.

fully_underspecified.text: Has there been work showing that the teacher model is size-matched or smaller than the student model, and for knowledge transfer to still be effective?
fully_underspecified.answer: Yes. Born-Again Multi-Task Networks reports a “born-again” setting where the student has the same model architecture as the teacher, and Born-Again Networks found that these students can “outperform their teachers”. More broadly, recent self-distillation work explicitly studies distillation from a single-model teacher to a single-model student with identical architecture. There is also work with a smaller teacher than the student: “Distillation from Weak Teacher (DWT)” is defined as transferring knowledge from a smaller, weaker teacher model to a larger student, and the paper states that this framework “facilitates enhancing larger student models through knowledge transfer from smaller, weaker” teachers. So the answer is: yes, both size-matched and smaller-teacher distillation have been shown to be effective.

without_scope.text: In knowledge distillation, the teacher model is typically a larger (more powerful) network than the student model. Has there been work showing that the teacher model is size-matched or smaller (but perhaps more targeted in knowledge) than the student model, and for knowledge transfer to still be effective?
without_scope.answer:
Yes. There is published work showing that <cite id="4d8028a1-2">the teacher and student can be identically parameterized</cite> and KD still helps: in Born-Again Networks, <cite id="4d8028a1-1">these Born-Again Networks (BANs), outperform their teachers significantly</cite>. Related self-distillation work likewise reports that <cite id="4d8028a1-5">a distinguished student model which outperforms its teacher model remains rare</cite> but proposes a framework that <cite id="4d8028a1-3">notably enhances the performance (accuracy) of convolutional neural networks</cite>, again without requiring a larger teacher.

There is also evidence for effective transfer from a smaller teacher in some settings. In Teacher Assistant distillation, Mirzadeh et al. report that <cite id="975a7d16-1">a student model distilled from a teacher with more parameters (and better accuracy) performs worse than the same one distilled from a smaller teacher</cite>. This motivated using <cite id="975a7d16-0">multiple teacher assistants that gradually decreases the model size</cite> to improve distillation across large teacher–small student gaps.

So the short answer is: <cite id="4d8028a1-1,4d8028a1-2,975a7d16-1">yes—both size-matched teachers and, in some cases, smaller/intermediate teachers have been shown to transfer knowledge effectively.</cite>

questions.original_query: Data selection has emerged as an important problem for training good language models (i.e., which datapoints to include). Has there been any research on the ordering of datapoints for LMs (i.e., easy to hard curriculum sequence of data points), such that a LM may be trained in a more sample-efficient manner?

query.text: Data selection has emerged as an important problem for training good language models (i.e., which datapoints to include). Has there been any research on the ordering of datapoints for LMs (i.e., easy to hard curriculum sequence of data points), such that a LM may be trained in a more sample-efficient manner?
query.answer: <cite id="8fffe42a-0,74026031-1">Yes—there is now explicit research on ordering LM training data via curriculum learning.</cite> <cite id="74026031-1,cfe96d95-7">This area was relatively underexplored until recently, but newer work studies easy-to-hard pretraining schedules directly for LLMs.</cite> For example, <cite id="74026031-0">recent LLM-pretraining curricula rank examples by a difficulty metric and then either strictly order data or split it into difficulty groups with pacing functions</cite>; <cite id="74026031-1">one systematic study trained over 200 models on up to 100B tokens across vanilla curriculum learning, pacing-based sampling, and interleaved curricula</cite>. The main takeaway so far is encouraging: <cite id="cfe96d95-1">curriculum learning consistently outperforms random data shuffling, particularly in the early and middle stages of training</cite>, and <cite id="cfe96d95-2">it can reduce the number of training steps needed by about 18–45%</cite>. So the short answer is <cite id="74026031-2">yes: data ordering has been studied for LMs, and evidence suggests it can improve sample/training efficiency</cite>, though the literature is still emerging.

fully_underspecified.text: Has there been any research on the ordering of data points for language models, such that a model may be trained in a more sample-efficient manner?
fully_underspecified.answer: Yes. <cite id="69842306-0">Curriculum learning (CL) ... improves model convergence and performance by ordering</cite> training samples by difficulty, and this idea has been studied for language models and closely related sequence models. In neural machine translation, <cite id="6ca812f0-1">a curriculum learning framework for NMT ... reduces training time</cite> and <cite id="6ca812f0-8">can help improve the training time and the performance of both recurrent neural network models and Transformers</cite>. For modern LLM pretraining, recent work reports that <cite id="a6e5a2cb-1">data ordering ... provides a practical mechanism for more efficient LLM</cite> pretraining, and that <cite id="a6e5a2cb-0">curriculum learning consistently outperforms random data shuffling, particularly in the early and middle stages</cite>. There is also LM-specific work on smaller models, where <cite id="895b7d0b-2">training language models using CL will lead to better performance compared to conventional training</cite>. So the short answer is: yes—this line of research exists, and it is usually discussed under curriculum learning, data ordering, or competence-based training.

without_scope.text: Has there been any research on the ordering of datapoints for language models, such as an easy-to-hard curriculum sequence, so that a language model may be trained in a more sample-efficient manner?
without_scope.answer: Yes. <cite id="f4eeee44-3">Recent work explicitly studies curriculum learning for language model pretraining, i.e., organizing training data from easy to hard</cite>, and <cite id="f3427deb-0">there is also work that systematically examines pretraining data ordering as an independent design variable for transformer-based language models</cite>. For example, <cite id="f4eeee44-0">“Irreducible Curriculum for Language Model Pretraining” proposes a curriculum algorithm for LM pretraining</cite> that <cite id="f4eeee44-1">prioritizes samples with higher learnability scores before lower-score samples</cite>; its reported results <cite id="e4360631-0">consistently outperform a baseline random order and an anti-curriculum on average 5-shot accuracy</cite>. Likewise, <cite id="f4eeee44-3">“Beyond Random Sampling: Efficient Language Model Pretraining via Curriculum Learning” frames curriculum learning as easy-to-hard ordering for LM pretraining</cite>, and its experiments <cite id="f4eeee44-4">consistently improve convergence in early and mid-training phases and can yield lasting gains</cite>, suggesting better training efficiency. That said, the literature is not uniformly positive: <cite id="f3427deb-1">analysis work notes that it is still unclear whether curriculum learning truly changes the learning trajectory or mainly reorders what the model would learn anyway</cite>, and <cite id="f3427deb-4">some LM-focused studies describe prior results as mixed</cite>. So the short answer is: <cite id="cb439737-3">the easy-to-hard curriculum idea has been around since classic curriculum learning work</cite>, and <cite id="f4eeee44-3,e4360631-0,f3427deb-0">there is now direct research applying it to language models, with evidence of improved convergence/sample efficiency in some settings, but not yet a universal consensus.</cite>

without_term.text: Data selection has emerged as an important problem for training good language models (i.e., which datapoints to include). Has there been any research on the ordering of datapoints for language models (i.e., easy to hard curriculum sequence of data points), such that a language model may be trained in a more sample-efficient manner?
without_term.answer: Yes—there is a real line of research on <cite id="f3ad0ded-8,f3ad0ded-3">curriculum learning, i.e., ordering training data from easier to harder</cite>, and it has been applied specifically to language models. For LM pretraining, <cite id="9ded2cb5-0">Campos (2021) explored “various linguistically motivated curricula” for language-model pretraining and transfer</cite>, although <cite id="9ded2cb5-1">that work reported “no clear improvement” overall</cite>. More recent results are more encouraging: <cite id="d8da8d50-0">one paper states that curriculum learning “improves stability and efficiency of language model pre-training”</cite>, <cite id="a4c6a045-0">a length-based curriculum for LM pretraining reported 1.5× faster convergence and better downstream performance</cite>, and <cite id="d8da8d50-1">a later study describes itself as the “first systematic investigation of curriculum learning in LLM pretraining”</cite> with <cite id="2ac3937e-2">improved convergence in early and mid-training phases</cite>. So the short answer is: <cite id="d8da8d50-0,a4c6a045-0,d8da8d50-1">yes, people have studied easy-to-hard ordering for language models, and there is evidence it can improve training/sample efficiency, though the benefits are not uniformly guaranteed across setups</cite>.

without_preference.text: Has there been any research on the ordering of datapoints for language models, such as easy-to-hard curriculum sequences, to make training more sample-efficient?
without_preference.answer: Yes. <cite id="b8353c87-0">Recent work explicitly studies curriculum learning for LLM pretraining, where data are organized from easy to hard based on a difficulty metric.</cite> <cite id="b8353c87-1">A 2025 paper reports “the first systematic investigation of curriculum learning in LLM pretraining,” training over 200 models on up to 100B tokens,</cite> and <cite id="f8823833-0,f8823833-1">finds consistent early- and mid-training convergence gains, with the goal of faster convergence and better best-model performance.</cite> Earlier LM-specific work also exists: <cite id="f8823833-6">the 2021 paper “Curriculum Learning for Language Modeling” explored linguistically motivated curricula for LM pretraining,</cite> but <cite id="574bf86a-0">reported no clear improvement over non-curriculum baselines.</cite> More specialized settings have shown benefits too—for example, <cite id="dce5b7b7-0">a 2024 study on small code language models found that a well-designed curriculum significantly improves accuracy.</cite> So the short answer is: <cite id="574bf86a-3">yes, there is research on ordering LM training data for sample/training efficiency, but the empirical evidence is mixed rather than uniformly positive.</cite>

questions.original_query: One desirable property for LMs is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the LM can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate LM confidence judgments?

query.text: One desirable property for LMs is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the LM can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate LM confidence judgments?
query.answer: Recent work on calibrating LM confidence includes both broad overviews and concrete methods. <cite id="d7511d63-0">Geng et al.’s 2024 survey, *A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in Large Language Models*, systematically categorizes confidence estimation and calibration techniques for LLMs.</cite> As motivation, <cite id="d7511d63-2">Xiong et al. find that LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident.</cite> Representative method papers include: <cite id="da6fb2b6-1">Zhao et al. (2024), *Fact-and-Reflection (FaR) Improves Confidence Calibration of Large Language Models*, which proposes a two-step prompting method that first elicits relevant known facts.</cite> <cite id="47e02f43-1">Zhang et al. (2024), *Calibrating the Confidence of Large Language Models by Eliciting Fidelity*, which decomposes LM confidence into uncertainty about the question and fidelity to the generated answer.</cite> <cite id="53739894-0">Han et al. (2024), *Enhancing Confidence Expression in Large Language Models Through Learning from Past Experience*, which aims to align expressed confidence with the true probability that an answer is correct.</cite> <cite id="5299ccda-0,5299ccda-1">Xiao et al. (2025), *Restoring Calibration for Aligned Large Language Models*, which studies how preference alignment harms calibration and proposes a calibration-aware fine-tuning approach.</cite> <cite id="3f5e2cca-0,3f5e2cca-1">Hu et al. (2025), *Rewarding Doubt*, which uses reinforcement learning to directly fine-tune LLMs to express calibrated confidence estimates alongside answers.</cite> And <cite id="4a7ab620-0">Bodhwani et al. (2025), *A Calibrated Reflection Approach for Enhancing Confidence Estimation in LLMs*, which presents a reflection-based framework for better confidence estimation.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate confidence judgments?

without_scope.text: One desirable property for LMs is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the LM can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some works that seek to properly calibrate LM confidence judgments?
without_scope.answer: Some representative works on calibrating LM confidence judgments include the following. <cite id="650eda0b-3">Geng et al.’s survey, *A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in Large Language Models*, provides a broad overview of confidence-estimation and calibration methods for LLMs.</cite> <cite id="4db309d7-2">Tian et al.’s EMNLP 2023 paper, *Just Ask for Calibration*, studies how to extract calibrated confidence scores from RLHF-tuned LMs</cite> and <cite id="bee9435c-4">reports that verbalized confidence from models such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Claude can be better calibrated than some alternatives.</cite> <cite id="35c878a5-0">Zhao et al.’s *Fact-and-Reflection (FaR) Improves Confidence Calibration of Large Language Models* proposes a two-step prompting method that improves LLM calibration.</cite> <cite id="650eda0b-4">Wang et al.’s *Calibrating Verbalized Confidence with Self-Generated Rationales* targets calibration of verbalized confidence estimates for LLM outputs.</cite> <cite id="650eda0b-2">Mastakouri et al.’s *Calibration of Language Model Confidence Scores for Generative Question Answering* finds that QA binning and scaling-QA-binning can reduce QA calibration error relative to elicited confidence and other baselines.</cite> Overall, these works span <cite id="650eda0b-1">both training-based and training-free calibration methods for LLMs.</cite>

without_term.text: One desirable property for language models is that they should be well-calibrated, in that the model can generate a confidence score that is well-calibrated to how likely its decision is actually correct. What are some recent works that seek to properly calibrate model confidence judgments?
without_term.answer:
Some recent papers on calibrating language-model confidence include:

- <cite id="51880b15-1">Tian et al. (EMNLP 2023), *Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback*, which focuses on eliciting calibrated confidence scores from RLHF-tuned LMs.</cite>
- <cite id="d36fbff5-0">Xiong et al. (ICLR 2024), *Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs*, which evaluates how well LLMs can express uncertainty via confidence elicitation.</cite>
- <cite id="236333b6-4">Kapoor et al. (2024), *Calibration-Tuning: Teaching Large Language Models to Know What They Don't Know*, which proposes a finetuning protocol to make LLMs output calibrated probabilities.</cite> <cite id="68ee7d19-8">The paper reports superior calibration performance on a variety of question-answering tasks.</cite>
- <cite id="68ee7d19-1">Krishnan et al., *Enhancing Trust in Large Language Models with Uncertainty Calibration Fine-Tuning*, which introduces an uncertainty-aware causal language-modeling loss for calibration-focused finetuning.</cite>
- <cite id="8ea81a4a-0,8ea81a4a-1">R-Tuning: Instructing Large Language Models to Say “I Don’t Know” improves models’ ability to answer known questions, refrain on unknown ones, and reports enhanced confidence calibration.</cite>
- <cite id="68ee7d19-4">Mastakouri et al. (2025), *QA-Calibration of Language Model Confidence Scores*, which introduces “QA-calibration” so confidence scores better reflect correctness within semantically related answer groups.</cite>

A useful way to think about this literature is that <cite id="68ee7d19-3">earlier work often used prompting-based confidence elicitation</cite>, while newer work adds <cite id="236333b6-4,68ee7d19-1">calibration-specific finetuning objectives</cite> and <cite id="68ee7d19-4">task-specific post-hoc calibration methods.</cite>

questions.original_query: Social bias in large language models is an endemic problem, as models often inherit and amplify stereotypical judgments due to naturally occurring, yet undesirable statistical associations from training corpora. What are some recent techniques on post-trained, aligned LMs that mitigate social bias?

query.text: Social bias in large language models is an endemic problem, as models often inherit and amplify stereotypical judgments due to naturally occurring, yet undesirable statistical associations from training corpora. What are some recent techniques on post-trained, aligned LMs that mitigate social bias?
query.answer:
## Recent post-training / alignment techniques A prominent recent line is preference-optimization-based debiasing. In BiasDPO, the authors employ Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to mitigate gender, racial, and religious biases in LLM-generated English text by developing a loss function that favors less biased over biased completions. They also build a manually designed dataset for training LLMs to recognize and correct biases, and report substantial reductions in biased outputs on Phi-2. A second family is inference-time activation steering, which operates on already aligned/chat models without another full fine-tune. FairSteer is a novel inference-time debiasing framework without requiring customized prompt design or model retraining; it assumes fairness-related features can be encoded into separable directions in the hidden activation space, then performs biased activation detection, debiasing steering vector (DSV) computation, and dynamic activation steering. The paper reports superiority of FairSteer across question-answering, counterfactual input evaluation and open-ended text generation tasks on six LLMs. A third family is self-debiasing / self-correction prompting. Recent work argues that LLMs can effectively self-correct their biased outputs through simple prompt, and task-specific follow-ups similarly propose a Self-Correction framework tailored to bias evaluation task that has potential in debiasing LLMs' responses. Related 2025 work further finds that clarifying intentions is essential for effectively reducing biases in LLMs through Self-Correction, suggesting that better self-reflection prompts can matter. That said, recent evidence also cautions that prompt-based debiasing in LLMs can be brittle. One 2025 study finds that prompt-based is often superficial, that some models misclassified over 90% of unbiased content as biased, and that the apparent gains of prior methods may reflect flawed evaluation metrics. So, among post-trained aligned LMs, the most credible recent mitigation strategies are: preference optimization, activation-space steering at inference time, and structured self-correction/self-debiasing prompts, with the last category needing especially careful evaluation.

In short: BiasDPO-style preference tuning, FairSteer-style dynamic activation steering, and self-debiasing/self-correction prompting are some of the clearest recent techniques for mitigating social bias in post-trained, aligned LMs.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some recent techniques that mitigate bias in language models?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Some recent techniques for mitigating bias in language models include:

- <cite id="68dd0eab-6">guiding prompts that explicitly direct the model to avoid stereotypes or engage in step-by-step reasoning</cite>, along with prompting-based methods such as <cite id="a5705fa0-0">Self-Reflection, Self-Awareness, [and] Self-Help</cite>.
- <cite id="ee5a77c3-6">zero-shot self-debiasing</cite> and <cite id="ee5a77c3-1">a progressive framework designed to instill intrinsic self-correction capabilities</cite>.
- Data-centric methods such as <cite id="ee5a77c3-0">a double data augmentation strategy</cite> and <cite id="ee5a77c3-2">Context-CDA</cite>, which <cite id="ee5a77c3-2">effectively mitigates bias without sacrificing language modeling performance</cite>.
- Training-time approaches like <cite id="67386a20-3">an adversarial training strategy designed to mitigate biases originating from pre-training data by improving model robustness</cite>.
- Alignment/fine-tuning methods such as <cite id="b9df2db8-0">fairness-aware fine-tuning methods</cite> and reward-learning approaches where <cite id="b9df2db8-2">FARO ... adds fairness constraints directly into the reward model fine-tuning process during preference learning</cite> or <cite id="b9df2db8-1">Fairness-Aware Offline RLHF</cite> is used to <cite id="b9df2db8-1">integrate fairness constraints into Offline Reinforcement Learning</cite>. This is especially relevant because <cite id="a5705fa0-1">instruction tuning and RLHF significantly amplify cognitive biases in language models</cite>.
- Representation-level debiasing, where <cite id="67386a20-1">small biased and anti-biased expert models</cite> are used to <cite id="67386a20-1">obtain a debiasing signal that will be added to the</cite> base model.

Broadly, recent work groups these into <cite id="67386a20-0">pre-processing, in-training, [and] post-processing</cite> interventions.

without_scope.text: What are some recent techniques on post-trained, aligned LMs that mitigate social bias?
without_scope.answer: Recent work on already post-trained/aligned LMs uses several <cite id="ccba6d56-1">post-processing</cite> or post-hoc debiasing strategies. One is <cite id="546eba3e-0">BiasDPO, a framework employing Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to mitigate gender, racial, and religious biases</cite> by <cite id="546eba3e-4">favoring less biased over biased completions</cite>. Another is <cite id="7ac61861-0">Social Contact Debiasing (SCD), based on the Contact Hypothesis</cite>, which aims <cite id="7ac61861-1">to debias LLMs by simulating various forms of social contact</cite>. A third family is self-editing at inference time: <cite id="62d127a3-3">self-debiasing via explanation and self-debiasing via reprompting</cite>, as well as <cite id="62d127a3-1">intent-aware self-correction</cite> that <cite id="62d127a3-1">divides self-correction into instruction, response, and feedback</cite> and finds that <cite id="62d127a3-2">clarifying intentions is essential for effectively reducing biases</cite>. Finally, recent post-hoc model editing includes <cite id="7ac61861-4">BiasUnlearn</cite>, where <cite id="7ac61861-4">BiasUnlearn outperforms existing methods in mitigating bias in language models while retaining language modeling capability</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the differences between encoder-decoder and causal/non-causal decoder-only LMs?

query.text: What are the differences between encoder-decoder and causal/non-causal decoder-only LMs?
query.answer: <cite id="6f42939f-0">Encoder-decoder models (for example, T5/BART) use two modules: an encoder to understand the input and a decoder to generate the output</cite>; <cite id="ba0e57f2-0">the decoder also has encoder-decoder attention, where queries come from the decoder and attend to the encoder’s representations</cite>. By contrast, <cite id="92c49a95-5,91d4850a-3">standard decoder-only LMs such as GPT-2 are causal/unidirectional autoregressive models</cite>, so <cite id="92c49a95-0,92c49a95-1">they are especially suited to text generation</cite>. A “non-causal decoder-only” model is not the usual GPT setup; it typically means a PrefixLM-style variant where <cite id="bebc5555-4">the prefix can use bidirectional attention while generation over the target remains causal</cite>, though <cite id="bebc5555-0">this kind of decoder-only bidirectional attention can have caching drawbacks</cite>. For full bidirectional context everywhere, the more standard design is encoder-style modeling such as BERT, where <cite id="91d4850a-7">BERT is explicitly a bidirectional Transformer representation model</cite>. Thus, the core differences are: <cite id="6f42939f-0,ba0e57f2-0">separate encoder plus decoder with cross-attention</cite> vs. <cite id="92c49a95-5">a single autoregressive decoder stack</cite>, and <cite id="91d4850a-3,91d4850a-7,bebc5555-4">left-to-right causal attention</cite> vs. <cite id="91d4850a-7,bebc5555-4">bidirectional/non-causal attention over some or all tokens</cite>.

questions.original_query: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in NLP. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language methods that have worked well?

query.text: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in NLP. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language methods that have worked well?
query.answer: Some of the strongest recent <cite id="1bbf6e0c-4">task-agnostic</cite> pruning methods for LLMs are <cite id="6273acc9-2">SparseGPT</cite>, <cite id="341d1108-2">Wanda</cite>, <cite id="c1f21809-4">SliceGPT</cite>, and <cite id="1bbf6e0c-0">LLM-Pruner</cite>. <cite id="6273acc9-2,6273acc9-0">SparseGPT is the first accurate one-shot method that works efficiently for 10B–100B+ parameter models and can prune GPT-family models to at least 50% sparsity</cite>. <cite id="341d1108-2,f1046338-2">Wanda is an unstructured pruning method that uses both weights and activations to estimate importance, and it significantly outperforms simple magnitude pruning while remaining competitive with heavier methods</cite>. <cite id="c1f21809-2,c1f21809-4">SliceGPT is a post-training structured method that deletes rows and columns to reduce model size, with reports of up to 25% parameter reduction without significant performance loss</cite>. <cite id="1bbf6e0c-0,1bbf6e0c-4">LLM-Pruner is a structural pruning framework that removes non-critical coupled structures based on gradient information and is explicitly presented as task-agnostic compression using only a small public post-training set</cite>. If you want the shortest practical shortlist, <cite id="6273acc9-2">SparseGPT</cite> and <cite id="341d1108-2">Wanda</cite> are the standard one-shot baselines, while <cite id="c1f21809-2">SliceGPT</cite> and <cite id="1bbf6e0c-0">LLM-Pruner</cite> are strong choices when you want structured pruning with actual architecture shrinkage.

fully_underspecified.text: What are some pruning methods that have worked well?
fully_underspecified.answer: Some pruning methods that have worked well are <cite id="3144da52-1,3144da52-2">magnitude-based pruning</cite>, <cite id="c09465b3-7,dd054690-3">iterative magnitude pruning (IMP)</cite>, <cite id="400c1bf4-1,400c1bf4-8">movement pruning</cite>, and <cite id="dd054690-0,dd054690-1,dd054690-9">structured pruning such as filter/channel pruning</cite>. In particular, <cite id="3144da52-1,3144da52-2">surveyed work reports that magnitude-based pruning often converges faster than magnitude-agnostic methods</cite>. For pretrained models and transfer learning, <cite id="c09465b3-4,400c1bf4-1,400c1bf4-8">movement pruning is often better than plain magnitude pruning, especially at high sparsity</cite>. And if your goal is actual wall-clock speedup rather than just sparsity, <cite id="c09465b3-0,dd054690-0,dd054690-1">structured pruning is the most reliable choice because only structured pruning is said to achieve universal neural network acceleration without special hardware or software</cite>.

without_scope.text: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in NLP. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language models that have worked well?
without_scope.answer:
Some of the strongest recent <cite id="48b19e27-2,48b19e27-3,d9c0516c-3,78c1117b-0,860605fc-3,9a59eb8b-6,9a59eb8b-8">general or task-agnostic LLM pruning methods</cite> are:

- <cite id="d9c0516c-3,d9c0516c-0">**SparseGPT**: the first accurate one-shot pruning method that works efficiently for 10B–100B+ parameter models, and it can prune GPT-family models to at least 50% sparsity in one shot.</cite>
- <cite id="48b19e27-2,48b19e27-4">**Wanda**: an unstructured method that uses both weights and activations as pruning signals; it substantially beats plain magnitude pruning and is competitive with SparseGPT.</cite>
- <cite id="9a59eb8b-6">**LLM-Pruner**: a structural pruning method that removes non-critical coupled structures using gradient information.</cite>
- <cite id="860605fc-3,48b19e27-8,860605fc-7">**FLAP**: a training-free structured pruning method that achieves strong results across language benchmarks and significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art structured pruning methods.</cite>
- <cite id="78c1117b-0,78c1117b-1,78c1117b-3">**SliceGPT**: a dense compression method that deletes rows and columns to reduce embedding dimension; it can remove up to 25% of parameters while retaining about 99% and 90% zero-shot task performance.</cite>
- <cite id="9a59eb8b-8">**MaGrIP**: a newer explicitly task-agnostic neuron-pruning method that uses magnitude and gradient information with a dual-threshold strategy.</cite>

In practice, <cite id="48b19e27-2,d9c0516c-3">**Wanda** and **SparseGPT** are the go-to post-training unstructured baselines</cite>, while <cite id="860605fc-3,9a59eb8b-6,78c1117b-0">**FLAP, LLM-Pruner, and SliceGPT** are strong structured/dense alternatives when actual wall-clock or hardware efficiency matters more than just parameter sparsity.</cite>

without_term.text: Pruning is a means of model compression that can improve model efficiency in natural language processing. What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language models that have worked well?
without_term.answer:
Some recent <cite id="b27001af-3,d6507ba5-4">general, task-agnostic</cite> LLM pruning methods with strong reported results are:

- <cite id="988a594f-1">Wanda, an unstructured pruning method for LLMs that uses both weights and activations as proxies</cite>; <cite id="afffc11a-6">it outperforms magnitude pruning by a large margin and competes favorably with SparseGPT</cite>.
- <cite id="a29a3229-2">SparseGPT, the first accurate one-shot pruning method reported to work efficiently at the scale of 10–100+ billion parameters</cite>; <cite id="a29a3229-5">it showed GPT-family models can be pruned to at least 50% sparsity in one shot</cite>.
- <cite id="b27001af-0">LLM-Pruner, a structural pruning method that removes non-critical coupled structures based on gradient information</cite>; <cite id="b27001af-3">its authors explicitly describe it as task-agnostic compression</cite>, and <cite id="8c01074c-3">a fine-tuned LLaMA-5.4B reached 62.36% average accuracy versus 63.25% for the original LLaMA-7B</cite>.
- <cite id="744ebf5a-8">FLAP, a retraining-free structured pruning framework for LLMs</cite>; <cite id="744ebf5a-0,744ebf5a-1">it achieved strong benchmark results and significantly outperformed LLM-Pruner and structured Wanda without retraining</cite>.
- <cite id="d6507ba5-1">SliceGPT, a post-training method that replaces weight matrices with smaller dense matrices by deleting rows and columns</cite>; <cite id="d6507ba5-4">it is framed as task-agnostic LLM compression</cite>, and <cite id="d6507ba5-0">one sliced model retained 90.3% of the original performance with about 2.2B parameters</cite>.

So, a good recent shortlist is <cite id="988a594f-1,afffc11a-6,a29a3229-2,a29a3229-5,b27001af-0,b27001af-3,744ebf5a-8,744ebf5a-1,d6507ba5-1,d6507ba5-4">Wanda, SparseGPT, LLM-Pruner, FLAP, and SliceGPT</cite>.

without_preference.text: What are some recent general, task-agnostic pruning methods for large language models that have worked well?
without_preference.answer:
Some strong recent <cite id="7d4ce8b4-2">task-agnostic</cite> or broadly applicable LLM pruning methods to look at are:

- <cite id="d7a776c4-1">Wanda</cite>: <cite id="d7a776c4-1">an unstructured pruning method for large language models that uses both weights and activations to estimate importance.</cite>
- <cite id="8174f80b-0,8174f80b-2">SparseGPT</cite>: <cite id="8174f80b-2">the first accurate one-shot pruning method that works efficiently at the scale of 10–100B-parameter models</cite>, and <cite id="8174f80b-0,8174f80b-1">it can prune GPT-family models to at least 50% sparsity, with reasonable perplexity even at 80% sparsity.</cite>
- <cite id="7d4ce8b4-1,7d4ce8b4-2">LLM-Pruner</cite>: <cite id="7d4ce8b4-1">the first framework specifically designed for structural pruning of LLMs while maintaining task performance</cite>, with <cite id="7d4ce8b4-2">task-agnostic compression</cite>.
- <cite id="7d4ce8b4-5,7d4ce8b4-8">FLAP</cite>: <cite id="7d4ce8b4-8">its zero-shot capability was evaluated across seven downstream tasks</cite>, and <cite id="7d4ce8b4-5">it achieves remarkable performance on a variety of language benchmarks.</cite>
- <cite id="8174f80b-3,8174f80b-5">SliceGPT</cite>: <cite id="8174f80b-3">it consistently outperforms existing structured sparsity approaches</cite>, and <cite id="8174f80b-5">can remove up to 25% of model parameters while maintaining 99%, 99%, and 90% of zero-shot task performance for the reported settings.</cite>
- <cite id="7774c933-0,7774c933-5">SlimGPT</cite>: <cite id="7774c933-0">a low-cost and fast structured pruning method</cite> that <cite id="7774c933-5">outperforms other methods and achieves state-of-the-art results on the LLaMA benchmark.</cite>

If you want the shortest practical shortlist, <cite id="d7a776c4-1">Wanda</cite> and <cite id="8174f80b-0,8174f80b-2">SparseGPT</cite> are strong one-shot baselines, while <cite id="7d4ce8b4-1,7d4ce8b4-2">LLM-Pruner</cite>, <cite id="7d4ce8b4-5,7d4ce8b4-8">FLAP</cite>, <cite id="8174f80b-3,8174f80b-5">SliceGPT</cite>, and <cite id="7774c933-0,7774c933-5">SlimGPT</cite> are notable structured options.

questions.original_query: Has there been any direct head-to-head comparison of techniques that involve learning from human feedback, e.g., DPO vs PPO vs SimPO (preferably under a fixed compute budget)?

query.text: Has there been any direct head-to-head comparison of techniques that involve learning from human feedback, e.g., DPO vs PPO vs SimPO (preferably under a fixed compute budget)?
query.answer: <cite id="5aff0496-0">Yes—there are direct head-to-head comparisons, but mostly in pairs rather than a single clean PPO-vs-DPO-vs-SimPO benchmark.</cite> <cite id="5aff0496-0">The original DPO paper reports that DPO “matches or improves response quality” relative to PPO-based RLHF and says DPO is “computationally lightweight.”</cite> <cite id="4e2d8c49-0">A later NeurIPS 2024 study (“Unpacking DPO and PPO”) systematically investigates preference-learning components and reports that PPO outperforms DPO by up to 2.5% in math and 1.2% in general domains.</cite> <cite id="53f6548f-1">That same study explicitly compares DPO and PPO “when the same base models and data are used,” so it is a reasonably controlled apples-to-apples comparison, though the snippet does not say it is under a fixed compute budget.</cite> <cite id="ba480d53-0">For SimPO, the primary comparison is against DPO and related variants, not PPO:</cite> <cite id="2239ab47-0">the SimPO paper reports that SimPO outperforms DPO by up to 6.4 points on AlpacaEval 2 and 7.5 points on Arena-Hard.</cite> So the short answer is: <cite id="5aff0496-0,4e2d8c49-0,2239ab47-0">yes for DPO↔PPO and SimPO↔DPO head-to-heads, but I did not find a primary-source three-way PPO↔DPO↔SimPO comparison under an explicitly fixed compute budget.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: Has there been any comparison of techniques that involve learning from feedback?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="b3813004-0">Yes—there are explicit comparisons of feedback-learning techniques in the literature.</cite> <cite id="b3813004-0">For example, a recent DPO survey says it “start[s] by comparing DPO with RLHF” to highlight DPO’s advantages and limitations.</cite> <cite id="e886222b-0">There is also a dedicated 2024 paper, *Is DPO Superior to PPO for LLM Alignment? A Comprehensive Study*, that directly compares DPO with PPO-based RLHF.</cite> <cite id="5861dd63-1">And the original DPO paper positions DPO against existing RLHF methods by arguing that it optimizes the same objective as RLHF while avoiding explicit reward modeling and reinforcement learning.</cite>

without_scope.text: Has there been any direct head-to-head comparison of techniques that involve learning from human feedback, e.g., DPO vs PPO vs SimPO?
without_scope.answer:
Yes. <cite id="487ab465-4">A NeurIPS 2024 paper (“Unpacking DPO and PPO”) directly evaluates PPO and DPO using “exactly the same models and initial training data” and reports that “PPO outperforms DPO across varied datasets.”</cite> <cite id="938210bb-0">The SimPO paper directly compares SimPO against DPO “across various state-of-the-art training setups.”</cite> And <cite id="e83a2669-3">at least one later study (“DPO Meets PPO”) explicitly compares against both RL-free methods “(DPO, SimPO)” and the standard online RL method “(PPO),”</cite> so there are now true head-to-head studies that include all three families in one experimental frame. 

The main caveat is that <cite id="938210bb-0">SimPO’s original paper is primarily SimPO-vs-DPO</cite> while <cite id="487ab465-4,143ea67e-5">the best-known controlled comparisons are PPO-vs-DPO.</cite> So the literature does contain direct comparisons, but the most rigorous and influential ones have mostly been pairwise rather than one universally accepted PPO-vs-DPO-vs-SimPO benchmark.

without_term.text: Has there been any direct head-to-head comparison of techniques that involve learning from human feedback, e.g., one method vs another vs another (preferably under a fixed compute budget)?
without_term.answer: Yes. <cite id="37e4bb9c-2">A 2024 study benchmarks DPO and PPO across “a collection of RLHF testbeds, ranging from dialogue to code generation.”</cite> There are also <cite id="ff8427e2-0">head-to-head comparisons among DPO variants that train “the zephyr-sft-full model with DPO, IPO, KTO”</cite>, and <cite id="4a83cade-0">Hugging Face reports that “DPO and IPO can achieve comparable results, outperforming KTO in a paired preference setting.”</cite> So the short answer is: <cite id="37e4bb9c-2,ff8427e2-0">yes, direct one-method-vs-another comparisons do exist</cite>. The main caveat is that, from the snippets retrieved here, the clearest evidence is <cite id="ff8427e2-0">same-model benchmarking</cite> rather than an explicitly stated <cite id="37e4bb9c-2">fixed-compute-budget</cite> protocol.

without_preference.text: Has there been any direct head-to-head comparison of techniques that involve learning from human feedback, such as DPO vs PPO vs SimPO?
without_preference.answer: <cite id="S17,S19">Yes—there have been direct head-to-head comparisons of these human-feedback alignment methods.</cite> <cite id="S19">For example, *Zephyr* says it “conduct[s] a preference alignment study comparing DPO and IPO with standard methods like PPO on two open models”</cite>, and <cite id="S17">another empirical study compares “DPO with PPO and other preference learning algorithms across four popular open-weight models, over three datasets”</cite>. <cite id="S23">For SimPO, the *SimPO* paper reports direct comparisons against DPO and says its experiments show “superior performance of SimPO over DPO”</cite>. <cite id="S33">And for all three together, *SPO: SimPO Meets PPO* explicitly says it is “the first to compare DPO, SimPO, and PPO in online RLHF”</cite>. <cite id="S26,S28">So the answer is yes, although the winner depends on the setup: some studies report PPO scaling very well with more rollout data, while others find DPO outperforming PPO in most tested settings.</cite>

questions.original_query: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only LMs. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only LMs, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this architecture?

query.text: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only LMs. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only LMs, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this architecture?
query.answer:
Yes. <cite id="eac96f18-0,7034ddb9-0">SimCTG (“A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation”) explicitly introduces a contrastive training objective for neural text generation</cite>, and <cite id="7034ddb9-2">reports that the trained model is “less confusing when making next token predictions,” leading to improved performance</cite>. There is also direct evidence on causal/decoder-only LMs specifically: <cite id="100e4322-0">CONTRA-CLM is a “contrastive learning framework” for causal language models at both token and sequence levels</cite>, and <cite id="100e4322-0">it reports that improving representation expressiveness “also boosts the source code generation capability” with a “9% relative improvement on execution accuracy on the HumanEval benchmark”</cite>. 

So the short answer is: <cite id="100e4322-0,eac96f18-0">yes—recent work shows that adding contrastive learning to causal, decoder-only LMs can improve generative performance, not just embedding quality</cite>. A useful distinction is that <cite id="7ea5b2d1-3">contrastive decoding also improves generation quality for frozen LMs</cite>, but that is an inference-time method rather than contrastive *training*.

fully_underspecified.text: Have there been any works showing that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this type of model?
fully_underspecified.answer: Yes. <cite id="9087ecfd-0">Google’s XMC-GAN uses cross-modal contrastive learning for text-to-image generation and reports that it “creates more realistic generated images” and “outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches in both image quality and text alignment.”</cite> <cite id="9ae25d28-0">Another text-to-image paper explicitly proposes “a contrastive learning approach to improve the quality and enhance the semantic consistency of synthetic images,” and says experiments on three benchmarks show effectiveness against state-of-the-art methods.</cite> <cite id="11121458-0">It is not limited to image generation either: CONT adds a contrastive objective to MLE-based neural text generation and reports improved results on machine translation, summarization, and image captioning.</cite> <cite id="9e1ce7b9-0">More recently, diffusion-based text-to-image work has also found that introducing a contrastive loss can “enhance generation quality and compositionality” and outperform prior approaches.</cite> So, <cite id="9087ecfd-0,9ae25d28-0,11121458-0,9e1ce7b9-0">there is clear prior evidence that contrastive learning can improve generative performance when integrated into generative models.</cite>

without_scope.text: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only LMs. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only LMs, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance?
without_scope.answer:
Yes. <cite id="446807f8-1">CONTRACLM is presented as “an effective contrastive learning approach that enhances both the generation and discrimination capability of causal language models.”</cite> <cite id="6c0f52cc-0">The ACL 2023 paper further states that CONTRACLM “enhances the discrimination of representations … which makes causal language models better suited” for downstream use</cite>, indicating that contrastive training is useful even for decoder-only/causal LMs.

A prominent earlier example is <cite id="041a2607-0">SimCTG, which proposes “a novel training framework … for open-ended text generation.”</cite> Its contrastive objective is designed <cite id="6ff6b8f2-3">“to encourage diversity while maintaining coherence”</cite>, and the reported results say <cite id="041a2607-4">“SimCTG achieves the best perplexity with more discriminative representations”</cite>. In the accompanying materials, <cite id="224f6415-3">SimCTG is described as calibrating the model representation space, while contrastive search generates “diverse and coherent text”</cite>.

So the short answer is: <cite id="446807f8-1,041a2607-0">yes—there are works, especially SimCTG and CONTRACLM, showing that contrastive objectives can improve generative behavior in causal/decoder-only language models.</cite>

without_term.text: Contrastive learning is an effective technique for learning good discriminative embedding representations, and was a popular training strategy for encoder-only language models. With the recent popularity of causal, decoder-only language models, have there been any works which show that contrastive learning can also help improve generative performance for this architecture?
without_term.answer: Yes. <cite id="172a6dd4-2">SimCTG proposed “a novel training framework” for open-ended text generation</cite> with <cite id="91bbc6dc-0">“a contrastive training objective to calibrate the model's representation space”</cite>. <cite id="68b0e4a0-8">CoNT adds “an additional contrastive learning objective” for “auto-regressive neural text generation models”</cite> and <cite id="68b0e4a0-3">reports that it “outperforms the MLE based training method on five generation tasks”</cite>. For explicitly decoder-only causal LMs, <cite id="d7d23b9a-1">ContraCLM introduces token-level and sequence-level contrastive learning for causal language models</cite>, and <cite id="d7d23b9a-8">describes this as enhancing “both the generation and discrimination capability of causal language models”</cite>. So, <cite id="68b0e4a0-8,d7d23b9a-8">there are indeed works showing that contrastive learning can improve generative performance in autoregressive / decoder-only language models</cite>.

questions.original_query: What methods can be used to simulate Binary Black Holes in numerical relativity?

query.text: What methods can be used to simulate Binary Black Holes in numerical relativity?
query.answer: <cite id="1f4ac818-1,b60e6318-4">One major method for simulating binary black holes in numerical relativity is to evolve Einstein’s equations in generalized-harmonic coordinates.</cite> <cite id="6fd8fa1b-2,1f4ac818-8">Another widely used method is the moving-puncture approach, which has become an important tool for long-term binary-black-hole simulations.</cite> <cite id="70b29bf6-4,1f4ac818-7">For treating the black-hole interiors, simulations typically use either moving punctures or singularity excision.</cite> <cite id="70b29bf6-4,f381163f-4">These approaches have been implemented with both finite-difference and spectral numerical codes,</cite> and <cite id="f381163f-8">more recently also with discontinuous-Galerkin methods.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What methods can be used to simulate black holes in relativity?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="2416b0a8-7">Black holes in relativity are usually simulated with numerical relativity</cite>, where Einstein’s equations are evolved in a <cite id="eb556a57-1">3+1 formulation such as ADM or, more commonly, BSSN</cite>, or in the <cite id="eb556a57-7">generalized harmonic formulation</cite>. To handle the singular interior, the main strategies are <cite id="d8277b06-0">excision algorithms</cite> and <cite id="d8277b06-0,87580edb-8">puncture / moving-puncture methods</cite>. For discretization, codes use <cite id="eb556a57-0,eb556a57-5">spectral or pseudospectral methods for black-hole spacetimes</cite> as well as <cite id="69531457-6,69531457-4">finite-difference methods, including for black-hole excision</cite>.

without_term.text: What methods can be used to simulate binary black holes in numerical relativity?
without_term.answer: <cite id="6cf3909a-1,03d58de9-1,299a577f-5">In numerical relativity, binary black holes are mainly simulated using two stable evolution formulations of Einstein’s equations: the BSSN formulation and the generalized-harmonic formulation.</cite> <cite id="03d58de9-1,ea2aee16-0">A standard BSSN-based approach is the moving-puncture method, which is used for binary black hole simulations and supports long-term compact-binary evolutions.</cite> <cite id="299a577f-5,6cf3909a-3">The other major approach is generalized-harmonic evolution, often paired with black-hole excision to handle the hole interiors.</cite> <cite id="6cf3909a-3,299a577f-1,299a577f-6">These systems are then solved numerically with either finite-difference methods or spectral/pseudospectral methods; spectral methods have been used for orbiting and merging binaries and are well suited to binary systems, especially with excision.</cite>

query.text: What messager are combined in multi-messenger astrophysics approach?
query.answer: <cite id="8bd435ac-0">Multi-messenger astrophysics combines electromagnetic radiation, gravitational waves, neutrinos, and cosmic rays.</cite> <cite id="8bd435ac-3">NASA likewise describes the four messengers as light in all its forms, cosmic rays, neutrinos, and gravitational waves.</cite>
