without_scope.answer: Compared with bi-directional encoders, the picture is: <cite id="ef926d03-0">GTR is a T5-encoder bi-encoder baseline</cite>, while <cite id="5499d4d7-6">Contriever is a 110M contrastively trained dense retriever</cite>; against such encoder baselines, <cite id="f48b1350-3,ef926d03-0">RepLLaMA’s 7B decoder-based bi-encoder reaches the top reported InstructIR score of nDCG@10 = 87.62 in a benchmark that includes GTR</cite>, <cite id="7273150f-0">and later summaries note that RepLLaMA outperforms earlier smaller retrieval models</cite>. <cite id="f974e003-0">BMRetriever’s 410M model is reported to beat baselines up to 11.7× larger, and its 2B model matches models above 5B parameters</cite>. So the current evidence suggests that fine-tuned autoregressive/decoder-only backbones are now clearly competitive with—and sometimes better than—strong bidirectional encoder retrievers, <cite id="3f15d5ae-5">but bi-encoders still remain the standard first-stage retrieval choice because of their efficiency advantages</cite>; many of the decoder-only gains also come from larger model scale or extra instruction/domain tuning rather than a universal architectural win.

without_term.text: What are the latest works on finetuning a language model for dense passage retrieval? How are their performance compared with bi-directional encoders?

without_preference.text: What are the latest works on finetuning an auto-regressive LM for dense passage retrieval, and how do they compare with bi-directional encoders?
without_preference.answer:
## Recent autoregressive/decoder-only retriever work

A good timeline of recent work is: <cite id="81556c67-0">RepLLaMA / “Fine-Tuning LLaMA for Multi-Stage Text Retrieval” (2023), which fine-tunes LLaMA “as a dense retriever (RepLLaMA) … for both passage retrieval and document retrieval using the MS MARCO datasets” and reports “strong zero-shot effectiveness” on BEIR</cite>; <cite id="6c2c998b-4">LLM2Vec (2024), which turns a decoder-only LLM into a text encoder via “1) enabling bidirectional attention, 2) masked next token prediction, and 3) unsupervised contrastive learning”</cite>; <cite id="1b41bc7b-0">NV-Embed (2024), which improves decoder-only LLM retrieval embeddings with a latent attention pooling layer, removes the causal mask during contrastive training, and reached “No. 1 on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB)” plus “the highest score of 59.36 on 15 retrieval tasks”</cite>; <cite id="c48537c8-7,375a6ba7-8">GritLM (2024), which “unifies representation and generation training by finetuning a decoder-only LLM” and uses “bidirectional attention for embedding and causal attention for generation”</cite>; <cite id="997b8cc3-0,ee2eb9f2-1">“Scaling Sparse and Dense Retrieval in Decoder-Only LLMs” (2025), a systematic study of dense vs. sparse retrieval and CL/KD objectives in decoder-only LLMs, finding that “Sparse retrieval models consistently outperform dense retrieval” on MSMARCO/TREC DL and BEIR</cite>; and very recent papers such as <cite id="d4db72ac-0">DREAM (2026), which “trains a dense retriever by feeding the retriever’s query-document scores into selected attention heads of a frozen decoder-only LLM”</cite> and <cite id="d4db72ac-2">“Effective Dense Retrieval using Only In-Context Examples” (2026), which notes that “turning decoder-only large language models (LLMs) into strong dense retrievers typically requires some form of retriever training”</cite>.

## How they compare with bi-directional encoders

The main baseline they are competing against is the classic dense-retrieval stack built from <cite id="6c2c998b-0,375a6ba7-3">“backbone encoders” such as BERT and T5, with early encoder-only embedding models “typically built on bidirectional Transformer architectures such as BERT, RoBERTa, or DeBERTa”</cite>. A striking pattern in the newer decoder-only retrievers is that <cite id="6c2c998b-4,1b41bc7b-0,375a6ba7-8">many of the strongest methods partially abandon strict autoregressive behavior by enabling bidirectional attention or removing the causal mask—LLM2Vec does this explicitly, NV-Embed “remove[s] the causal attention mask,” and GritLM uses “bidirectional attention for embedding”</cite>. That is, <cite id="1b41bc7b-0">the best-performing decoder-only retrieval models increasingly look encoder-like during representation learning</cite>, which suggests that bidirectional context is still very valuable for dense passage retrieval.

Performance-wise, the gap has narrowed a lot: <cite id="1b41bc7b-0">NV-Embed states that decoder-only embedding models are “beginning to outperform BERT or T5-based embedding models” on general-purpose embedding tasks including dense retrieval</cite>, and <cite id="81556c67-0">RepLLaMA reports that LLM-based retrieval “surpasses that of smaller models” while also benefiting from longer-context document representations</cite>. But the comparison is not fully settled: <cite id="375a6ba7-0">Causal2Vec (2025) argues that “shifting from causal attention to bidirectional attention is not necessary”</cite>, while <cite id="ee2eb9f2-1">the 2025 scaling study still finds substantial limits for dense retrieval in decoder-only LLMs relative to sparse alternatives</cite>. 

**Bottom line:** <cite id="81556c67-0,1b41bc7b-0,6c2c998b-4">the latest autoregressive-LM retriever work includes RepLLaMA, LLM2Vec, NV-Embed, GritLM, DREAM, and newer 2025–2026 scaling/in-context studies</cite>. <cite id="6c2c998b-4,1b41bc7b-0,375a6ba7-8">Compared with bidirectional encoders, they are now competitive—and sometimes stronger on broad embedding/retrieval benchmarks—but the highest-performing approaches usually add bidirectional-style attention during retriever finetuning, rather than relying on a purely causal/autoregressive encoder</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do people train a long-context Transformer model over 32K context length using sequence parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?

query.text: How do people train a long-context Transformer model over 32K context length using sequence parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
query.answer:
## How sequence parallelism is used for 32K+ context training

For context lengths beyond 32K, the standard idea is to <cite id="2f038e10-0,9f946fa3-7">parallelize along the sequence-length dimension and partition a long sequence into multiple subsets across GPUs</cite>. In NVIDIA/Megatron guidance, <cite id="2f038e10-1">sequence parallelism is enabled with tensor parallelism to reduce activation memory</cite>, while <cite id="2f038e10-1,2f038e10-3">context parallelism is used for long-sequence training by partitioning activations across GPUs</cite>.

A common practical recipe is to use one of the long-context attention variants rather than only classic tensor-parallel training. <cite id="d2a75eff-2">Both Ulysses and Ring Attention enable long-context training</cite>, and recent work <cite id="d2a75eff-0,9f946fa3-3">explicitly studies DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Ring-Attention as the state-of-the-art sequence-parallel approaches and proposes a unified approach</cite>.

## Main methods

### 1) DeepSpeed-Ulysses
DeepSpeed-Ulysses <cite id="9f946fa3-9">partitions input data along the sequence dimension and employs an efficient all-to-all collective communication for attention</cite>. Mechanistically, it <cite id="73c7524e-4">uses all-to-all to change hidden states partitioned along the token dimension to the attention-head dimension</cite>, so attention can be computed normally after the redistribution. Its appeal is that <cite id="73c7524e-2,9f946fa3-1">by trading sequence locality for head locality, it achieves relatively low communication overhead and is communication- and memory-efficient</cite>. Reported systems <cite id="9f946fa3-0">enable efficient training with sequence lengths up to one million</cite>.

The main limitation is architectural: <cite id="73c7524e-1">Ulysses is sensitive to the number of attention heads, and its parallelism degree cannot exceed the number of heads</cite>. That means it is often easiest to use when the model has enough heads and the required sequence-parallel degree is moderate.

### 2) Ring Attention
Ring Attention instead <cite id="73c7524e-3">uses ring-based peer-to-peer communication with a sharded sequence</cite>. Its design target is extreme scale: the original work is titled <cite id="5e7521e-0">“Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context”</cite>, and the paper snippet states it <cite id="5e7521e-1">essentially achieves near-infinite context size</cite>.

In practice, Ring Attention is the contrasting design to Ulysses: instead of all-to-all redistribution around heads, it relies on a ring/P2P schedule over sequence shards. This makes it attractive when the desired context scale is so large that head-limited all-to-all becomes awkward.

### 3) Unified / hybrid sequence parallelism (USP)
Recent work argues these two methods should not be treated as mutually exclusive. The USP paper <cite id="73c7524e-0">organizes SP-Ring and SP-Ulysses in a hybrid parallel manner named USP-Attention</cite>. More concretely, <cite id="f6b04534-2">Ring-Attention operates across columns and Ulysses operates across rows, enabling hybrid parallel strategies</cite>.

This hybridization is motivated by complementary strengths. <cite id="f6b04534-5">Ulysses and Ring-Attention are orthogonal and can be composed arbitrarily, forming hybrid 4D meshes</cite>, and <cite id="4f9d115f-6">Unified-SP has lower communication cost than Tensor Parallel with Megatron-LM sequence parallelism</cite>.

## How the methods are compared

### Communication pattern
The cleanest comparison is by communication topology. <cite id="73c7524e-3,73c7524e-4">Ulysses uses all-to-all to convert token sharding into head-dimension work, while Ring-Attention uses ring-based P2P communication over a sharded sequence</cite>. USP is then compared as a hybrid of those two patterns: <cite id="73c7524e-0,f6b04534-2">it combines SP-Ring and SP-Ulysses in one hybrid arrangement</cite>.

### Scalability limits
Another major comparison axis is how far each method scales. <cite id="73c7524e-1">Ulysses cannot scale its parallelism degree beyond the number of attention heads</cite>, whereas Ring Attention is presented as <cite id="5e7521e-1">achieving near-infinite context size</cite>. This is why papers often position Ulysses as efficient but head-limited, and Ring as more extreme in context scaling.

### Communication/performance trade-offs
The USP comparison summarizes the trade-off succinctly: <cite id="f6b04534-0">DeepSpeed-Ulysses maintains constant communication volume, while Ring-Attention hides P2P communication costs</cite>. Empirically, implementations also report that <cite id="f6b04534-1">if the head number is enough, Ulysses outperforms Ring-Attention</cite>, and that <cite id="f6b04534-1">the all-to-all communication of Ulysses is highly efficient within a single machine</cite>.

### Comparison to older Megatron-style sequence parallelism
These newer methods are also compared against earlier Megatron-style sequence parallelism. One recent comparison states that <cite id="4f9d115f-8">Megatron-SP’s sequence parallelism increases linearly with the sequence length regardless of the number of compute devices</cite>. This is part of the motivation for moving from “activation-memory saving” SP toward explicit long-context methods such as <cite id="2f038e10-1">context parallelism for long sequence training</cite>, Ulysses, Ring, and USP.

## Practical takeaway

For 32K+ training, people usually <cite id="2f038e10-0,9f946fa3-7">shard the sequence itself across GPUs</cite> and then choose the communication scheme that best matches model structure and cluster topology. <cite id="f6b04534-1,73c7524e-1">If the model has enough attention heads and the job fits a fast intra-machine all-to-all, Ulysses is often the stronger choice; its main cap is the head-count limit</cite>. <cite id="5e7521e-1,73c7524e-0">If the target context is much larger or the deployment needs more scalable sequence parallelism, Ring Attention or the hybrid USP design is the usual alternative</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How do people train a model over a long context length using parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
fully_underspecified.answer:
### The basic idea

<cite id="bd23043e-0">Long-context training is hard because attention computation scales quadratically with sequence length, which quickly exceeds GPU memory beyond tens of thousands of tokens.</cite>  
<cite id="35a7333d-4">The common parallelism-based fix is sequence parallelism: split one input sequence into several sub-sequences and compute them on different GPUs/cards in parallel.</cite>  
<cite id="52dfe794-0,52dfe794-4">In the broader “context parallelism” framing, the model shards inputs—and often activations as well—along the sequence-length dimension so attention can be computed in parallel across multiple devices.</cite>

### Main ways people do it

**1) Megatron-style sequence/context parallelism**  
<cite id="52dfe794-1,52dfe794-3">Megatron-LM sequence parallelism is essentially an optimization of tensor-parallel communication, replacing or splitting some all-reduce behavior into all-gather and reduce-scatter on sequence-parallel parts.</cite>  
<cite id="52dfe794-0">Megatron Core’s context parallelism generalizes this idea by partitioning network inputs and activations along the sequence dimension.</cite>

**2) DeepSpeed-Ulysses**  
<cite id="bd23043e-0">Ulysses distributes attention computation across multiple GPUs through attention-head parallelism.</cite>  
<cite id="8de0bc87-4,8de0bc87-5">Operationally, it uses all-to-all communication to transform token-partitioned hidden states into head-partitioned attention work; one description summarizes it as gathering tokens and scattering heads among GPUs.</cite>  
<cite id="35a7333d-3">Its appeal is that it is designed to be communication- and memory-efficient for long-sequence transformer training.</cite>  
<cite id="8de0bc87-1">Its main limitation is that the sequence-parallel degree is bounded by the number of attention heads.</cite>

**3) Ring Attention**  
<cite id="636de2ed-4">Ring Attention distributes long sequences across multiple devices.</cite>  
<cite id="636de2ed-0">It can train sequences up to roughly device-count-times longer than baseline approaches</cite> <cite id="636de2ed-7">and has been reported to enable training large models with over 1M context size with negligible overheads.</cite>  
<cite id="8de0bc87-1">Unlike Ulysses, its scaling is tied to sequence length rather than head count, so it can scale arbitrarily farther in that dimension.</cite>

**4) Hybrid / unified methods (USP)**  
<cite id="ac1245f0-0,35a7333d-1">Recent work explicitly tries to unify DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Ring Attention in one sequence-parallel method, with the goal of overcoming the shortcomings of each individual approach.</cite>  
<cite id="35a7333d-2,8de0bc87-6">These hybrid methods combine Ulysses-style all-to-all communication with Ring-style peer-to-peer communication to exploit the strengths of both.</cite>

### How these methods are compared

<cite id="f35689a5-1,a605bc9e-0">In practice, Ulysses and Ring Attention are often compared directly as two leading long-context training approaches.</cite>  
The main comparison axes are:

**Communication pattern**  
<cite id="8de0bc87-4,8de0bc87-5">Ulysses is characterized by all-to-all communication that swaps token-parallel work into head-parallel work.</cite>  
<cite id="8de0bc87-6">Hybrid USP methods are compared partly by how they mix all-to-all with peer-to-peer communication.</cite>

**Scalability limit**  
<cite id="8de0bc87-1">Ulysses is limited by attention head count</cite>, while <cite id="8de0bc87-1">Ring Attention scales with sequence length.</cite>  
<cite id="636de2ed-0">That is why Ring-style methods are favored when the target context must grow by roughly the number of devices or more.</cite>

**Runtime / communication overhead**  
<cite id="35a7333d-6">One comparison notes that DeepSpeed Ulysses is overall faster, while Ring Attention suffers from too many communications.</cite>  
<cite id="35a7333d-3">Ulysses is also explicitly marketed as communication- and memory-efficient.</cite>

**Achievable context length**  
<cite id="636de2ed-7">Ring Attention is often highlighted for demonstrated million-token-scale training, including reports of over 1M context size.</cite>  
<cite id="bd23043e-0">Ulysses is also used for million-token contexts, but its scaling behavior is constrained by head parallelism.</cite>

### Bottom line

<cite id="52dfe794-0,35a7333d-4">People train over long contexts by parallelizing along the sequence/context axis rather than trying to fit the full token dimension on one GPU.</cite>  
<cite id="8de0bc87-1,35a7333d-6">Ulysses is usually preferred when head-parallel all-to-all gives enough scale and better speed; Ring Attention is preferred when you need sequence-parallel scaling beyond the number of heads, even at higher communication cost.</cite>  
<cite id="ac1245f0-0,35a7333d-1">Current state-of-the-art systems increasingly compare themselves as hybrids that try to combine the efficiency of Ulysses with the scalability of Ring Attention.</cite>

without_scope.text: How do people train a long-context Transformer model using sequence parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
without_scope.answer:
### How long-context training is done with sequence parallelism

<cite id="c11ea7df-0">Sequence parallelism (SP) divides the sequence dimension of input tensors across multiple computational devices</cite>, which <cite id="c11ea7df-0">has become a key way to unlock long-context capabilities in generative AI models</cite>. In practice, teams <cite id="c11ea7df-0">partition input sequences</cite> and then choose a distributed attention algorithm that lets each GPU process only a shard of the tokens while coordinating with the others.

A common baseline is <cite id="a525d5ee-0">Context Parallelism (CP), a parallelization scheme on the sequence-length dimension</cite>. Another widely used method is DeepSpeed-Ulysses: <cite id="a4abeff9-8">it partitions input data along the sequence dimension and uses a one-step Alltoall to gather tokens and scatter heads among all GPUs</cite>. Ulysses is attractive because <cite id="a14af02b-0">it is described as a simple but highly communication- and memory-efficient sequence-parallel approach</cite>, and <cite id="a14af02b-5">its sequence length scales linearly with the number of GPUs</cite>.

The other landmark method is Ring Attention. The Ring Attention paper <cite id="624cce1c-0">proposes a way of implementing softmax dense attention where the attention operation is distributed over multiple GPUs</cite>, and <cite id="624cce1c-3">it leverages blockwise computation of self-attention on multiple GPUs</cite>. Its main benefit is scale: <cite id="624cce1c-2,624cce1c-6">Ring Attention enables training and inference with context size that scales linearly with the number of devices</cite>.

More recent systems combine these ideas. <cite id="2b2240a8-0">USP explicitly investigates DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Ring-Attention and proposes a unified sequence-parallel approach</cite>; the authors say it is <cite id="c11ea7df-0">more robust to transformer model architectures and network hardware topology</cite>. Practitioner summaries also note that <cite id="a4abeff9-2,b3ebd193-6">Ulysses and Ring Attention are not mutually exclusive and can be combined in a hybrid strategy</cite>. Sequence parallelism is usually deployed as part of <cite id="c11ea7df-0">hybrid 4D parallelism involving data, tensor, pipeline, ZeRO, and SP choices</cite>.

### How the methods are compared

The main comparison axes are <cite id="c11ea7df-0">communication cost</cite>, <cite id="c11ea7df-0">memory cost</cite>, and how well a method fits <cite id="c11ea7df-0">transformer model architectures and network hardware topology</cite>. Recent benchmarking work also emphasizes <cite id="b3ebd193-9">communication cost and overlap for Ulysses, Ring-AllGather, Ring-P2P, USP, and LoongTrain</cite>, while systems papers report <cite id="b3ebd193-0">end-to-end training speed and memory use</cite>.

In head-to-head trade-offs, <cite id="2b2240a8-4,a4abeff9-0">DeepSpeed-Ulysses is often faster overall, and if the head number is large enough it can outperform Ring-Attention</cite>. But Ulysses has an architectural limit: <cite id="a4abeff9-3,a4abeff9-4">it requires num_heads ≥ sp_size, so its maximum context/sequence parallelism degree is limited by the number of attention heads</cite>. It can also interact poorly with tensor parallelism because <cite id="a14af02b-8">tensor parallelism partitions the model in the head dimension, so DeepSpeed Ulysses and tensor parallelism are in conflict</cite>.

By contrast, Ring Attention is typically judged as the more scalable ultra-long-context option, but <cite id="2b2240a8-1,b3ebd193-2,2b2240a8-4">it is considered less efficient than Ulysses in computation and communication and can suffer from too many communications</cite>. This is why unified or hybrid methods are popular: they try to keep <cite id="a4abeff9-0">Ulysses’s efficient all-to-all behavior</cite> while still benefiting from <cite id="624cce1c-2">Ring Attention’s linear context scaling with device count</cite>.

A good summary of the current landscape is: <cite id="c11ea7df-0">SP works by sharding the sequence across devices</cite>; <cite id="a4abeff9-8">Ulysses does this with all-to-all token/head redistribution</cite>; <cite id="624cce1c-0,624cce1c-3">Ring Attention does it with distributed blockwise attention over multiple GPUs</cite>; and newer methods such as <cite id="2b2240a8-0,c11ea7df-0">USP unify the two</cite>. Empirically, newer variants can improve results further: <cite id="b3ebd193-0">LoongTrain reports better end-to-end speed and lower memory use than DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Megatron Context Parallelism</cite>.

without_term.text: How do people train a long-context transformer model over 32K context length using sequence parallelism techniques? How are these methods compared with each other?
without_term.answer:
## What people do in practice

To train a transformer at <cite id="c1b88cc5-0">contexts beyond tens of thousands of tokens</cite>, people usually <cite id="177670ed-0">divide the sequence dimension of input tensors across multiple computational devices</cite> so that <cite id="10493163-5">the network inputs and all activations are partitioned along the sequence-length dimension</cite>. This is the core idea behind modern <cite id="177670ed-0">sequence parallelism (SP)</cite> or <cite id="10493163-5">context parallelism (CP)</cite>. The motivation is straightforward: <cite id="c1b88cc5-0">attention computation scales quadratically with sequence length</cite>, so a naive single-GPU implementation quickly runs out of memory once context grows past roughly 32K.

In a full training stack, SP is usually combined with ordinary distributed training tools rather than replacing them. For example, <cite id="7d0d911d-0">DeepSpeed-Ulysses incorporates Flash attention, sparse attention, and ZeRO optimizer</cite>, and <cite id="177670ed-0">USP discusses hybrid 4D parallelism involving sequence parallelism alongside other forms of parallelism</cite>. So the common recipe is: shard tokens across GPUs for activations and attention memory, then still use data/model/pipeline/optimizer sharding as needed for model size and throughput.

## The main sequence-parallel methods

### 1) DeepSpeed-Ulysses

In Ulysses, the model <cite id="7d0d911d-0">partitions input tensors along the sequence dimension</cite> and then <cite id="7d0d911d-0">uses a communication-efficient all-2-all collective for distributed attention computations</cite>. Intuitively, it <cite id="00bba275-2">leverages all-to-all to change the hidden states partitioned along the token dimension to attention head dimension</cite>, which is why one summary describes it as <cite id="f1684cc5-4">trading sequence locality for head locality</cite>. The practical appeal is that <cite id="86c835fa-0">Ulysses requires two all-to-all operations per attention layer</cite> and <cite id="86c835fa-0">benefits from lower latency</cite>.

Its main weakness is a structural limit on parallelism degree. <cite id="00bba275-3">Ulysses requires num_heads >= sp_size</cite>, and equivalently <cite id="00bba275-1">the parallelism degree in Ulysses cannot exceed the number of heads</cite>. That is why Ulysses is often strongest when the model has enough heads and when communication is mostly intra-node, since <cite id="98601cbd-0">if the head number is enough, Ulysses outperforms Ring-Attention</cite> and <cite id="98601cbd-0">the All-to-All communication of Ulysses is highly efficient within a single machine</cite>.

Ulysses has already been used at very large context lengths. DeepSpeed’s tutorial states that <cite id="7d0d911d-0">DeepSpeed-Ulysses can handle sequences up to 1 million in length on 64 A100 GPUs</cite>, which shows how sequence sharding is used in practice for far more than 32K context.

### 2) Ring Attention / context parallelism

Ring Attention is the other major family. The original paper describes it as <cite id="b20d14a8-0">leverag[ing] blockwise computation of self-attention to distribute long sequences across multiple devices</cite>, and LoongTrain summarizes its communication pattern by saying <cite id="10493163-0">Ring-Attention performs context-parallel computation, and organizes communication in a ring fashion</cite>. Another summary notes that <cite id="b20d14a8-1">by cleverly distributing sequence data across multiple devices and overlapping communication with computation, Ring Attention allows context length to scale</cite>.

Compared with Ulysses, Ring Attention is usually more flexible but more communication-heavy. The clearest practical distinction is that <cite id="00bba275-3">Ring Attention has no</cite> <cite id="00bba275-3">num_heads >= sp_size</cite> <cite id="00bba275-3">limitation</cite>, whereas <cite id="86c835fa-0">Ring Attention serializes over P</cite> and therefore tends to pay more in latency/communication steps. This is why practitioners often reach for ring-style CP when they need very large SP degree across many GPUs or across nodes, but prefer Ulysses when head count and topology make all-to-all cheap.

Megatron’s context parallelism is the production-oriented version of this general idea. NVIDIA describes CP as <cite id="10493163-5">a parallelization scheme on the sequence-length dimension</cite> that <cite id="10493163-5">partitions the network inputs and all activations along the sequence dimension</cite>. In practice, that makes Megatron CP a good baseline for long-context training systems, even though papers may differ in whether they benchmark against “Ring Attention,” “context parallelism,” or a specific Megatron implementation.

### 3) Unified/hybrid methods: USP

A newer direction is to combine Ulysses and Ring rather than treat them as mutually exclusive. The USP paper says <cite id="177670ed-0">it investigates the state-of-the-art SP approaches, i.e. DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Ring-Attention, and proposes a unified SP approach</cite> that is <cite id="177670ed-0">more robust to transformer model architectures and network hardware topology</cite>. A concise summary is that <cite id="24dc5cf6-1">USP integrates DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Ring-Attention, overcoming the shortcomings of both</cite>.

The underlying idea is straightforward: use Ulysses where all-to-all is efficient and use ring-style communication where head-count limits or cross-node topology make pure Ulysses awkward. The public implementation describes itself as <cite id="bea61bea-4">a sequence parallel approach that synergizes the strengths of two popular distributed attentions, i.e. DeepSpeed-Ulysses-Attention and Ring-...</cite>. The paper also reports strong efficiency, stating <cite id="177670ed-0">47% MFU on two 8xA800 nodes using SP for LLAMA3-8B model training with sequence length 208K</cite>.

### 4) LoongTrain

LoongTrain is another hybridized long-context training system. Its core proposal is <cite id="bea61bea-8">the 2D-Attention mechanism</cite>, and one summary describes it as <cite id="bea61bea-8">a novel system to efficiently train LLMs with long sequences at scale</cite>. In benchmarking claims, <cite id="bea61bea-5">LoongTrain outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, i.e., DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Megatron Context Parallelism, in both end-to-end training speed and scalability</cite>.

Conceptually, LoongTrain belongs to the same trend as USP: do not rely on a single communication pattern everywhere. Instead, use a more 2D or hybrid decomposition so the system can reduce the bottlenecks seen in pure head-parallel all-to-all or pure ring-based context parallelism. The evidence we retrieved is limited on the exact algorithmic details, but the paper’s stated benchmark position is clear: <cite id="0a75579d-0">LoongTrain outperforms DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Megatron Context Parallelism in both end-to-end training speed</cite>.

## How these methods are compared

### Communication pattern

The first comparison axis is the communication primitive. Ulysses is usually characterized by <cite id="7d0d911d-0">communication-efficient all-2-all</cite> and more specifically <cite id="86c835fa-0">two all-to-all operations per attention layer</cite>, while Ring Attention uses <cite id="10493163-0">communication in a ring fashion</cite> and is often described as <cite id="86c835fa-0">serializ[ing] over P</cite>. That makes Ulysses attractive when low-latency all-to-all is available, and Ring more natural when scaling SP degree without the head-count restriction matters more.

### Parallelism limits

The second axis is scalability constraints. The best-known hard constraint is that <cite id="00bba275-3">Ulysses requires num_heads >= sp_size</cite>, or equivalently <cite id="00bba275-1">the parallelism degree in Ulysses cannot exceed the number of heads</cite>. Ring-style methods are favored when one needs larger sequence-parallel groups because <cite id="00bba275-3">Ring Attention has no such limitation</cite>.

### Hardware topology

The third axis is network topology sensitivity. The USP paper explicitly argues for a design that is <cite id="177670ed-0">more robust to transformer model architectures and network hardware topology</cite>, which is a direct response to the fact that different communication patterns behave differently on intra-node versus inter-node links. The YunChang/USP implementation makes the same practical point more bluntly: <cite id="98601cbd-0">the All-to-All communication of Ulysses is highly efficient within a single machine</cite>, while <cite id="98601cbd-0">if the head number is enough, Ulysses outperforms Ring-Attention</cite>.

### End-to-end efficiency

The fourth axis is empirical efficiency: throughput, latency, MFU, and maximum reachable context length. For Ulysses, public evidence includes <cite id="7d0d911d-0">sequences up to 1 million in length on 64 A100 GPUs</cite>. For USP, the paper reports <cite id="177670ed-0">47% MFU</cite> at <cite id="177670ed-0">208K sequence length</cite>, and for LoongTrain the headline comparison is that <cite id="bea61bea-5">it outperforms DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Megatron Context Parallelism in end-to-end training speed and scalability</cite>.

## A concise takeaway

If you want to train a model above 32K context, the standard move is to <cite id="177670ed-0">shard the sequence dimension across devices</cite> so that <cite id="10493163-5">inputs and activations are partitioned along sequence length</cite>, then choose an attention communication scheme. <cite id="7d0d911d-0">Ulysses</cite> is usually best when <cite id="00bba275-3">num_heads >= sp_size</cite> and all-to-all is fast; <cite id="b20d14a8-0">Ring Attention</cite> is better when you need larger SP groups without the head-count cap; and <cite id="24dc5cf6-1">USP</cite> or <cite id="bea61bea-8">LoongTrain</cite> are attempts to combine the strengths of both and improve robustness and end-to-end performance.

query.text: Could you explain the LLaVA series or variants? How they envolve over time?
query.answer:
A simple way to read the LLaVA family is as a <cite id="237b5b1b-4,237b5b1b-2">progression from image instruction-tuning to broader, unified multimodal models</cite>.

- <cite id="237b5b1b-4">Original LLaVA (2023) introduced visual instruction tuning as the “first attempt to extend instruction-tuning to the language-image multimodal space”</cite>, and <cite id="237b5b1b-2">it combined “a vision encoder and Vicuna” for general-purpose visual-language understanding</cite>.
- <cite id="0481b13f-0,a0988649-5">LLaVA-1.5 (late 2023) was mainly an improved baseline: it made “simple modifications” to the original LLaVA, used only public data, and achieved strong benchmark results</cite>. <cite id="a0988649-2">Its training recipe was also notably efficient, finishing in about one day on a single 8×A100 node</cite>.
- <cite id="3f99f35f-3">LLaVA-NeXT is also called LLaVA-1.6</cite>. <cite id="3f99f35f-0,8b54b46d-0">This version focused on stronger reasoning, better OCR, better world knowledge, and higher-resolution visual input, including “4x more pixels”</cite>.
- <cite id="d3fec4b6-0">LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave extended the line toward more complex multimodal settings; the project reports that “with a single model,” it achieved leading results on multi-image benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="0481b13f-3">Its stated scope explicitly includes multi-image, video, and 3D</cite>.
- <cite id="702b694e-1,8b54b46d-4">LLaVA-OneVision then tried to consolidate these lessons into a unified open LMM family</cite>. <cite id="53f343b3-0,53f343b3-3">The key claim of OneVision is that a single model can perform strongly across single-image, multi-image, and video tasks</cite>.
- <cite id="3f99f35f-1">LLaVA-Video was previously called LLaVA-NeXT-Video</cite>. <cite id="f3fc65e9-1,702b694e-0">It specialized the family for video instruction tuning by introducing LLaVA-Video and training with the LLaVA-Video-178K synthetic dataset, described as a high-quality video instruction-tuning dataset with 178,510 caption entries</cite>.

So, in short, the series evolved from <cite id="237b5b1b-4,237b5b1b-2">a single-image visual assistant</cite> to <cite id="0481b13f-0,a0988649-5">a stronger and more efficient baseline</cite>, then to <cite id="3f99f35f-0,8b54b46d-0">better reasoning/OCR and higher resolution</cite>, and finally to <cite id="d3fec4b6-0,53f343b3-3,f3fc65e9-1">unified multi-image/video models and dedicated video-tuned variants</cite>.

If you want, I can next give you a <cite id="237b5b1b-2,53f343b3-3">variant-by-variant table</cite> with architecture, training data, and what each one is best for.

- <cite id="afff9c54-2">On November 6, 2023, OpenAI announced an updated GPT-3.5-Turbo model that became the default and came with 16k context.</cite>
- <cite id="30fd10de-4,30fd10de-1">GPT-4 was released first in March 2023, and OpenAI described it as a large multimodal model that accepts image and text inputs and emits text outputs.</cite>
- <cite id="30fd10de-4,30fd10de-8">GPT-4 Turbo followed as the next generation of GPT-4, with a 128K context window, and OpenAI positioned it as a cheaper, better version of GPT-4.</cite>
- <cite id="30fd10de-0">GPT-4o then became the new flagship model, designed to reason across audio, vision, and text in real time.</cite>
- <cite id="afff9c54-3,afff9c54-6">GPT-4o mini is the smaller, cost-efficient variant; it has a 128K context window, supports up to 16K output tokens, and OpenAI says it surpasses GPT-3.5 Turbo and other small models on academic benchmarks.</cite>
- <cite id="30fd10de-3">The GPT-4.1 series added major improvements on coding, instruction following, and long context, and it also introduced OpenAI’s first-ever nano model.</cite>
- <cite id="30fd10de-2,30fd10de-5">More recently, OpenAI has also referred to separate reasoning-oriented models such as o1, o3-mini, and o4-mini, while describing GPT-4.5 as a more general-purpose model.</cite>

So, in plain English, <cite id="30fd10de-1,30fd10de-8,30fd10de-0,30fd10de-3">the family evolved from earlier text-centric chat models, to stronger multimodal GPT-4 models, to cheaper long-context variants like GPT-4 Turbo, and then to real-time multimodal models like GPT-4o plus smaller “mini”/“nano” versions and distinct reasoning-focused “o” models.</cite> If you want, I can also turn this into a simple year-by-year timeline or a comparison table of GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 vs GPT-4o vs 4.1/4.5.

without_preference.text: Could you explain the LLaVA series or variants and how they evolved over time?
without_preference.answer:
The LLaVA family evolved from a <cite id="f4404f5e-4">first attempt to use language-only GPT-4 to generate multimodal language-image instruction-following data</cite>, which turned an LLM into a vision-language assistant via <cite id="1588df06-9">an effective visual instruction tuning method to turn Large Language Models (LLMs) into multi-modal LLMs</cite>. In practice, the early LLaVA recipe connected a vision encoder to an LLM and trained it end-to-end for general-purpose visual chat <cite id="cdb254fe-1">as a novel end-to-end trained large multimodal model that combines a vision encoder and Vicuna for general-purpose visual and language</cite>.

LLaVA-1.5 was the next major step. Rather than radically changing the architecture, it focused on better design choices and training: <cite id="1588df06-0">the fully-connected vision-language cross-modal connector in LLaVA is surprisingly powerful and data-efficient</cite>, and the paper framed itself as <cite id="1588df06-5">the first systematic study to investigate the design choices of LMMs in a controlled setting under the LLaVA framework</cite>. So 1.5 is best understood as a stronger, cleaner baseline built from the original LLaVA recipe.

LLaVA-NeXT, often called LLaVA-1.6, pushed capabilities further by improving visual fidelity and downstream reasoning. The official release highlights that <cite id="2af60b9d-2">LLaVA-NeXT has several improvements: Increasing the input image resolution to 4x more pixels</cite>, which was intended to help the model capture more detail for reasoning, OCR, and world knowledge. This stage also broadened the scope of LLaVA from single-image chat toward richer multimodal settings.

After that, the NeXT line expanded into video and interleaved multimodal understanding. The video release states that <cite id="2af60b9d-4">a mixed training regimen of video and image data is essential for optimizing the performance of "LLaVA-NeXT-Video"</cite>, while the later LLaVA-Video work introduced <cite id="e5cd7959-2">LLaVA-Video, a new video LMM</cite> trained with synthetic video instruction data. This reflects a shift from image-only instruction tuning to explicitly temporal multimodal learning.

LLaVA-OneVision is the more unified culmination of these ideas. Its paper presents <cite id="2af60b9d-6">a family of large multimodal models that aims to achieve strong performance across single-image, multi-image, and video</cite>, and describes the model family as <cite id="f4404f5e-1">developed by consolidating our insights into data</cite> (with the full abstract also emphasizing models and training recipes). In other words, OneVision is not just another point release: it is the attempt to make the LLaVA line transfer smoothly across visual task formats instead of treating image, multi-image, and video as separate systems.

So, in one sentence: LLaVA evolved from <cite id="f4404f5e-4">GPT-4-generated visual instruction tuning</cite> for image chat, to <cite id="1588df06-5">stronger controlled baselines</cite> in 1.5, to <cite id="2af60b9d-2">higher-resolution and stronger reasoning</cite> in NeXT/1.6, and finally to <cite id="2af60b9d-6">unified single-image, multi-image, and video understanding</cite> in OneVision.

questions.original_query: What are ways to cool the center-of-mass (CoM) motion of levitated nanoparticles?

query.text: What are ways to cool the center-of-mass (CoM) motion of levitated nanoparticles?
query.answer:
The main ways to cool the center-of-mass motion of levitated nanoparticles are:

1. <cite id="1bd7d61a-3">Feedback cooling, where a damping force is applied in proportion to the particle’s speed</cite>. In practice this includes <cite id="983678a0-2">parametric feedback cooling</cite>, <cite id="1bd7d61a-6">all-optical cold damping</cite>, and <cite id="1bd7d61a-2,983678a0-1">electrical feedback cooling</cite>.

2. <cite id="983678a0-6">Cavity cooling of the center-of-mass motion</cite>, including <cite id="dbc6cbcc-7,983678a0-9">3D cavity cooling of a levitated nanoparticle inside an optical cavity</cite>. This is often implemented as cavity-assisted or sideband cooling.

3. <cite id="5a7b0830-1,dbc6cbcc-0">Sympathetic cooling of the center-of-mass motion</cite>, where the nanoparticle is cooled indirectly by coupling it to another cooled object or mode; for example, <cite id="5a7b0830-0">one nanoparticle can be sympathetically cooled via Coulomb coupling to a second nanoparticle that is feedback cooled</cite>.

More recently, <cite id="983678a0-0,5a7b0830-3">coherent, measurement-free optical feedback</cite> has also been demonstrated as another feedback-based route to CoM cooling.

fully_underspecified.text: What are ways to cool motion of particles?
fully_underspecified.answer: Common ways to cool particle motion include <cite id="39809504-1,39809504-0">laser cooling, especially Doppler cooling, which uses light to slow atoms and can cool gases from room temperature to the microkelvin regime</cite>; <cite id="ceff3aa4-1,ceff3aa4-5">resolved sideband cooling, which is used for tightly trapped atoms or ions and can bring their motion near the ground state, beyond the Doppler limit</cite>; <cite id="2cc8ff13-6,39809504-9">evaporative cooling, where the highest-energy particles leave and the remaining sample becomes colder</cite>; <cite id="2cc8ff13-1">sympathetic cooling, where a hard-to-cool species transfers energy to another species that is easier to cool</cite>; and <cite id="39809504-5,2cc8ff13-2">buffer-gas or collisional cooling, where particles thermalize through collisions with a cold inert gas, with related charged-particle methods such as electron cooling also used in traps</cite>.

questions.original_query: What recent experiments have verified the existence of the Casimir force at the micro- and nanoscale?

query.text: What recent experiments have verified the existence of the Casimir force at the micro- and nanoscale?
query.answer: Recent micro-/nanoscale verification of the Casimir force comes from <cite id="9e5e5449-0">2025 experiments showing that 3D nanostructures can significantly alter the Casimir force, both increasing and suppressing it</cite>, and from <cite id="73d98151-1">a measurement method that aligned and measured the force between two microscale objects on the nanoscale</cite>. Another notable recent result is <cite id="d34856d3-0">a 2024 experiment demonstrating magnetic-field tuning of the Casimir force for a gold sphere and a silica plate immersed in water-based ferrofluids</cite>. In addition, <cite id="14cf442c-0">recent precision work directly measured the Casimir force between a silver-coated microsphere and a gold-coated silicon plate</cite>. These measurements fit into a broader recent experimental literature: <cite id="e5ca2717-0">a 2024 review states that recent advances include precision Casimir-force measurements with non-magnetic and magnetic materials, geometric-dependence measurements, and thermal Casimir-force measurements in graphene</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What recent experiments have verified the existence of a force at small scales?
fully_underspecified.answer: If by “a force at small scales” you mean <cite id="f6bef338-2,1b9553a4-3">gravity</cite>, two recent experiments stand out. In 2021, <cite id="f6bef338-2">an exquisitely sensitive experiment measured force between two tiny spheres</cite>, and <cite id="f6bef338-1,f6bef338-7">showed that Newton’s law of gravity holds even for masses as small as about 90 milligrams, with a gold ball just 2 millimeters wide having its gravitational pull measured</cite>. More recently, in 2024, <cite id="1b9553a4-1,1b9553a4-3">researchers measured a force of around 30 attonewtons on a levitated particle weighing just under half a milligram (about 0.43 mg), which was described as the smallest gravitational pull yet recorded</cite>. So the recent small-scale force experiments that verified a force’s existence were <cite id="f6bef338-2,f6bef338-1,f6bef338-7,1b9553a4-1,1b9553a4-3">tabletop measurements of gravity at millimeter and sub-milligram scales</cite>, rather than confirmation of a new fifth force.

without_scope.text: What experiments have verified the existence of the Casimir force?
without_scope.answer: <cite id="51671b0b-8,c888a202-2">The Casimir force has been verified by several landmark experiments, beginning with Steven Lamoreaux’s 1997 direct measurement in a sphere–plate geometry, which measured the force to within about 5% of the theoretical prediction.</cite> <cite id="1db82d5f-0,1db82d5f-2,1db82d5f-8">This was followed by Mohideen and Roy’s 1998 atomic-force-microscope experiment, which made precision measurements over roughly 0.1–0.9 μm using a gold-coated sphere and flat plate.</cite> <cite id="51671b0b-0,51671b0b-1">Bressi et al. (2002) then provided a quantitative measurement in the original parallel-plate configuration.</cite> <cite id="c888a202-3">Later high-precision confirmations include Decca et al. (2005), who measured the Casimir pressure between two plane plates with a micromachined torsional oscillator.</cite> <cite id="38cfce3b-3">Subsequent experiments have also observed variants such as the thermal Casimir force between two gold plates.</cite>

without_term.text: What recent experiments have verified the existence of the force at the micro- and nanoscale?
without_term.answer: Recent experiments verifying the <cite id="a2d4a39b-0">Casimir force</cite> at micro- and nanoscale include <cite id="f44e49e3-6">precision measurements of the Casimir force from 0.1 to 0.9 micrometers</cite> and <cite id="f44e49e3-6">measurements of the Casimir force between parallel metallic surfaces</cite>. Another key demonstration is that <cite id="a2d4a39b-0">Munday and Capasso measured the Casimir force between two gold surfaces immersed in a fluid, and they experimentally proved that repulsive forces exist</cite>. More recently, nanostructure-based experiments have shown control of the effect: <cite id="a2d4a39b-6">they experimentally demonstrate strong suppression of the attractive Casimir force by nanostructuring one of the interacting surfaces</cite>. Overall, recent reviews describe <cite id="f44e49e3-0">recent advances in precision Casimir force measurements with both non-magnetic and magnetic materials</cite>, showing that the force is now well verified in MEMS/NEMS-relevant micro- and nanoscale setups.

questions.original_query: What are the large systems in which quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated?

query.text: What are the large systems in which quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated?
query.answer:
Examples of comparatively large or macroscopic systems with experimentally demonstrated quantum effects include <cite id="a4e4a28f-8">superconductors and superfluids, which are “macroscopic quantum phenomena” that can be experimentally observed</cite>. This category also includes <cite id="a4e4a28f-1">Josephson/SQUID-type superconducting circuits, where the Josephson effect is a “remarkable example of a macroscopic quantum phenomenon”</cite>.  

Other major examples are <cite id="a4e4a28f-5">Bose–Einstein condensates, in which macroscopic quantum effects have been used in ultrasensitive detectors</cite>; <cite id="02a48348-0,02a48348-1">large molecules and macromolecules, for which high-contrast quantum interference has been demonstrated, including fullerenes, molecular clusters, and tailor-made macromolecules</cite>; and <cite id="dca9ffbf-6,dca9ffbf-3,dca9ffbf-9">mechanical resonators, where experiments have reached the quantum ground state, created single-phonon excitations, generated entanglement between mechanical resonators, and measured non-classical phonon superpositions</cite>. More recently, <cite id="dca9ffbf-2">quantum interference has also been demonstrated for sodium nanoparticles containing more than 7,000 atoms</cite>.  

So, in short: <cite id="a4e4a28f-8,a4e4a28f-5,02a48348-0,dca9ffbf-6,dca9ffbf-2">quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated in macroscopic condensed-matter systems, ultracold atomic condensates, large molecules, mechanical resonators, and even nanoparticles containing thousands of atoms</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the large systems in which effects have been successfully demonstrated?
fully_underspecified.answer: Assuming you mean <cite id="P13">quantum effects in unusually large or macroscopic systems</cite>, the main classes where they have been successfully demonstrated include <cite id="P11,P14">superconductors and superfluids</cite>, <cite id="P12">Bose–Einstein condensates</cite>, and <cite id="P7,P8">superconducting circuits such as SQUIDs and Josephson-junction devices</cite>. Quantum interference has also been shown for <cite id="P4,P5">large molecules such as C70 and fullerene systems</cite>, and later for <cite id="P3">macromolecules with over 800 atoms and masses beyond 10,000 amu</cite>. More recently, <cite id="P15,P16">micromechanical and nanomechanical resonators have shown quantum behavior, including devices containing billions of atoms</cite>. <cite id="P18">Which of these counts as the “largest” system depends on whether one measures size by mass, particle number, spatial extent, or complexity.</cite>

questions.original_query: What progress has been made in trapping and controlling multiple nanoparticles?

query.text: What progress has been made in trapping and controlling multiple nanoparticles?
query.answer: <cite id="c5770651-3">A major step was the experimental demonstration of strong, controllable optical and electrostatic interactions in arrays of levitated solid-state particles</cite>, and <cite id="c5770651-4,06f1dac6-2">two levitated nanoparticles were shown to realize a tunable nonreciprocal dipole–dipole interaction</cite>. <cite id="c5770651-0,06f1dac6-1">By 2023, researchers had built reconfigurable optically levitated nanoparticle arrays in vacuum with full control of individual nanoparticles, allowing arbitrary patterns to be formed and their motion detected</cite>. <cite id="18823b30-0,6134177c-4">At the same time, programmable optical tweezers enabled scalable all-optical cold damping with independent control of each tweezer’s trap frequency and position</cite>. <cite id="18823b30-6,6134177c-0">In 2024, programmable cavity-mediated long-range interactions between nanoparticles in vacuum were demonstrated</cite>, and <cite id="6134177c-3,06f1dac6-9">chip-based hybrid optical–electrostatic platforms achieved levitation and motion control of a silica nanoparticle in high vacuum</cite>. Overall, <cite id="c5770651-0,18823b30-6">the field has progressed from trapping single particles to independently positioning, cooling, coupling, and reconfiguring multiple levitated nanoparticles</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What progress has been made in trapping and controlling multiple particles?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="a342efe3-0">Progress has advanced from early demonstrations of 3D trapping of “two or more beads” within a single optical tweezer</cite> to <cite id="5ccc401d-4">programmable holographic optical tweezers used for manipulating microsized samples</cite>. <cite id="5ccc401d-1">Researchers also showed automated multi-particle handling by combining real-time feature recognition with holographic optical tweezers to automatically trap, assemble, and sort micron-sized colloidal particles</cite>. More recently, <cite id="5ccc401d-2">dynamic holographic optical tweezers have been highlighted as programmable methods for particle assembly and transformation</cite>, while <cite id="5ccc401d-7">improved algorithms have generated large numbers of point traps in a tilted plane with 94% uniformity</cite>. <cite id="7cd21c47-0,7cd21c47-5">Closed-loop holographic tweezer systems now aim for higher efficiency and stability when manipulating multiple microparticles and cells on microfluidic chips</cite>, and <cite id="667d0884-4">new optical tweezers have also achieved stable trapping of large, irregularly shaped particles that were previously difficult to trap</cite>.

questions.original_query: Which integrated phononic devices have been realized?

query.text: Which integrated phononic devices have been realized?
query.answer: <cite id="8cbc91f5-1">Integrated phononic waveguides have been realized</cite>, including <cite id="68c36bbb-7">a diamond phononic waveguide platform for generating, guiding, and detecting gigahertz-frequency surface acoustic wave phonons</cite>. <cite id="154a1250-1">High-Q surface-acoustic-wave resonators have also been demonstrated as key elements for integrated phononic systems</cite>. For multiport routing, <cite id="68c36bbb-0">a 4-port integrated directional coupler</cite>—that is, a <cite id="68c36bbb-2">phononic beam splitter</cite>—has been demonstrated. And for circuit-level functionality, <cite id="154a1250-0">on-chip phononic Mach–Zehnder interferometers (MZIs) have been shown for tunable microwave interferometry</cite>. Therefore, the integrated phononic devices clearly realized so far include <cite id="8cbc91f5-1,68c36bbb-7">waveguides</cite>, <cite id="154a1250-1">resonators</cite>, <cite id="68c36bbb-0,68c36bbb-2">directional couplers/beam splitters</cite>, and <cite id="154a1250-0">Mach–Zehnder interferometers</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: Which devices have been realized?
fully_underspecified.answer: \boxed{\text{Laser diodes, detectors, and transistors}} <cite id="409bdfbc-6">a variety of advanced optoelectronic devices, including laser diodes, detectors, and transistors, have been realized</cite>

questions.original_query: Which experiments have demonstrated quantum effects in microwave-optics transducers?

query.text: Which experiments have demonstrated quantum effects in microwave-optics transducers?

fully_underspecified.text: Which experiments have demonstrated quantum effects in transducers?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="1c4819fb-5,1e6ae93d-0">A key quantum-effect demonstration in a transducer was the 2020 superconducting-qubit-to-optical-photon experiment, which generated optical photons from a qubit and observed the qubit’s quantum Rabi oscillations through single-photon detection of the converted light, with low added noise.</cite> <cite id="cb9d8e89-2,1c4819fb-1">Another major milestone was the 2024 demonstration of quantum entanglement between optical and microwave photonic qubits using a chip-scale piezo-optomechanical transducer.</cite> <cite id="a8c98d15-6">More recently, experiments have also demonstrated interference of photons from two simultaneously operated microwave-to-optical transducers, showing single-photon-level quantum interference across transducers.</cite>

questions.original_query: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated nanospheres have been experimentally studied?

query.text: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated nanospheres have been experimentally studied?

fully_underspecified.text: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated particles have been studied?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="169745b1-4">A levitated nanoparticle has 6 degrees of freedom: three translational modes and three rotational modes.</cite> <cite id="169745b1-1">Besides studying translational motion, levitated anisotropic particles are especially suited for exploring the control of rotational degrees of freedom.</cite> <cite id="169745b1-2">For levitated particles, it allows separating the trapping frequencies of libration and centre-of-mass motion</cite>, so the studied motional degrees of freedom are the <cite id="169745b1-4">three center-of-mass translational</cite> and <cite id="169745b1-4">three rotational</cite> degrees of freedom, with <cite id="169745b1-2">libration</cite> studied as confined rotational motion.

without_term.text: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated nanoparticles have been experimentally studied?
without_term.answer: <cite id="a0d9f6a7-1">A levitated nanoparticle has 6 degrees of freedom: three translational modes and three rotational modes</cite>. Experimentally, <cite id="a0d9f6a7-7">motional and rotational degrees of freedom can be controlled</cite>; in particular, <cite id="a0d9f6a7-0">all three libration degrees of freedom</cite> have been cooled in recent work, and <cite id="a0d9f6a7-4">all external degrees of freedom of a nanoparticle</cite> have been feedback-controlled. So the experimentally studied motion DOFs are the <cite id="a0d9f6a7-1">three center-of-mass translational DOFs and the three rotational DOFs</cite> (often observed as <cite id="a0d9f6a7-0">librations</cite> when the particle’s orientation is trapped).

questions.original_query: What physical quantities can be precisely measured using a levitated nanosphere?

query.text: What physical quantities can be precisely measured using a levitated nanosphere?
query.answer: <cite id="S18,S21">A levitated nanosphere can be used for precision measurement of ultra-weak forces, acceleration/inertial effects, torque or rotation, and electric and magnetic fields.</cite> <cite id="S18,S19">It can also serve as a local probe of pressure and temperature, and in some setups even mass.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What physical quantities can be measured using a particle?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="49ea3788-0">Measurable properties of particles include mass, charge, spin, and decays.</cite> <cite id="49ea3788-0">Like macroscopic objects, particles can also have energy and momentum.</cite> For a localized particle, one can also specify <cite id="49ea3788-8">mass, energy, momentum and position, and orientation.</cite>

without_term.text: What physical quantities can be precisely measured using a levitated small sphere?
without_term.answer: A levitated small sphere is used most directly for <cite id="fec321b3-0,8f57fd13-1">precision force and acceleration sensing</cite>. Reviews also describe levitated-particle sensing for <cite id="28fa7fa7-0">torque measurement, inertial sensing, and electric and magnetic field detection</cite>. In addition, individual levitated microspheres have been used for <cite id="12f59f0d-0">in situ mass measurement</cite> and <cite id="b9775efe-5">density measurement</cite>. There are also proposals and ongoing efforts to use levitated microspheres for <cite id="bac11f25-0,12f59f0d-4">precision gravitation-related measurements, including accelerometry and the Newtonian constant of gravitation</cite>.

questions.original_query: What experiments can be conducted to verify or further study the non-Hermitian skin effect?

query.text: What experiments can be conducted to verify or further study the non-Hermitian skin effect?
query.answer: Experiments to verify or further study the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE) should focus on its defining signature: <cite id="2ed21c52-5,ec132250-0">the accumulation or concentration of a macroscopic number of bulk eigenstates near system boundaries.</cite> A strong first test is to build <cite id="ec132250-3,5639b3c6-8">electric-circuit realizations and directly measure localized voltage distributions or skin/interface states,</cite> since circuits have already been used to observe <cite id="5639b3c6-8">anomalous skin effects by measuring localized voltage distributions</cite> and <cite id="ec132250-3">one- and two-dimensional non-Hermitian skin interface states.</cite> A second route is <cite id="ec132250-4,5639b3c6-2">acoustic metamaterial experiments, especially in 2D, to image spin-polarized higher-order NHSE and corner accumulation,</cite> because these platforms have demonstrated <cite id="5639b3c6-2">spin-polarized, higher-order non-Hermitian skin effect in two-dimensional acoustic higher-order topological insulators.</cite> Third, <cite id="2ed21c52-0,ec132250-0">photonic quantum walks or photonic lattices can track whether averaged eigenmodes cluster at boundaries or corners as gain/loss and nonreciprocity are tuned,</cite> with reported evidence that <cite id="2ed21c52-0">the averaged eigenmodes of the quantum walk exhibit clustering</cite> and that NHSE appears in <cite id="ec132250-0">photonic quantum walks.</cite> Finally, <cite id="ec132250-2,5639b3c6-9">ultracold-atom optical lattices offer a clean, tunable platform to simulate 2D non-Hermitian topological bands with controllable parameters,</cite> making them promising for precision studies of how NHSE depends on dimensionality, disorder, topology, and interactions. In practice, the most informative experiments would systematically vary boundary conditions, nonreciprocity, and lattice geometry, then compare the resulting <cite id="5639b3c6-8,5639b3c6-2,2ed21c52-0">boundary-localized voltage, acoustic, or optical mode profiles</cite> to theoretical predictions.

questions.original_query: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue due to residual optical absorption in the a levitated nanoparticle?

query.text: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue due to residual optical absorption in the a levitated nanoparticle?
query.answer: <cite id="f1d28781-1">Laser recoil heating and particle absorption limit stable levitation in high vacuum.</cite> Practical ways to reduce that problem are to <cite id="07405700-5,7cc6a9a2-2">use very low-absorption materials—optical levitation is limited to low-absorption objects, and silica spheres usually heat up very little because of their inherently low optical absorption</cite>, <cite id="1655167a-2">choose trapping wavelengths that avoid unwanted optical absorption bands</cite>, and <cite id="54729cf4-6">operate in cryogenic free space, which suppresses thermal effects sufficiently</cite>. To counter the motional consequences of heating, researchers also use <cite id="78e26d42-0">optical feedback cooling, which has reached phonon occupations of a few hundred phonons</cite> and <cite id="7ca820b7-2,7ca820b7-8">cavity/coherent-scattering cooling, including 3D cooling and ground-state cooling</cite>. If optical absorption remains the bottleneck, another route is to <cite id="07405700-0">switch to a Paul-trap or other non-optical/hybrid levitation scheme, since particles in Paul traps do not inherently suffer from heating due to optical absorption</cite>.

questions.original_query: If we have a lot of specialized language models, how can we combine them to build a general system that combine the abilities of different models? Can this unified model be as good as the single large LM?

query.text: If we have a lot of specialized language models, how can we combine them to build a general system that combine the abilities of different models? Can this unified model be as good as the single large LM?
query.answer: Can such a unified model be as good as one large LM? In a nutshell, GLaM outperforms GPT-3 across 21 natural language tasks with only one third of energy consumption compared to training GPT-3, so mixture-of-experts systems can sometimes match or exceed a large dense LM. But this is not guaranteed: long fine-tuning of experts that optimizes for their individual performance leads to degraded merging performance. So the best summary is: yes, a unified system can sometimes be as good as or better than a single large LM, especially with good routing or expert composition, but in practice it depends heavily on how the experts are combined, and naive merging often loses quality.

fully_underspecified.text: How can we combine multiple models to build a general system that combines their abilities? Can this unified model be as good as a single large model?
fully_underspecified.answer: You can build a general system from multiple models in at least two main ways: <cite id="371de18f-1">Mixture of experts (MoE) uses multiple specialized submodels, or “experts,” and routes inputs to the most relevant ones</cite>, while <cite id="016c9483-2">model merging combines two or more models, or model updates, into a single model</cite>. This can produce a unified system because <cite id="3757f7ce-2">task-specific models can be merged into a single unified model that executes all tasks concurrently</cite>, and more broadly <cite id="016c9483-0">combining multiple models can enhance a model with diverse capabilities</cite>. As for whether it can be as good as one large model: sometimes yes, especially under fixed compute, because <cite id="a71c79b7-8">MoE models select different parameters for different inputs instead of reusing the same parameters for all inputs</cite> and <cite id="398fe582-0">FLOP-matched sparse variants gain sample efficiency as the number of experts increases</cite>; in practice, <cite id="a71c79b7-9">the Switch Transformer compares favorably to dense counterparts in speed and sample efficiency</cite>. But not always: <cite id="fb4a4f6a-1">existing model merging methods often suffer from significant performance degradation or require extra tuning data/training</cite>, so a unified model can match or exceed a single large model in some regimes, but there is no guarantee unless the routing, merging, and training are done well.

questions.original_query: What are papers that train multilmodal language models that can input and output both text and images?

query.text: What are papers that train multilmodal language models that can input and output both text and images?
query.answer:
Some papers that fit your criterion are:

- <cite id="8a2e7c2b-2,8a2e7c2b-3">**Generating Images with Multimodal Language Models (GILL, 2023)**, which is described as “the first multimodal language model capable of conditioning on image-and-text inputs” and can “generate coherent image (and text) outputs.”</cite>
- <cite id="8dd55377-0,8dd55377-1">**Unified-IO 2: Scaling Autoregressive Multimodal Models (2024)**, where the model “can use text, images, audio, and/or videos as input and can generate text, image, or audio outputs,” and is “capable of understanding and generating image, text, audio, and action.”</cite>

questions.original_query: How do machine unlearning methods perform? Can they be used to remove knowledge from language models?

query.text: How do machine unlearning methods perform? Can they be used to remove knowledge from language models?
query.answer:
## Short answer

<cite id="180e90e0-2">Machine unlearning methods are usually divided into exact and approximate approaches</cite>, and <cite id="180e90e0-1">approximate unlearning explicitly trades off performance, efficiency, and feasibility</cite>. In practice, that means unlearning can often reduce a model’s dependence on selected data or suppress answers about target facts, but it rarely gives a free lunch: effectiveness, utility retention, and computational cost must be balanced.  

For language models specifically, <cite id="b484b106-2">benchmarks such as RWKU are designed to evaluate unlearning specific knowledge in LLMs</cite> and <cite id="b651c853-9">TOFU was introduced to deepen understanding of unlearning in LLMs</cite>. So yes, unlearning methods can be used to make LLMs *less likely* to produce targeted information. But the strongest recent evidence suggests that <cite id="46efabf9-0">existing benchmarks can give an overly optimistic and potentially misleading view of effectiveness</cite>, <cite id="46efabf9-2">forget/retain benchmark splits can overestimate unlearning success</cite>, and <cite id="f60be665-1">supposedly “unlearned” information can still leak when sampling top-k outputs instead of using deterministic decoding</cite>. Consistent with that, <cite id="f60be665-0">current approaches may provide only an illusion of forgetting</cite> and <cite id="f60be665-3">knowledge leakage persists across methods and tasks</cite>.  

## What “performance” looks like in machine unlearning

At a high level, machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specified training data after training. The literature distinguishes <cite id="180e90e0-2">exact and approximate unlearning approaches</cite>. Exact methods try to match the model that would have been obtained if the data had never been included, while <cite id="180e90e0-0">approximate unlearning aims to minimize the influence of unlearned data to an acceptable level while achieving an efficient unlearning process</cite>. That efficiency goal is why approximate methods are common, but it also explains why guarantees are weaker.  

Because of this, performance is usually judged by a tradeoff: how much forgetting is achieved, how much normal capability is preserved, and how expensive the procedure is. Surveys emphasize that <cite id="180e90e0-1">approximate unlearning involves deliberate tradeoffs among performance, efficiency, and feasibility</cite>. So the practical answer is that machine unlearning can work partially or usefully, but not perfectly in all settings.  

## Can unlearning remove knowledge from language models?

Partially, yes. Reliably and completely, not with current evidence. LLM-specific work treats this as a real target: <cite id="b484b106-2">RWKU is a benchmark for unlearning specific knowledge in large language models</cite>, and <cite id="b651c853-9">TOFU is a benchmark aimed at helping deepen understanding of unlearning in LLMs</cite>. This means researchers can already train post hoc methods that reduce recall of targeted facts or documents.  

However, the harder question is whether the underlying knowledge is actually gone, rather than just harder to elicit. Recent work raises major doubts. A position paper reports that <cite id="46efabf9-0">existing benchmarks provide an overly optimistic and potentially misleading view on the effectiveness of candidate unlearning methods</cite>. More specifically, <cite id="46efabf9-2">benchmarks that separate prompts into a “forget set” and a “retain set” can overestimate effectiveness</cite>. And auditing work argues that <cite id="5d7d7b91-0">a comprehensive auditing framework is needed, covering multiple benchmark datasets, unlearning algorithms, and prompt-attack settings</cite>, which implies simple evaluations are not sufficient.  

The strongest negative evidence comes from alternative prompting and decoding. <cite id="f60be665-1">Leak@$k$ reports that “unlearned” language models can still leak supposedly removed information when one considers top-k sampling rather than greedy decoding</cite>. The paper’s summary claim is blunt: <cite id="f60be665-0">current approaches to LLM unlearning provide only an illusion of forgetting</cite>. It further states that <cite id="f60be665-3">knowledge leakage persists across methods and tasks</cite>. That suggests many current methods are better understood as suppressing common outputs or inducing refusals than as truly deleting internalized knowledge.  

## Bottom line

Machine unlearning methods do have practical value: they can often <cite id="180e90e0-0">minimize the influence of selected data</cite> and, in LLMs, can reduce the model’s tendency to answer with targeted knowledge on standard benchmarks <cite id="b484b106-2">designed for knowledge unlearning</cite>. But the field’s own recent evaluations indicate that current LLM unlearning results are fragile: <cite id="46efabf9-0">standard benchmarks may overstate progress</cite>, and <cite id="f60be665-1">the supposedly forgotten information may still be recoverable under different decoding or prompting strategies</cite>.  

So the best current answer is: **machine unlearning can weaken or hide knowledge in language models, but there is not yet strong evidence that today’s methods reliably and completely remove that knowledge.**

fully_underspecified.text: How do methods perform? Can they be used to remove knowledge from models?
fully_underspecified.answer: <cite id="c72ba6e7-0">Current methods can work reasonably well on benchmark-style unlearning tasks: certain knowledge-editing approaches, especially WISE and AlphaEdit, are reported as effective unlearning baselines, particularly for pretrained knowledge.</cite> <cite id="25ef0946-9">There is also evidence that newer mechanistic approaches can achieve better trade-offs between successful edits/unlearning and preserving general model performance.</cite> But <cite id="d1a376d2-1,d1a376d2-6">the stronger evidence says most current approximate unlearning methods often suppress outputs rather than robustly erase the underlying knowledge.</cite> For example, <cite id="1541ca5e-4">one adversarial evaluation found that supposedly unlearned knowledge was recovered in 54% of questions using adversarial suffixes, even without revealing the target entities,</cite> and <cite id="1541ca5e-2">other work shows a tension between keeping model utility and preventing knowledge recovery, including recovery after quantization.</cite> So the short answer is: <cite id="c72ba6e7-0,25ef0946-9,d1a376d2-1,1541ca5e-4">these methods can improve benchmark performance and sometimes hide or weaken access to specific facts, but they generally should not yet be treated as reliable, guaranteed knowledge removal from models.</cite>
